Turks regard the campaign as a defining moment in their national history, and 25 April is ANZAC Day in Australia and New Zealand. Greek troops occupied the town on 4 August 1920 during the Greco-Turkish War, and it returned to Turkish rule on 26 November 1922. From November 1920 to May 1922 a camp near Gelibolu held White Russian exiles, 26,590 of them transferred from Constantinople.

Between 1923 and 1926 Gallipoli was the centre of Gelibolu Province. It later became a district centre in Çanakkale Province. The Gallipoli Peninsula Historical National Park preserves battlefields, cemeteries and memorials of the campaign.
gallipoli-campaign: The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on 31 October 1914 after the Black Sea raid. Allied planners wanted to take control of the Turkish straits, expose Constantinople to bombardment by warships and cut it off from the Asian part of the empire. Success could have opened the Bosphorus and Dardanelles to Allied supplies for Russia and given Western control of the Suez Canal. The campaign began on 19 February 1915 with an Anglo-French bombardment of the Dardanelles forts. On 18 March the Entente fleet of 18 battleships tried to force the narrowest point. The French battleship Bouvet struck a mine and capsized in two minutes, and the battleships Irresistible and Ocean were also lost.

After the naval failure, General Sir Ian Hamilton was appointed to command 78,000 men of the Mediterranean Expeditionary Force. Landings were made on 25 April 1915 at five beaches. The 29th Division landed at Cape Helles, while the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed north of Gaba Tepe at a place that became known as ANZAC. The French made a diversion at Kum Kale. The Ottoman 5th Army, a conscript force commanded by Sanders, held the high ground, and Lieutenant Colonel Mustafa Kemal had predicted the likely landing areas. The Allies were checked at Krithia in three battles, and trench warfare followed.

A force of 42,000 Ottoman troops attacked Anzac on 19 May and suffered about 13,000 casualties. In August the Allies tried a new offensive at Sari Bair and Suvla, which failed. Criticism of Hamilton's performance was smuggled out by journalists, and he was replaced by Sir Charles Monro. Autumn and winter brought gales, blizzards and flooding. The Allies evacuated the peninsula, and the campaign ended on 9 January 1916.

Casualty figures vary. Edward J. Erickson wrote in 2001 that over 100,000 men were killed, including 56,000 to 68,000 Ottoman soldiers and around 53,000 British and French. Fisher resigned in May 1915, and the crisis led H. H. Asquith to form a coalition government with the Conservatives. Churchill was demoted from First Lord of the Admiralty, and the Dardanelles Commission investigated the failure.

In Turkey the campaign is regarded as a defining moment, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who rose to prominence at Gallipoli, became the first president of the Republic of Turkey in 1923. In Australia and New Zealand it is regarded as a baptism of fire, linked to the emergence of a national identity and the Anzac spirit, and 25 April is Anzac Day. About 50,000 Australians and 16,000 to 17,000 New Zealanders served there. Analysis of the campaign led many to believe that amphibious assaults could not succeed against modern defences.
galway: Galway, in Irish Gaillimh, lies on the River Corrib between Lough Corrib and Galway Bay, and is the county town of County Galway. Its name comes from the river, which formed the western boundary of the earliest settlement, Dún Gaillimhe, the fort at the mouth of the Gaillimh. Residents are called Galwegians, and the Latin name of the city is Galvia. It bears the nickname City of the Tribes, from the fourteen merchant families who led it in its Hiberno-Norman period. The climate is oceanic, mild, moist and changeable, with about 1,156 mm of rain a year spread through the seasons.

During the Norman invasion of Connacht in the 1230s, Dún Gaillimhe was captured by Richard Mor de Burgh, who had led the invasion. As the de Burghs eventually became Gaelicised, the merchants of the town, the Tribes of Galway, pushed for greater control over the walled city. A municipal charter of 1484 allowed the citizens to form a council and mayoralty, and the first mayor, Peirce Lynch Fitzjohn, was elected in 1485. Controlled largely by the merchant families, the city grew into a trading port, before a period of decline.

Local government changed several times in the twentieth century. In 1937 the Urban District of Galway became the Borough of Galway, remaining part of County Galway; in 1986 it became the County Borough of Galway and ceased to be part of the county; and in 2001 it was renamed Galway City. Queen's College, Galway, was founded in 1845 and is now the University of Galway. The patron saint of the city since the 14th century has been St Nicholas of Myra, and the Roman Catholic diocese of Galway was created in 1831.

Galway is the capital of Connacht and, with a population of 85,910 at the 2022 census, the most populous settlement in the province. St. Nicholas' Collegiate Church, founded in 1320 and enlarged in the following two centuries, is the largest medieval church still in everyday use in Ireland. Lynch's Castle on Shop Street is a medieval townhouse built by the Lynch family in the 16th century, and Galway Cathedral, built on the site of the old gaol, was consecrated in 1965.

The city has a reputation for the Irish language, music, song and dance, and the Galway Gaeltacht lies on its doorstep. It holds many festivals, among them the Galway Arts Festival, and the Galway Races, first held in the 1860s. UNESCO designated it a City of Film in 2014.
gamal-abdel-nasser: Gamal Abdel Nasser Hussein was born in Bakos, Alexandria, on 15 January 1918, the son of a postal worker from Upper Egypt. His family moved often, which showed him the class divisions of Egyptian society, and he read widely, including biographies of Napoleon, Atatürk, Bismarck and Garibaldi. In 1937 his police record of anti-government protest at first blocked his entry to the Royal Military Academy; he briefly studied law before reapplying. His first battlefield experience was in Palestine in the 1948 Arab–Israeli War. On his return he began organising dissenting officers. In 1944 he had married Tahia Kazem.

On 25 January 1952 about 7,000 British soldiers attacked the police station in Ismailia, killing 50 Egyptian policemen, and the Cairo Fire riots followed. Nasser published a six-point programme to dismantle feudalism and British influence. In January 1953 he overcame Mohamed Naguib's opposition and banned all political parties in favour of the Liberation Rally. After a Muslim Brotherhood member fired eight shots at him in Alexandria on 26 October 1954, he cracked down on the Brotherhood, placed Naguib under house arrest and assumed executive office; he was formally elected president in June 1956. At the Bandung Conference in April 1955 he was treated as the leading representative of the Arab countries.

On 19 July 1956 the US and UK withdrew their offer to finance the Aswan Dam, and Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company. The UK, France and Israel secretly agreed to take the canal and topple him, but the Suez Crisis ended in what was seen as his political victory, and his prestige across the Arab world rose. His Cairo radio station, the Voice of the Arabs, spread his ideas of Arab unity. From 1961 he nationalised much of the economy, and the National Charter of 1962 promised universal health care, affordable housing and wider women's rights. Egypt's intervention in North Yemen from 1962 cost 26,000 Egyptian soldiers, and Nasser later called it a miscalculation.

Egypt's defeat in the Six-Day War of 1967 led Nasser to resign, but demonstrations brought him back; he named himself prime minister and began the War of Attrition in January 1968. After the Arab League summit closed on 28 September 1970 he suffered a heart attack and died at 52. His funeral in Cairo drew five to six million mourners. Supporters credit him with making Egypt independent of British influence and widening access to housing, education and health services; critics point to authoritarianism and the dominance of the military over civil institutions. His successor Anwar Sadat later departed from Nasserist policies.
gamprin: Gamprin is a municipality of Liechtenstein, on the Rhine, on the border with the Swiss municipality of Sennwald. It lies in the hilly landscape west of the Eschnerberg and consists of the villages of Gamprin and Bendern, in a scattered settlement that includes the old hamlets of Au, Bühl, Badäl, Salums and Gölla. It covers 6.188 square kilometres. It also has an exclave on the Nendler Berg, and its Gampriner Seele, a lake of 2.6 hectares, is the only lake in Liechtenstein. A flood of the Rhine in 1927 created it.

Settlement here goes back to the Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages, and the archaeological site of Lutzengüetle lies within the parish. The name comes from the Old Romansh camp Rin, a field on the Rhine. It was first mentioned about 1150 as Camporin, and in 1253 as Gamperin. The Bendern Parish Church, dedicated to Mary, has a nave dating from the 8th or 9th century, enlarged in the 14th century, and a Gothic chancel inaugurated in 1481. In 1499, during the Swabian War, Swiss Confederates pillaged the village. The oldest surviving village charter, of 1643, describes the villagers' rights and duties in using pastures and forests, and in 1699 the men of the Unterland swore allegiance to the Prince at Bendern.

In the 18th and 19th centuries Bendern ran one of the five ferries on the Liechtenstein stretch of the Rhine, linking it with Haag on the opposite bank. A wooden bridge was built across the river in 1867–68.

Until 1950 Gamprin had neither a coat of arms nor an official flag. A committee designed them, and the municipality adopted them in 1958. The yellow ribbon stands for the Rhine, and the roses come from the arms of the knight Rüdiger von Limpach, who owned property in Gamprin in the Middle Ages. The municipality contains the Liechtenstein Institute and the LGT Group.
ganapati-kakatiya: Ganapati's father Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Seuna, or Yadava, kingdom in 1198–1199, and Ganapati himself was taken captive. During his captivity the kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and the commander-in-chief Rudra of the Recherla Reddi family appears to have governed in his name. An inscription at Manthena dated 26 December 1199 calls Ganapati the establisher of all the kingdom, which suggests that he had been freed by then. Yadava inscriptions claim that their king Jaitrapala released him out of compassion; the Yadavas may rather have wanted a quiet eastern border while they fought the Hoysalas.

Helped by the decline of the Kalyani Chalukya and Chola empires, Ganapati first turned to coastal Andhra, which the Kakatiyas had lost. The Krishna delta was conquered by 1201, and his general Chaunda plundered the island of Divi, whose Ayya chiefs submitted; Ganapati married two daughters of their chief, and their brother Jayapa became his commander. The Velanati Choda ruler Prithvishvara probably died fighting the Kakatiyas about 1206, and by 1209 Vela-nadu and Kamma-nadu were annexed. At Nellore Ganapati installed the Telugu Choda chief Tikka on the throne.

Repeated campaigns in Kalinga and Vengi from 1212 against the Eastern Ganga kings Ananga Bhima III and Narasimha I had mixed results, and Kakatiya control was probably limited to the land south of the Godavari River. In 1250 an army under Samanta Bhoja won a decisive victory at Palaiyaru and restored Tikka's son Manuma-siddhi II at Nellore. Around 1257, however, the Pandya king Jatavarman Sundara I attacked; the Pandyas captured Nellore and killed Manuma-siddhi II at the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263.

Ganapati continued the removal of the capital from Anumakonda to Orugallu, where he built a fortification of 75 bastions, each protected by a nayaka, comprising a stone fort and a mud fort one within the other. He also subdued the petty chiefs who had been harassing foreign merchants at the port of Motupalli.

Ganapati apparently retired after his defeats by the Pandyas in the late 1250s. He had no male heir and two daughters, Rudrama-devi, married to the Vengi Chalukya prince Virabhadra, and Ganapama-devi. Rudrama began to rule as co-regent in 1259–1260 under the regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja, though an inscription at Duggi shows that Ganapati was alive at least until 1269. The 17th-century Pratapa-charita says that two sons of his by junior queens, Hari-hara and Murari-deva, rebelled against her; no other source knows these sons. Inscriptions listing distant kings as his vassals follow literary convention and can be dismissed.
gandaki-river: The Gandaki drains a catchment of 46,300 square kilometres, most of it in Nepal. Its upper course, the Kali Gandaki, rises at the Nhubine Himal Glacier in the Mustang region at 6,268 metres, on the border with Tibet. It then runs south through the Kali Gandaki Gorge between Dhaulagiri (8,167 metres) and Annapurna (8,091 metres), one of the deepest canyons in the world, and the river is older than the Himalayas, cutting through the mountains as they rise. Near Devghat the Kali Gandaki is joined by the Trishuli, a larger tributary.

Below Gaindakot the river is called the Narayani or Sapt Gandaki, the Seven Gandakis, after seven tributaries that rise in the Himalaya. In India it enters Uttar Pradesh, passes Kushinagar District and flows about 300 kilometres south-east across Bihar, building an immense megafan across eastern Uttar Pradesh and north-western Bihar.

The river is mentioned as Sadanira in the Shatapatha Brahmana, and in the Mahabharata. Its origin is told in the Shiva Purana. Between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna it flows past Muktinath, whose stones, the saligrama silas found in the riverbed, are of great significance to Hindus, who regard them as a representation of Narayana. Srivaishnavas and followers of Madhvacharya count the Muktinath temple among the 108 Divyakshetrams.

Along the river lie places of archaeological interest. At Lauriya-Nandangarh stands a lion pillar of Ashoka, a single block of polished sandstone 11 metres high, believed to be over 2,300 years old, beside brick stupas said to hold ashes from the Buddha's funeral pyre. Near the Kali Gandaki in Upper Mustang some 10,000 man-made caves have yielded partly mummified bodies and skeletons at least 2,000 to 3,000 years old, and religious paintings, sculptures and manuscripts of the 12th to 14th century. Mahatma Gandhi began the Champaran Satyagraha from his ashram at Bhitiharawa near the river.

Under an agreement signed on 4 December 1959 between Nepal and India, the Gandak Barrage was built at Valmikinagar in 1968–69 to supply irrigation to Nepal, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Chitwan National Park in Nepal, established in 1973 and a World Heritage Site since 1984, lies beside India's Valmiki National Park around the barrage. The river's valleys also have many hydroelectric stations.
ganesha: Ganesha is mentioned in Hindu texts between the 1st century BCE and the 2nd century CE, and a few images from the 4th and 5th centuries CE have been documented. An elephant-headed figure on Indo-Greek coins of the 1st century BCE has been proposed as an early depiction, but this is strongly contested. The first terracotta images date from the 1st century CE, and the earliest stone icons were carved at Mathura in Kushan times. The title gaṇapati appears twice in the Rig Veda, but there it refers to Brahmanaspati and Indra, not to Ganesha. The detailed stories of his birth and elephant head come from the later Puranas, composed from about 600 onwards.

Ganesha is identified by his elephant head and four arms. He is also called Ganapati, Vinayaka and Pillaiyar. Hindu texts name him as the son of Shiva and Parvati, though the Puranas give different accounts of his birth. In the most recurrent story Parvati made him from clay to guard her, and Shiva beheaded him when he came between them and replaced the head with an elephant's.

Devotees honour him as Vighneshvara, the Lord of Obstacles, held both to place obstacles in the way of those who need to be checked and to remove them for those who begin something new. He is also the patron of letters and learning. In the Ganapatya tradition he is the Supreme Being, and the Ganesha Purana and Mudgala Purana are its principal texts.

Hindus of all denominations invoke Ganesha at the beginning of prayers and ceremonies, and dancers and musicians, particularly in southern India, begin performances with a prayer to him. He is placed at the doorway of many temples, and the Ashtavinayak, eight shrines near Pune, are dedicated to him. The ten-day festival of Ganesh Chaturthi begins with the bringing in of clay idols, which are immersed in water at its end. In 1893 Lokmanya Tilak turned it from private family celebrations into a public event, to build unity against British rule in Maharashtra.

From about the 10th century he became the principal deity of traders. In Mahayana Buddhism he appears as the god Vināyaka, often dancing. Some Jains worship him, and the earliest known Jain statue dates to about the 9th century.
gang-of-four: The Gang of Four was a Maoist faction of four Chinese Communist Party officials who came to prominence during the Cultural Revolution of 1966-1976. Its leading figure was Jiang Qing, the wife of Mao Zedong, a former film actress who had taken no public political role before 1966 and whom Mao placed in charge of the country's cultural apparatus. Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen were party leaders in Shanghai who had played leading roles in securing that city for Mao. Yao Wenyuan's article of 10 November 1965 attacking the play Hai Rui Dismissed from Office is cited as the spark of the Cultural Revolution.

The Cultural Revolution began to lose momentum around the death of Lin Biao in 1971. Premier Zhou Enlai regained his authority and brought Deng Xiaoping back into the leadership at the 10th Party Congress in 1973. Near the end of Mao's life a power struggle developed between the Gang and an alliance of Deng, Zhou and Ye Jianying. After Zhou died in January 1976, the Gang used their newspapers to attack Deng and mobilised their urban militia units. It remains unclear which decisions were Mao's and which the Gang's own.

Mao died on 9 September 1976. Premier Hua Guofeng attacked the radicals' media line at a Politburo meeting, and Jiang Qing insisted that she be named party chairman. Hua won the army over to his side, and on 6 October 1976 he had the four leading radicals arrested in a bloodless coup. Nationwide denunciations began on 21 October. Government media blamed the Gang and Lin Biao for the excesses of the Cultural Revolution, and many Chinese saw the arrests as the sign of a new era.

The four were tried in late 1980 by the Supreme People's Court, with Jiang Hua presiding, and convicted in January 1981 of anti-party activities. The trial was broadcast daily on television. The prosecution separated political errors from crimes, among them the usurpation of state power and the persecution of some 750,000 people, 34,375 of whom died in 1966-1976. Jiang Qing alone argued her own case, saying she had obeyed Mao at all times; Zhang Chunqiao admitted nothing, while Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen expressed repentance.

Jiang Qing and Zhang Chunqiao received death sentences later commuted to life imprisonment, Wang Hongwen life, and Yao Wenyuan twenty years. Jiang Qing died by suicide in 1991 and Wang Hongwen died in 1992; Yao Wenyuan and Zhang Chunqiao died in 2005. The term was later used for Hua Guofeng's four closest collaborators, who were demoted in 1980 for grave errors in the struggle against the Gang.
ganghwa-island: Ganghwa Island lies in the Yellow Sea, in an estuary of the Han River, and belongs to Ganghwa County in Incheon, South Korea. A narrow channel separates it from Gimpo on the mainland and is crossed by two bridges, while the main channel of the Han River separates it from Kaesong in North Korea. Its position controls access to the river, which runs through Seoul, the capital of Joseon and of South Korea.

Before the 10th century the island had several names, among them Haegu, meaning mouth of the sea, and Gangha, meaning below the rivers. In 940, in the Goryeo period, it received its present name, which means a beautiful town by the river. It was originally joined to the mainland and became separate through erosion. Mudflats now surround it, and land reclamation for farming has enlarged it. Its highest mountain is Manisan, at 469 metres.

In the early Goryeo period the island formed part of Ganghwa-hyeon. It became part of Ganghwa-bu in 1377, and in 1914 part of Ganghwa County in Gyeonggi Province. It remained so until 1994, when it was placed under Incheon Metropolitan City. A palace site of Goryeo on the island, Goryeogung, dates from 1232 to 1270.

Its fortifications were repeatedly attacked in the 19th century. The island was the site of the French expedition to Korea of 1866, the American expedition of 1871, the Battle of Ganghwa and the Ganghwa Island incident with Japan in 1875. In 1876 Korea was forced to sign a treaty with Japan, which took its name from the island as the Treaty of Ganghwa.

Stone tombs on the island belong to the UNESCO World Heritage series Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites. On Manisan stands the Chamseongdan Altar, where Dangun Wanggeom is said to have performed ancestral rites; a foundation day festival is held there each autumn. The Ganghwa Bridge was built to the mainland in 1969 and replaced in 1997, and the Ganghwa Choji Bridge opened in 2002. The island's turnip has been cultivated for more than a thousand years.
gangotri: Gangotri is a town and municipality in the Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand, 99 km from the district headquarters at Uttarkashi. It stands on the banks of the Bhagirathi, from which the Ganges takes its origin, in the Greater Himalayan Range at a height of approximately 3,200 metres. The source of the Bhagirathi is the Gangotri Glacier. Once the river joins the Alakananda at Devprayag it takes the name Ganga. According to Hindu belief Gangotri is the seat of the goddess Ganga.

A popular Hindu legend says that the goddess Ganga descended here when Shiva released the river from the locks of his hair. Near the river is a stone where, according to tradition, King Bhagiratha performed penance to Shiva in order to bring the Ganga down to earth and absolve the sins of his ancestors. According to another legend, the Pandavas performed the great Deva Yajna here to atone for the deaths of their kinsmen in the battle of the Mahabharata.

The original Gangotri Temple was built by the Nepalese general Amar Singh Thapa and was restored in the 19th century. Hindus believe that ancestral rites on the banks of the Bhagirathi free the spirit of the ancestor from the cycle of rebirth, and that a holy dip in its waters cleanses sins of the present life and of past births.

Gangotri is one of the four sites of the Chota Char Dham pilgrimage circuit. The temple is closed from Diwali each year and reopens on Akshaya Tritiya, and during that time the idol of the goddess is kept at Mukhba village, near Harsil. The ritual duties of the temple are supervised by the Semwal family of pujaris, who come from Mukhba. The 2011 census of India recorded a population of 110 in 47 families, all of whom identified as Hindu.
gangtok: Gangtok stands at an elevation of 1,650 m in the lower Himalayas, on the side of a hill. A promenade called The Ridge runs between the Raj Bhawan, the governor's residence, at one end and the palace at the other. Two streams, the Roro Chu and the Ranikhola, flank the city and flow south to join the Teesta at Singtam. Mount Kanchenjunga is visible to the west. The slopes are prone to landslides, and in June 1997 a landslide disaster killed 38 people and destroyed hundreds of buildings. Most agree that the name means hill top in Tibetan.

Little is known of Gangtok's early history. The earliest records date from the building of a hermitic monastery in 1716, and the town remained a small hamlet until the Enchey Monastery, built in 1840, made it a pilgrimage centre. After the English conquest of Sikkim in the mid-19th century it became the capital of what was left of Sikkim, and after the British defeated the Tibetans it became a major stopover in the trade between Tibet and British India. In 1894 Thutob Namgyal, the Sikkimese monarch under British rule, shifted the capital from Tumlong to Gangtok, and a new palace and other state buildings were built.

After India's independence in 1947 Sikkim became a nation-state under Indian suzerainty, by a treaty that gave India control of its external affairs. Trade through the Nathula and Jelepla passes flourished, but it declined after 1959 and the passes were sealed after the Sino-Indian War of 1962. In 1975, after years of political uncertainty including riots, the monarchy was abolished and, following a referendum, Sikkim became India's twenty-second state, with Gangtok as its capital.

Gangtok is the capital of Sikkim and the seat of the Sikkim High Court. Its residents include Nepalis, who settled in the region under British rule and form the majority, Lepchas, who are native to the land, Bhutias and Tibetans. Hinduism and Buddhism are the most significant religions. The Enchey Monastery is the city's oldest and the seat of the Nyingma order, and the Rumtek Monastery on the outskirts, built in the 1960s on the model of one in Lhasa, is the seat of the Kagyu order. Tourism is the main part of the city's economy.
ganja-azerbaijan: Ganja lies 400 to 450 metres above sea level on the Ganja-Dashkasan plain in the west of Azerbaijan, 375 km from Baku. It stands at the north-eastern foothills of the Lesser Caucasus on the Ganjachay river. The name comes from the Persian word ganj, meaning treasure or treasury; Arabic sources call the city Janza and Armenian sources Gandzak. The tale that its founder found treasure nearby is considered a folk etymology.

The anonymous Arabic history Tarikh Bab al-abwab says Ganja was founded in 859–60 by Muhammad ibn Khalid, the Arab governor of the region under the caliph Al-Mutawakkil, after he unearthed a treasure there. The medieval Armenian historian Movses Kaghankatvatsi supports a 9th-century Arab foundation, while the Persian name suggests an older pre-Islamic town. From the 9th to the 12th century the area was known as Arran, and its urban population mainly spoke Persian. The city was damaged by an earthquake in September 1139, when King Demetrius I of Georgia took it and carried off its gates, and again by the Mongol invasion of 1231. It revived after the Safavids came to power in 1501 and was occupied briefly by the Ottomans in 1578–1606 and 1723–1735.

After the death of Nader Shah in 1747 Ganja became the centre of the Ganja Khanate, whose khans were subordinate to the rule of Iran. Russia, after annexing eastern Georgia in 1801, met strong opposition at Ganja. In 1804 Russian forces under General Pavel Tsitsianov invaded and sacked the city, sparking the Russo-Persian War of 1804–1813. Some western sources claim that up to 3,000 inhabitants were massacred. The Treaty of Gulistan forced Iran to cede the khanate, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 made its inclusion in the Russian Empire permanent. It was renamed Yelizavetpol after Alexander I's wife, Elizabeth, and became capital of the Elizavetpol Governorate in 1868, though local Azerbaijanis continued to call it Ganja.

In 1918 Ganja was the temporary capital of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. The Red Army occupied Azerbaijan in April 1920, and in May an anti-Soviet rebellion in Ganja was put down, heavily damaging the city. In 1935 it was renamed Kirovabad after Sergei Kirov, and it regained its original name in 1989. A pogrom in November 1988 forced the local Armenian population to leave.

Ganja is a major city of western Azerbaijan, divided into the Kapaz and Nizami districts, which were established in 1980. The poet Nizami Ganjavi was born there, and its old landmarks include the Nizami Mausoleum, the Shah Abbas Caravanserai, the Imamzadeh complex and the Chokak Hamam. Most of its people are Muslim, mainly Shia, and most of its Armenians, Slavs, Jews and Germans have emigrated. The city is known for Ganja silk, and metallurgical and food industries operate there.
gansu: Gansu lies between the Tibetan Plateau and the Loess Plateau, bordering Xinjiang and Qinghai to the west, Sichuan to the south, Shaanxi to the east and Inner Mongolia and Ningxia to the north. The Yellow River passes through the south of the province and flows through Lanzhou. The Qilian Mountains rise in the south, and parts of the Gobi Desert lie within the province. The Hexi Corridor, a natural passage of some 1,000 kilometres from Lanzhou to the Jade Gate, runs between the Gobi to the north and the Qilian Mountains to the south.

The name Gansu is a compound of Ganzhou, around Zhangye, and Suzhou, around Jiuquan, two prefectures of the Sui and Tang periods; the compound was first used under the Song dynasty. Before that the region was known as Longxi or Longyou, after Mount Liupan.

In prehistoric times Gansu was home to Neolithic cultures. The Dadiwan culture flourished in the east from about 6000 BCE to about 3000 BCE, and the Majiayao and Qijia cultures took root there in later millennia. The Yuezhi lived in the far west until the Xiongnu forced them to emigrate around 177 BCE. The state of Qin grew out of the south-east, around Tianshui, and Qin tombs and artefacts have been excavated at Fangmatan.

The Han dynasty extended the Great Wall across the corridor and built the fort towns of Yumenguan and Yangguan along it. The Ming dynasty built the Jiayuguan outpost, begun around 1372 and then at the western edge of China. By the Qingshui treaty of 823 between the Tibetan Empire and the Tang dynasty, China lost much of western Gansu for a significant period. Uyghurs who had migrated from their fallen khaganate set up the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom, which lasted from 848 to 1036, and the Western Xia later controlled much of the province.

Along the Silk Road, Gansu was both an economic route and a path of cultural transmission. The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang were begun in 366 CE, when a monk named Le Zun is said to have had a vision and carved the first grotto. The Bingling and Maijishan grottoes also date from the early centuries of Buddhist art. The Dungan Revolt of 1862–77 began in Gansu, and an earthquake on 16 December 1920 killed some 180,000 people.

Gansu is a province of north-western China with Lanzhou as its capital and largest city. Its population is about 26 million, mostly Han, with Hui, Dongxiang and Tibetan minorities. Labrang Monastery, built in 1710 in the south, is one of the six great monasteries of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, and the Jiayuguan pass preserves a section of the Great Wall.
gao: Gao lies on the eastern bank of the Niger River, 320 km east-southeast of Timbuktu, at the junction with the Tilemsi Valley. The climate is arid, with rain only from June to September, and almost all local agriculture depends on the river's annual flood, which reaches Gao later than the upper river and peaks in December. In flood the river is 4 km wide at the city.

Excavations at Gao-Saney show that the site was occupied by about 700 CE, as a centre of manufacturing, iron smelting and trade reaching as far as Mesopotamia. Al-Khwārizmī gives the earliest written mention in the first half of the 9th century, and about 872 al-Yaqubi called the kingdom of Kawkaw the most important and most powerful of the realms of the Sūdān. By the 10th century the ruler was said to be a Muslim and the city had two towns. More than 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions survive from Gao and Gao-Saney, the oldest dated 1042. Towards the end of the 13th century Gao became part of the Mali Empire, and Ibn Battuta stayed there in 1352–53.

In the first half of the 15th century Sunni Sulayman Dama threw off Malian rule, and his successor Sunni Ali Ber, who ruled from 1464 to 1492, expanded Songhai territory and made Gao his capital. Leo Africanus, who visited between 1506 and 1510 under Askiya Muhammad I, found a large town without a wall, full of rich merchants, with a market where many slaves were sold. A survey under Askiya Al-Hajj, who reigned from 1582 to 1586, counted 7,626 houses, suggesting about 45,000 people. After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 the invaders made Timbuktu their capital, and Gao declined. When Heinrich Barth visited in 1854 he found a poor village of about 300 huts.

Gao is the capital of the Gao Region and the largest town in eastern Mali. The Tomb of Askia, a World Heritage Site, is a mosque tomb of some 2,500 square metres with a minaret 12 metres high. The town also has a mosque associated with Kankou Moussa, a museum of the Sahel and the sand dune La Dune Rose. Most people speak Koyraboro Senni, and the population includes Bozo, Fulani, Tuareg, Arab and Bambara groups. The city is regarded as a Songhay cultural capital.
garden-of-the-hesperides: In Greek mythology the Hesperides are the nymphs who tend the garden in which grow the trees of Hera that bear golden apples. They were also called the Atlantides, from their reputed father Atlas. Their name means originating from Hesperos, the evening, which also shares a root with the English word west. Their parents, number and names vary between sources. They are listed as daughters of Night, of Atlas and Hesperis, of Phorcys and Ceto, or of Zeus and Themis. Apollonius of Rhodes gives three, Aigle, Erytheis and Hespere, while Apollodorus gives four, Aigle, Erytheia, Hesperia and Arethusa. Euripides calls them minstrel maids for their sweet song.

The garden is Hera's orchard in the far west, near the Atlas Mountains, at the edge of the ocean of Oceanus. According to the legend, the goddess Gaia brought branches bearing golden apples as a wedding gift when Zeus and Hera married, and Hera had them planted in her gardens, which extended as far as Mount Atlas. The Hesperides tended the grove, and Hera set the immortal, never-sleeping, hundred-headed dragon Ladon to guard the apples. Pliny the Elder places the garden at Lixus in modern Morocco, and elsewhere says the Hesperides live on two islands in the Atlantic. Diodorus gives a variant in which the Hesperides had flocks of sheep so beautiful that the poets called them golden apples, guarded by a shepherd named Dracon.

Euesperides, modern Benghazi, might have mythological associations with the garden. Diodorus gives a variant in which the Hesperides had flocks of sheep so beautiful that the poets called them golden apples, guarded by a shepherd named Dracon.

The eleventh Labour of Heracles was to steal the apples. In one version Heracles tricked Atlas into fetching them by offering to hold up the heavens for a while, and then walked away with them; in another he killed Ladon. According to Apollodorus, Eurystheus gave the apples back to Heracles, and Athena returned them to the garden. The Argonauts came to the Hesperian plain the next day, and the Hesperides directed them to a spring that Heracles had struck from a rock near Lake Triton. Heracles appears sitting in bliss in the garden on Attic pottery, especially from the late fifth century BCE.

By Roman times the garden had dwindled to a poetic convention. It returned in Renaissance poetry, where Robert Greene, Shakespeare and John Milton mention it, and Robert Herrick's collection of verse, Hesperides, was published in 1647. Later it was thought the golden apples might have been oranges, and the Greek botanical name for citrus species is Hesperidoeidē.
gargano: The Gargano is a historical and geographical sub-region of the province of Foggia in Apulia, a wide, isolated mountain massif of highland and several peaks that forms the backbone of a promontory projecting into the Adriatic Sea. Its highest point is Monte Calvo, at 1,065 metres. The peninsula is partly covered by the Foresta Umbra, the only remaining part in Italy of the ancient oak and beech forest that once covered much of Central Europe. The Latin poet Horace spoke of the oaks of Garganus in his Ode II, ix. Two large salt lakes, Lesina and Varano, lie in the north, and the coast has beaches and resorts such as Vieste, Peschici and Mattinata.

Between the Miocene and the early Pliocene the area was a large island, which also included adjacent parts of peninsular Italy. Its animals, known as the Gargano fauna or Terre Rosse fauna, were unbalanced in the way of island communities and included giant rodents, a marine otter, a ruminant with five horns and flightless and giant birds. Fossils have been recovered from fissures in the limestone, filled with red clays. Paleontologists have argued over whether the animals arrived by a single land bridge or in several waves by rafting or flying. Later, as the ice ages began, sea levels sank and the island became joined to the mainland.

The Gargano is the site of the oldest shrine in Western Europe dedicated to the archangel Michael, the Sanctuary of Saint Michael the Archangel at Monte Sant'Angelo, and pilgrimages (cumpagnie) to it are made on 8 May and 29 September.

Most of the upland, about 1,200 square kilometres, forms the Gargano National Park, founded in 1991. Other sites include the Sanctuary of Saint Pio of Pietrelcina in San Giovanni Rotondo, the Abbey of Saint Mary of Ripalta and the Sanctuary of Saint Nazario, whose pilgrimage falls on 28 July. On Good Friday San Marco in Lamis holds the procession of the Fracchie. The varieties of Southern Italo-Romance spoken here are each particular to their town.
garonne: The Garonne flows from the central Spanish Pyrenees to the Gironde estuary at the French port of Bordeaux, a length of 529 km, of which 47 km lies in the Val d'Aran in Spain. Its basin covers 56,000 square kilometres. The name comes from Garumna, a Latin form of an Aquitanian name meaning stony river. Three places have been proposed as its source, and by the usual convention of the United States Geological Survey and others it is the Ratera-Saboredo cirque, the most distant point of the basin.

The river follows the Aran Valley northwards into France and passes Toulouse and Agen on its way to Bordeaux. The Ariège, the Tarn and the Lot join it, and just after Bordeaux it meets the Dordogne at the Bec d'Ambès to form the Gironde estuary, which runs about 100 km to the Atlantic. It is one of the few rivers in the world with a tidal bore. The European sea sturgeon, critically endangered, breeds only in its basin.

Umayyad and Aquitanian forces fought the Battle of the River Garonne in 732 beside the river near present-day Bordeaux. The river has long served shipping. Seagoing vessels reach Bordeaux, and it forms part of the Canal des Deux Mers between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Before the lateral canal was built between 1838 and 1856, shallow-draught boats used the river as far as Toulouse, though navigation on the upper river was uncertain. The canal now takes boats through 53 locks to Toulouse, where it meets the Canal du Midi.

Floods have been recorded since around 1177, with others in 1220, 1258 and many later years. At Toulouse, where the left bank is inhabited, they were frequent. In 1827 the river rose four metres above its usual level and filled the arches of the Pont de Pierre and Pont Neuf, and the floods of 1835, 1855 and 1875 were higher.

The river passes Vielha, Saint-Gaudens, Muret, Toulouse, Agen, Marmande, Langon and Bordeaux. Upstream of Toulouse it depends mainly on snow and snow melt, and downstream it is fed by rain, as are its main tributaries. The Saint-Martory canal and the lateral canal both draw water from the river.
garoua: Garoua lies on the Benue River in northern Cameroon and serves as the gateway to Benoue National Park. Its neighbourhoods include Commercial Centre, Lopere, Quartier de Marouare, Poumpoumre and Roumde Adjia, with the suburb of Yelwa in the north-west, near Garoua International Airport. The city has a tropical savanna climate, with a wet season and a dry season and heat throughout the year. The coolest months are December and January, with an average temperature of 26.0 °C, and the hottest is April, at 33.0 °C. December, January and February receive no rain at all, while August is the wettest month. The city receives about 997 millimetres of rain a year.

Garoua was established by the Fulani emir Modibbo Adama in the first half of the 19th century. During the steamship era it developed into a major river port, and goods were carried by ship along the Benue between Garoua and Burutu in Nigeria. The population of the city was 30,000 in 1967. By 2022 it had grown to approximately 900,000 people, among them a large Fulbe, or Fulani, population.

Garoua is the capital of the North Region of Cameroon and the fourth largest port in the country. It became a centre of trade in petroleum, cement, hides, peanuts and cotton, and has long been a centre of the cotton industry, with several textile processing facilities and factories. The cotton company Sodecoton has one of its major centres there. Leatherwork and fishing are also notable industries.

Most places of worship are mosques, but there are also Christian churches, including those of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Garoua, the Evangelical Church of Cameroon, the Presbyterian Church in Cameroon and the Cameroon Baptist Convention. The city stands on National Highway 1, at a junction of the road between Maroua and Ngaoundéré. Among its notable natives are the storyteller Goggo Addi, who worked to preserve Fulani cultural heritage, and Ahmadou Ahidjo, the first president of Cameroon.
gascony: Gascony was a province of south-western France that succeeded the Duchy of Gascony, dated 602 to 1453. The region is vaguely defined: it lies between the Atlantic Ocean and the Pyrenees and extends north to the Garonne, with the Adour as its other main river. Most definitions put it east and south of Bordeaux. Its historical capital was Auch. Gascony was historically inhabited by Basque-related people, and the Gascon language, usually classified as a variety of Occitan, has been spoken there from the Middle Ages. The name comes from the same root as the word Basque, through Vasconia, Wasconia and Gasconia.

Before Roman rule the inhabitants were the Aquitanians, who spoke a language related to Basque. Julius Caesar's lieutenants conquered Aquitania in the 50s BCE. In 297 Emperor Diocletian made the territory south of the Garonne the province of Novempopulania, the land of the nine tribes, which corresponds mostly to modern Gascony. It was given to the Visigoths in 416 to 418 and passed to the Franks after their victory in 507. Viking raiders devastated towns including Bayonne and Dax in 842 to 844, until Duke William II Sánchez defeated them at Taller in 982. The duchy then splintered into counties and viscounties such as Fézensac, Armagnac, Astarac, Bigorre and Béarn.

The 1152 marriage of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine gave Henry control of Aquitaine and Gascony. The duchy functioned as an overseas English possession, sometimes called England's first colony. Philip IV of France confiscated it in 1294, beginning the Gascon War, and Edward I's three expeditions of 1294 to 1298 failed to recover it before the Treaty of Paris in 1303. In 1337 Philip VI of France took Gascony back into his hands, which precipitated the Hundred Years' War. The English were finally defeated at the Battle of Castillon on 17 July 1453, and Gascony remained French. From the 17th century its government was united with Guyenne, with its capital at Bordeaux, until 1792.

Gascony is divided between the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine, with the departments of Landes, Pyrénées-Atlantiques, south-western Gironde and southern Lot-et-Garonne, and the region of Occitanie, with Gers, Hautes-Pyrénées, south-western Tarn-et-Garonne and western Haute-Garonne. Its towns include Auch, Bayonne, Dax, Lourdes, Mont-de-Marsan, Pau and Tarbes. It was the home of Henry III of Navarre, who became king of France in 1594, and it is the land of d'Artagnan, who inspired the character in Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers.
gaston-thorn: Gaston Thorn was born in Luxembourg City on 3 September 1928, but spent his early childhood in Strasbourg, where his father worked for the French railways. The family returned to Luxembourg at the outbreak of World War II. While still at school he took part in resistance activities during the German occupation and spent several months in prison. After the war he studied medicine in Montpellier, then law in Montpellier, Lausanne and Paris, and practised law in Luxembourg from 1955. He entered politics in 1959 for the liberal Democratic Party, sat in the European Parliament from 1959 to 1969 and chaired his party from 1962 to 1969.

Thorn was Foreign Minister and Foreign Trade Minister from 1969 to 1980 and Prime Minister from 1974 to 1979. His socialist-liberal coalition of the Democratic Party and the Luxembourg Socialist Workers' Party was the first government since World War II not to include the Christian Social People's Party, and he was the first prime minister since the war from outside it, though his party had fewer seats than its partner. He also served as Minister of Economics from 1977 to 1980 and as President of the United Nations General Assembly for its 30th session, in 1975-1976.

In 1980 he was chosen to succeed Roy Jenkins as president of the Commission of the European Communities, and took office on 12 January 1981. France and Britain had opposed his appointment. His term coincided with economic and political crisis, and relations with the British government of Margaret Thatcher declined over her demand for compensation for Britain's budget payments. He reached agreement on a common fisheries policy and laid the basis for the accession of Spain and Portugal; Greece had just joined.

After leaving the commission in 1985 Thorn went into business, chairing Luxembourg's largest media company CLT and serving as president of the Banque Internationale à Luxembourg from 1985 to 1999. He remained active in the International European Movement and Liberal International. He died in Luxembourg City on 26 August 2007 and received a state funeral at Notre-Dame Cathedral on 30 August.
gatling-gun: Richard J. Gatling designed the gun in Indiana in 1861 and patented it on 4 November 1862. He wrote that he made it to reduce the size of armies and so the number of deaths from combat and disease. Inventors had explored grouped barrels since the 18th century, but poor engineering and the lack of a unitary cartridge had defeated earlier designs. Gatling's first version used reloadable steel cylinders, each holding a ball and a black-powder charge with a percussion cap. He later used paper cartridges, because self-contained brass cartridges were not yet fully available. Brass cartridges replaced paper in the 1860s.

The gun had six barrels, in some models up to ten, revolving around a central shaft as a hand crank was turned. Each barrel loaded a cartridge from a hopper on top, fired when it reached a set position and ejected the spent case, then cooled while it turned back to the top. Each barrel had its own firing mechanism, so the gun needed no single reciprocating bolt and did not overheat quickly. Unskilled operators could reach about 200 rounds per minute, and by 1886 a model could fire more than 400.

Because it needed a person to crank it, it was not a true automatic weapon; the Maxim gun of 1883 was the first fully automatic one. Black-powder smoke made concealment impossible until smokeless powder arrived, and the weight of the gun and its carriage made it hard to move over rough ground.

The American Civil War saw its first use in combat. Twelve guns bought personally by Union commanders served in the trenches at the Siege of Petersburg, and eight others were fitted to gunboats. The US Army accepted the gun only in 1866.

It was later used in the Boshin War, the Anglo-Zulu War and by Russia, which called it the Gorloff gun, at Nikopol and Plevna in the Russo-Turkish War. It served most successfully in expanding European colonial empires, defeating massed attacks by the Zulu, the Bedouin and the Mahdists; the British first deployed it in the Anglo-Ashanti wars of 1873 and 1874. At San Juan Hill in 1898 a four-gun battery under Lieutenant John H. Parker fired 18,000 rounds in eight and a half minutes. The US military declared all Gatling models obsolete in 1911, after 45 years of service, and the idea of rotating barrels returned after World War II in the Minigun and the M61 Vulcan.
gatun-lake: Gatun Lake, in Spanish Lago Gatún, is a reservoir south of Colón in Panama. Its water is mostly fresh and slightly saline near the locks. It covers about 470 square kilometres and carries ships along 33 kilometres of their passage across the Isthmus of Panama, at roughly 26 metres above sea level.

Rainforest around the lake is impassable in places, and these areas remain practically free from human interference. The largest island in the lake is Barro Colorado Island, which was set aside for scientific study when the lake was formed and is operated by the Smithsonian Institution. Many discoveries about tropical animals and plants originated there.

The lake was created by damming the Chagres River. It came into being on 27 June 1913, when the gates of the spillway at Gatun Dam were closed. The water stood then at about 14.6 metres above sea level and was expected to rise to operating levels within the following six months. When it was made, Gatun Lake was the largest artificial lake in the world.
It supplies the millions of litres of water needed to operate the locks of the Panama Canal each time a ship passes through. It also provides drinking water for Panama City and Colón.

Angling is one of the main recreations on the lake. Peacock bass, a species native to the Amazon, Rio Negro and Orinoco basins, were accidentally introduced around 1967 by a local businessman. Known locally as sargento, they have become the dominant game fish. Their introduction had severe effects on the local species: a Smithsonian report found that native fish populations had still not recovered, and only one quarter the number of native fish species was found in a sampling taken in 2016.
gaudeamus-igitur: The claim that the lyrics date from 1287 rests on a manuscript held in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris. A poem there beginning Subscribere proposui has two verses that closely resemble later verses of the song, though neither the first verse nor the words Gaudeamus igitur appear, and its music bears no relation to the present melody. A German translation of these verses was made in about 1717 and published in 1730 without music. A Latin version in a handwritten student songbook, dating from between 1723 and 1750 and kept in the Berlin State Library, differs considerably from the modern text.

The lyrics endorse the bacchanalian mayhem of student life while keeping in view that everyone will die, in the tradition of memento mori and carpe diem. The song contains humorous and ironic references to sex and death, and many versions are bowdlerized for public ceremonies, while students in private typically sing ribald words. The Neo-Latin word Antiburschius refers to opponents of the politically active German student fraternities of the 19th century. Centuries of use have produced many slightly different versions.

The current Latin text was published at Halle in 1781 in Studentenlieder by Christian Wilhelm Kindleben, who admitted to making significant changes. The present melody first appeared in print in Leipzig in 1782 in Lieder für Freunde der Geselligen Freude, though it was evidently well known earlier. The present text and melody were probably first printed together in Ignaz Walter's operatic setting of Goethe's Faust in 1797.

Johannes Brahms quoted the tune in his Academic Festival Overture, and Franz Liszt wrote a paraphrase and, in 1870, a humoresque on it. Pyotr Tchaikovsky arranged it for male chorus in 1874. Johann Strauss II quoted it in his Studenten-Polka, first performed on 24 February 1862, and Franz von Suppé in his operetta Flotte Bursche of 1863. It is the official anthem of the International University Sports Federation.
gauja: The Gauja flows through the Vidzeme region of Latvia. It is the only large river of Latvia that begins and ends its flow in the country. About 93.5 kilometres of the Gauja lie within Gauja National Park. There the river flows through the Gauja Valley, which is between 1 and 2.5 kilometres wide and reaches a maximum depth of 85 metres near Sigulda. The sandstone rocks on the banks of the Gauja and of the rivers that join it began to form 370 to 300 million years ago, during the Devonian period.

Before the 13th century the Gauja served as a trade route and as a border river between the Livonian and Latgalian lands. While Livonian languages were still spoken along the river and the sea, it was called Koivo, the Birch River, from the Livonian keùv or the Estonian kõiv. In Latvian the name once meant a great amount or a crowd, and so the river was called the big river. The Livonians suffered greatly during the Great Northern War and from a plague in the 18th century, when the remaining Livonians assimilated with the Latvians.

The Gauja changes its bed rapidly and has a reputation for being deceitful. Its bed is made of unconsolidated sand and gravel that move with the current. In places the bed is pebbly and forms boulder rapids, among them Kazu, Raiskuma, Rakšu and Ķūķu. Within the national park the river bottom is 60 to 120 metres wide and the depth changes quickly, from 0.3 to 7 metres. In low water the current runs at 0.2 to 0.4 metres a second, and in the spring flood at 2 to 3 metres a second.

The river usually freezes over in mid-December, and the ice starts moving in late March, though in warm winters it does not freeze. Much underground water flows into it, so its water is cooler than that of the other large rivers of Latvia, and the river changes level and current speed a good deal through the year.
gaul: Little is written about the peoples of Gaul before the Romans, so their early history rests largely on archaeology. Eastern and southern France shared in the Urnfield culture of the Late Bronze Age, from which the Hallstatt culture developed. The La Tène culture arose in the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, probably under Greek, Phoenician and Etruscan influence, and spread across the whole of Gaul by the late 5th century BCE. In the 4th and early 3rd centuries BCE Gallic tribal confederations expanded into northern Italy, Transylvania and Asia Minor.

Rome intervened in southern Gaul in 154 BCE and again in 125 BCE, when it stayed, and by 121 BCE it held the Mediterranean region called Provincia. Julius Caesar entered Gaul in 58 BCE, ostensibly to help Rome's allies against the migrating Helvetii, and conquered nearly all of it. Vercingetorix tried to unite the Gauls and checked Caesar at Gergovia, but Caesar captured him at the Battle of Alesia in September 52 BCE. The Gallic Wars are said to have killed as many as a million people, probably one in twelve of the Gauls, and to have enslaved another million.

Gaul's inhabitants gradually adopted Roman culture, producing a Gallo-Roman culture, and all received citizenship in 212 CE. From 260 to 273 the Gallic Empire broke away from Rome. After Frankish victories in 486, 507 and 532, Gaul except for Brittany and Septimania came under the Merovingians, the first kings of France.

The basic unit of Gallic politics was the tribe or civitas, which had a council of elders and at first a king; later the executive was an annually elected magistrate. The Gauls were seldom united. Caesar divided the people of Gallia Comata into the Aquitani, the Belgae and the Celtae. The druids presided over sacrifices, kept the agricultural calendar, educated the aristocracy and claimed the right to decide questions of war and peace. The Gaulish language is thought to have survived into the 6th century and helped shape the Vulgar Latin that became French.
gaullism: Gaullism took shape around Charles de Gaulle, who as head of the Free French Forces became the symbol of resistance to the Nazi occupation and the Vichy government. The historian Serge Berstein divides its history into phases. In the first, from 1940 to 1945, it meant those who rejected the armistice with Germany and followed de Gaulle. From 1946 to 1958 it was an opposition to the Fourth Republic, whose unstable parliamentary government Gaullists wanted replaced by a president with pre-eminent constitutional powers. In 1947 de Gaulle founded the Rally of the French People, whose membership reached one million within six months.

Berstein holds that Gaullism is neither a doctrine nor a political ideology, but a pragmatic exercise of power. Its fundamental principle is what de Gaulle called a certain idea of France, which required a strong state able to ensure that the nation's interests came first. De Gaulle disliked the regime of the parties, which he held responsible for the military disaster of 1940, and wanted a strong executive embodying national unity. He admired Louis XIV, Napoleon and Georges Clemenceau as makers of consensus. In foreign policy Gaullists sought independence from allies, which led to France's own nuclear force, the withdrawal of French forces from NATO's command structure and the removal of US bases.

After 1945 Gaullists at first defended the French Empire. De Gaulle later accepted decolonisation, and he ended the Algerian crisis of 1954 to 1962 by granting independence, which he judged to be in France's interest. Social Gaullism also proposed an association of capital and labour in place of class struggle.

De Gaulle returned to power in 1958 and served as president of the new Fifth Republic from 1959 until his resignation in 1969. His followers organised the Union for the New Republic, which became the largest force after the November 1958 elections. His successor Georges Pompidou consolidated Gaullism between 1969 and 1974. The Cross of Lorraine became the symbol of later parties, among them the Rally for the Republic, founded by Jacques Chirac in 1976. Scholars distinguish traditional, social and neo-Gaullism, and the strong presidency was kept by all de Gaulle's successors, including the socialist François Mitterrand.
gauls: The Gauls were a group of Celtic peoples of mainland Europe in the Iron Age and the Roman period, roughly from the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE, and they spoke Gaulish, a Continental Celtic language. Their culture developed over the first millennium BCE, from the Urnfield culture through the Hallstatt culture of the 8th century BCE to the La Tène culture from around the 5th century BCE. By the 4th century BCE they were spread over much of what is now France, Belgium, Switzerland, southern Germany, Austria and the Czech Republic, controlling trade routes along the Rhône, Seine, Rhine and Danube. Their name Galli is generally derived from a Celtic root meaning power or ability.

Gallic invaders settled the Po Valley in the 4th century BCE and defeated Roman forces under Brennus in 390 BCE. In the early 3rd century BCE they expanded into the Balkans, and in 279 BCE they defeated the Macedonians and killed King Ptolemy Keraunos. Those who crossed to Asia Minor settled in Galatia, and the Seleucid king Antiochus I checked them with war elephants in 275 BCE. Many Gauls served as mercenaries in the armies of Carthage, and Hannibal used them in his invasion of Italy, including at Cannae.

Roman pressure grew after the First Punic War. The Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE began a gradual decline of Gallic power. The Romans conquered the area later called Gallia Narbonensis by 121 BCE, and the Cisalpine Gauls were subdued in the early 2nd century BCE. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar began the Gallic Wars, and a mixed Gallo-Roman culture emerged after the annexation. In the crisis of the third century a Gallic Empire briefly broke away under the Batavian general Postumus.

Gaul was never united under a single ruler. The fundamental unit of politics was the tribe, each with a council of elders and at first a king, later an annually elected magistrate. Among the Aedui the executive was called a Vergobret. Many tribes built large fortified settlements called oppida, such as Bibracte, Gergovia and Alesia, and minted their own coins. They imported Mediterranean wine in large quantities, as the Vix grave's 1.63 m vessel shows. Their religion was polytheistic and overseen by druids, and they produced the Coligny calendar.

The Roman civitates, based on the tribes, later became the basis of the French dioceses, which lasted until the French Revolution. In modern France the Gauls have been evoked as ancestors, in the phrase of Ernest Lavisse's school textbook, our ancestors the Gauls.
gautama-buddha: Siddhartha Gautama was a wandering religious teacher of the eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains who lived in the 6th or 5th century BCE. Buddhist legends place his birth at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, to royal parents of the Shakya clan. Most scholars accept that he lived, taught and founded a monastic order during the reign of Bimbisara of Magadha and died in the reign of Bimbisara's successor Ajatashatru, making him a contemporary of Mahavira, the Jain tirthankara.

His dates are uncertain. The long chronology of the Sri Lankan chronicles gives 624 to 544 BCE, while most scholars who accept it but date Ashoka's coronation to about 268 BCE put his life at 566 to 486 BCE. The oldest surviving written mention of the Buddha is from the middle of the 3rd century BCE, in the Edicts of Ashoka, whose Lumbini pillar inscription commemorates the emperor's pilgrimage to the birthplace. The earliest biographies already contain supernatural elements, and the scholar Rupert Gethin holds that the life story is not history, nor meant to be.

According to Buddhist tradition, he renounced home life to live as a wandering ascetic and attained nirvana at Bodh Gaya in what is now Bihar. He then taught across the lower Indo-Gangetic Plain and built a monastic order, the sangha. Tradition describes a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism, summarised in the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. The earliest biographical material in the Pali Nikayas describes a forty-five-year career as a teacher.

He left no writings. His teachings were compiled by the Buddhist community as the Vinaya Pitaka, on monastic discipline, and the Sutra Pitaka, discourses attributed to him, passed down orally in Middle Indo-Aryan dialects. How far later doctrine reflects his own words is disputed. Scholars such as Richard Gombrich and A. K. Warder hold that early texts contain material traceable to him, while others doubt that the beliefs of pre-sectarian Buddhism can be recovered.

Buddhist tradition holds that he died at Kushinagar, in modern Uttar Pradesh, and reached parinirvana. Buddhism later developed into the Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions and spread beyond the Indian subcontinent. It declined in India and largely disappeared there after the 8th century CE, but became more prominent in Southeast and East Asia. Mahayana sutras present Shakyamuni as a transcendent being, and the Hindu tradition incorporated the Buddha as the ninth avatar of Vishnu.

The earliest artistic depictions, at Bharhut and Sanchi, are aniconic, showing an empty throne, footprints, a Dharma wheel or a Bodhi tree. Images in human form became widespread after the first century CE, and those of Gandharan and Central Asian Buddhism were influenced by Hellenistic art, a style known as Greco-Buddhist art.
gauteng: Gauteng lies on the Highveld, a high-altitude grassland at about 1,500 m above sea level. Its southern border is the Vaal River, which separates it from the Free State, and it also borders North West, Limpopo and Mpumalanga. It is the only landlocked South African province without a foreign border. Between Johannesburg and Pretoria lie low parallel ridges and undulating hills, part of the Magaliesberg Mountains and the Witwatersrand. The Witwatersrand area, also called the Rand or the Reef after its gold reefs, is a conurbation about 120 km wide, historically divided into the East Rand, Central Rand and West Rand. The name comes from the Sotho-Tswana word gauta, meaning gold.

At the Sterkfontein caves some of the oldest hominid fossils have been found, including Mrs Ples and Little Foot. Events in the area were not written down until the 19th century. The first records are from the early 19th century, when settlers from the Cape Colony defeated the chief Mzilikazi and began to establish villages. Pretoria, founded in 1855 as capital of the South African Republic, grew rapidly until the discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 led to the founding of Johannesburg. Pretoria remained significant, notably in the Second Boer War. In 1905 the Cullinan Diamond, the largest diamond ever found, was mined at the nearby town of Cullinan.

Many events of the anti-apartheid struggle took place in what is now Gauteng: the Freedom Charter of 1955, the Women's March of 1956, the Sharpeville massacre of 1960, the Rivonia Trial of 1963 and 1964, the Soweto uprising of 1976 and the Boipatong massacre of 1992. The Apartheid Museum documents this era. The province was formed from part of the old Transvaal after South Africa's first multiracial elections on 27 April 1994, first as Pretoria–Witwatersrand–Vereeniging, and was renamed Gauteng on 28 June 1995.

Gauteng is the smallest of South Africa's nine provinces by land area and the most populous. Its capital, Johannesburg, is the country's largest city, and Pretoria is the administrative capital. Soweto is its largest township. The province is governed by a 73-member provincial legislature, and the Constitutional Court sits in Johannesburg. Its southern half is a financial and commercial centre and is home to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. The Cradle of Humankind, which includes the Sterkfontein caves, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The first FIFA world cup match on African soil took place at Soccer City on 11 June 2010.
gavrilo-princip: Gavrilo Princip was born on 25 July 1894 in the hamlet of Obljaj, near Bosansko Grahovo, in western Bosnia, the second of nine children, six of whom died in infancy. His parents, Petar and Marija, were poor Serb farmers who gave a third of their income to a landlord. At thirteen he went to Sarajevo, where his brother Jovan paid for his schooling at the Merchants' School and then the Sarajevo Gymnasium.

Bosnia had been annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908, and student groups there took up nationalist and anti-imperial ideas. In 1911 Princip joined Young Bosnia, a secret society with Serb, Croat and Muslim members that sought the liberation of Bosnia and the unification of the South Slavs. After taking part in a demonstration in February 1912 he was expelled from school and walked to Belgrade.

In 1914 Nedeljko Čabrinović showed Princip a newspaper cutting announcing Archduke Franz Ferdinand's visit to Sarajevo. Princip drew Čabrinović and Trifko Grabež into a plot. Milan Ciganović, an associate of the Serbian secret society known as the Black Hand, obtained five Browning pistols, six grenades and vials of poison for them and trained them in Belgrade. The three crossed into Bosnia, and Danilo Ilić recruited further conspirators in Sarajevo.

On 28 June 1914 the conspirators stood along the Appel Quay. Čabrinović threw a grenade that wounded occupants of another car, and the motorcade sped on. After the Archduke decided to visit the injured in hospital, his driver took a wrong turn into a side street where Princip stood. As the car stalled, Princip fired twice, killing Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and the conflict widened to the First World War.

Tried with twenty-four others in October 1914, Princip said he was a Yugoslav nationalist and that he regretted the death of the Duchess. He was too young to be executed, being twenty-seven days short of twenty, and received a sentence of twenty years. Held in the Small Fortress at Theresienstadt, he developed tuberculosis, which led to the amputation of his right arm, and he died on 28 April 1918. In 1920 he and the other conspirators were reburied in Sarajevo.

His memory remains contested. The Habsburg monarchy saw a terrorist, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and socialist Yugoslavia a hero, and many Serbs still honour him, while many Bosniaks and Croats regard him as a terrorist.
gayatri-mantra: The mantra is the verse Rigveda 3.62.10, dedicated to Savitr. In recitation it is preceded by the syllable oṃ and the formula bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, known as the mahāvyāhṛti or great mystical utterance, as the Taittiriya Aranyaka prescribes. The verse is composed in the metre called gāyatrī, which in principle has three lines of eight syllables each. The text preserved in the Samhita is one syllable short in its first line. A proposed historical form of vareṇyaṃ, vareṇiyaṃ, would restore the eight syllables, and in practice reciters may keep seven, prolong the final m, or use the reconstructed word. The word Gāyatrī also names the metre, the goddess of the mantra, and other verses in the same metre addressed to other deities.

Translators have rendered the verse in many ways. Ralph T. H. Griffith in 1896 gave it as a prayer that the worshipper may attain the excellent glory of the god Savitar so that he may stimulate our prayers. Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton render the same wish as making our own the desirable effulgence of god Savitar, who will rouse forth our insights.

The mantra is cited widely in Hindu texts, including the listings of the Śrauta liturgy, the Srauta-sutras, the grhyasutras, the Mahabharata, the Harivamsa and the Manusmṛti. Several Upanishads treat it esoterically. It has a significant role in the upanayana ceremony, which marks the start of Vedic study. Traditionally this verse was given only to a Brahmana, while other verses were used for a kshatriya and a vaishya. Reciting it is used as a method of atonement, and practitioners hold that it bestows wisdom through the Sun.

The Buddha knew the mantra. In Majjhima Nikaya 92 he calls the Sāvittī the foremost of metres, and in Sutta Nipata 3.4 he asks a man who claims to be a brahmin for the chant of Sāvitrī, in three lines of four and twenty syllables. Among Balinese Hindus it is the first of seven sections of the Trisandhyā Puja, said three times a day.

In 1827 Ram Mohan Roy published a dissertation on the mantra that analysed it against various Upanishads, and from 1830 the Brahmos used it in private devotion. In the later 19th century Hindu reform movements spread the chant beyond the Brahmin class: in 1898 Swami Vivekananda held that a person became a Brahmana through learning, not birth, and gave the mantra to non-Brahmins in the Ramakrishna Mission. Its use is now very widespread.
gdansk: Gdańsk lies at the mouth of the Motława River on the southern edge of Gdańsk Bay. The low-lying Lower Terrace covers part of the Vistula Fens, while the Upper Terrace is an area of uneven highlands that belongs to the Kashubian Lake District. The name most likely comes from Gdania, the old name of the Motława. Its German form, Danzig, developed from forms such as Danzc and Danczk.

The first written mention is in a biography of Saint Adalbert, which records his visit in 997 to a town called Gyddanyzc, then ruled by Bolesław I the Brave of Poland. The city grew into a trading town and later joined the Hanseatic League. In 1308 the Teutonic Knights, called in to relieve the Polish garrison, seized the town and killed many of its inhabitants; estimates of the dead range from about 60 to about 1,000. In 1454 the Prussian Confederation rejected the authority of the Teutonic Order and appealed to King Casimir IV of Poland, which led to the Thirteen Years' War, and on 16 June 1454 the king granted Danzig extensive privileges.

With considerable autonomy it served as the Polish Crown's main seaport and largest city until the early 18th century. Prussia annexed it in 1793 in the Second Partition of Poland, and it joined the German Empire in 1871. It was a free city from 1807 to 1814 and again from 1920 to 1939. A military clash at Westerplatte on 1 September 1939 was one of the first events of the Second World War. After 1945 the German population fled or was expelled and Poles settled in their place. The Solidarity trade union began in the city in the 1980s.

Gdańsk is the capital of the Pomeranian Voivodeship and Poland's sixth-largest city, with a population of 486,492, and a major seaport. With Gdynia and Sopot it forms a metropolitan area called the Tricity. Parts of the old city destroyed in the war were rebuilt in the 1950s and 1960s. Its landmarks include the Town Hall, the Green Gate, Artus Court, Neptune's Fountain and St. Mary's Church, one of the largest brick churches in the world. St. Dominic's Fair, which dates back to 1260, is still held there.
gdynia: Gdynia is historically and culturally part of Kashubia and Eastern Pomerania. It lies in a conurbation with the spa town of Sopot and the city of Gdańsk, which together form the Tricity, a metropolitan area of around a million inhabitants. In prehistoric times the area was the centre of the Oksywie culture. In the late 10th century the region was united with the emerging state of Poland by Mieszko I, and the district of Oksywie was first mentioned in 1209, as Oxhöft. For centuries Gdynia remained a small fishing village, and by the 20th century it attracted visitors as a seaside resort.

The Polish government decided to build a major seaport at Gdynia in the winter of 1920, during the Polish–Soviet War. German dockworkers in the Free City of Danzig had struck and refused to unload military supplies sent from the West to aid the Polish army, and Poland concluded that it needed a port it controlled economically and politically. A special committee began building the city in 1925, city rights were granted in 1926 and tax privileges for investors in 1927. Growth became rapid after 1928, with a new railway station and post office, and by 1939 the population had grown to over 120,000.

Gdynia was the site of fierce Polish defence during the German invasion of September 1939. The Germans captured the whole city on 14 September and occupied it until 1945, carrying out mass arrests of some 7,000 Poles on 15 and 16 September. The occupiers set up prisons and camps, and Poles were deported to concentration camps or executed. The Red Army captured the city on 28 March 1945 and it was restored to Poland. Settlers arrived from destroyed Warsaw and from Wilno and Lwów, and Greek refugees from the Greek Civil War also came through the port. Protests in and around Gdynia in 1970 contributed to the rise of the Solidarity movement in Gdańsk.

Gdynia is a seaport on the Baltic coast of northern Poland, and the largest city in Poland that is not a voivodeship capital. Its modernist centre, laid out in 1926 by Adam Kuncewicz and Roman Feliński as a grand maritime façade for the newly independent state, is built around an axis that runs from 10 Lutego Street through Kościuszko Square to the Southern Pier. Its architecture shows monumentalism, early functionalism and interwar modernism. The oldest building is the 13th-century church of St Michael the Archangel in Oksywie, and two museum ships, the destroyer ORP Błyskawica and the sailing ship Dar Pomorza, are moored in the harbour. The port is the home of the 3rd Ship Flotilla of the Polish Navy.
gebhard-leberecht-von-blucher: Blücher was born on 16 December 1742 in Rostock, then in the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the son of a retired army captain from an old landowning noble family. At sixteen he joined the Swedish Army as a hussar. Prussian hussars captured him in a skirmish in 1760, and the colonel of their regiment, Wilhelm Sebastian von Belling, a distant relative, had him join it.

In peacetime his ardent spirit led him into excesses, including the mock execution of a priest in 1772. Passed over for promotion, he sent a rude letter of resignation in 1773, and Frederick the Great replied, "Captain Blücher can take himself to the devil". He farmed until Frederick died in 1786, then returned as a major in 1787.

He received the Pour le Mérite in 1789 and became a major general in 1794 after his victory at Kirrweiler. As a cavalry general in 1806 he fought at Auerstedt, but he was defeated at Lübeck and surrendered at Ratekau on 7 November, insisting that the document record a lack of provisions and ammunition. In 1813, aged 71, he returned to high command.

As commander-in-chief of the Army of Silesia he defeated Marshal MacDonald at the Katzbach and Marshal Marmont at Möckern, and his army stormed Leipzig on the last day of the Battle of the Nations. He was made field marshal on 16 October 1813 and, with his chief staff officers, pressed the Coalition sovereigns to carry the war into France.

In 1814 he suffered defeats at Champaubert, Vauchamps and Montmirail, then won at Laon on 9 and 10 March, after which a breakdown cost him his sight for a time. The allies entered Paris, and Frederick William III made him Prince of Wahlstatt. When Napoleon returned in 1815 Blücher commanded the Army of the Lower Rhine. At Ligny on 16 June he lay trapped for hours under his dead horse and the Prussians retreated, but he led his army to join Wellington at Waterloo, where its arrival was decisive. The two armies entered Paris on 7 July.

Blücher retired to Krieblowitz in Silesia and died there on 12 September 1819, aged 76. Napoleon called him very brave but no talent as a general, and admired his readiness to rise again after a defeat. Later Prussian soldiers spoke of a Prussian way of war built on the quick, decisive battle. He was made an honorary citizen of Berlin, Hamburg and Rostock, and statues were raised at Berlin, Breslau, Rostock and Kaub, where his troops crossed the Rhine.
gediminas: Gediminas was born in about 1275. Written sources of the era are scarce, so his ancestry and early life remain obscure and are debated by scholars. Theories make him the son, the brother or the cousin of his predecessor, Grand Duke Vytenis, or even his hostler. Chronicles written long afterwards by the Teutonic Knights, long-standing enemies of Lithuania, claimed that he was Vytenis' hostler who killed his master and took the throne. The Lithuanian Chronicles, also late, made him Vytenis' son, though the two men were almost the same age.

Gediminas inherited Lithuania proper, Samogitia, Navahrudak, Podlasie, Polotsk and Minsk, all threatened by the Teutonic Knights and the Livonian Order. He allied with the Tatars against the Teutonic Order in 1319, and in 1322 he wrote to Pope John XXII asking for protection and offering to be baptised. On 25 January 1323 he sent circular letters to the Hanseatic towns inviting people of every order and profession to settle in his lands.
