Holstein-Glückstadt stayed under the Danish Crown until Denmark's defeat in the Second Schleswig War of 1864. Austria occupied it, and after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 it was incorporated into the Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein.

The Marsh Railway reached Glückstadt in 1845 from Elmshorn and was extended to Itzehoe in 1857. Trains now run from Hamburg-Altona to Westerland on Sylt, and a ferry crosses the Elbe to Wischhafen in Lower Saxony. The town lies on the Deutsche Fährstraße theme road and the Elbe Cycle Route.
glyptothek: Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria, later Ludwig I, commissioned the Glyptothek as a monument to ancient Greece. He envisioned a German Athens in which Greek culture would be remembered, and had it built in front of the gates of Munich. It stands beside the Königsplatz and the building that houses the State Collection of Greek and Roman Antiquities, and it is the oldest public museum in Munich. The architects Karl von Fischer and Leo von Klenze laid out the Königsplatz in 1815, and Klenze arranged it like a forum, with the Glyptothek on its north side.

Between 1806 and the opening in 1830 Ludwig built up a notable collection through his agents. It came to include the Medusa Rondanini, the Barberini Faun and, in 1813, the figures from the temple of Aphaea on Aegina. Frescoes and stuccos by Peter von Cornelius, Clemens von Zimmermann and Wilhelm von Kaulbach once adorned the walls.

The building is neoclassical. Twelve Ionic columns form the portico, and thirteen rooms are arranged around a courtyard. The gable carries a group by Johann Martin von Wagner showing Athena as protector of the plastic arts.

The collection runs from the Archaic age, about 650 BCE, to the Roman era, about 550 CE. Archaic works include the Munich Kouros and the temple figures from Aegina. Classical pieces include the portrait of Homer, the Medusa Rondanini and the Alexander Rondanini, and the Hellenistic period is represented above all by the Barberini Faun. The Roman galleries hold busts of Augustus, Nero and Septimius Severus. A bust of Caligula excavated in Córdoba in 1937 was acquired in 2017, so the museum owns portraits of all five Julio-Claudian emperors.

The Second World War did not destroy much of the sculpture, but the frescoes did not survive, and when the museum reopened in 1972 only lightly plastered bricks were visible. Klenze's Assyrian Hall of 1864 was not rebuilt, and the Assyrian reliefs from the palace of Ashur-nasir-pal II and a lion from the Ishtar Gate of Babylon went to the Staatliche Sammlung für Ägyptische Kunst. It is now part of the Kunstareal, and its sculptures are complemented by the terracotta and bronze collections of the Antikensammlung opposite.
gnaeus-julius-agricola: Agricola was born on 13 June 40 at the colonia of Forum Julii in Gallia Narbonensis, now Fréjus in France. Both his grandfathers had served as imperial governors. His father, Lucius Julius Graecinus, a senator noted for his interest in philosophy, was put to death on the order of the emperor Caligula for refusing to prosecute the emperor's second cousin Marcus Junius Silanus. His mother was Julia Procilla, whom Tacitus describes as a lady of singular virtue. Agricola was educated at Massilia (Marseille).

He served as a military tribune in Britain under Gaius Suetonius Paulinus from 58 to 62 and almost certainly took part in the suppression of the Boudican uprising in 61. He was quaestor in the province of Asia in 64, tribune of the plebs in 66 and praetor in 68. In the Year of the Four Emperors he gave his support to Vespasian, and was given command of the Legio XX Valeria Victrix in Britain, where he reimposed discipline and fought the Brigantes under Quintus Petillius Cerialis. He then governed Gallia Aquitania for almost three years and in 76 or 77 was made suffect consul.

Returning to Britain as governor in the summer of 77, he found that the Ordovices had virtually destroyed the Roman cavalry in their territory, and defeated them before subduing Anglesey. In 79 he pushed his armies to the estuary of the river Taus, usually taken to be the Firth of Tay. He reformed the corn levy and encouraged the building of towns on the Roman model, and had the sons of native nobles given a Roman education, which Tacitus calls a means of pacifying the tribes. In 83 he faced the Caledonians under Calgacus at Mons Graupius. Tacitus puts their numbers above 30,000 and their losses at about 10,000 against 360 Roman dead, and two thirds of their army escaped into the Highlands.

Agricola was recalled after an unusually long tenure. Tacitus claims that the emperor Domitian ordered this because Agricola's successes outshone his own modest victories in Germany. He was awarded triumphal decorations and a statue but never held another civil or military post, and he declined the governorship of Africa, from ill health or, as Tacitus claims, because of Domitian's machinations. He died on 23 August 93 on his family estates in Gallia Narbonensis, aged fifty-three. Rumours of poisoning by Domitian circulated, but no evidence for them was ever produced. His career is known mainly from the biography by Tacitus, his son-in-law, and from archaeological evidence in northern Britain.
gniezno: Gniezno lies about 50 km east of Poznań and was founded, like Rome, on seven hills. At the beginning of the 10th century the site held several places sacred to the Slavic religion. A ducal stronghold was founded on Lech Hill just before 940. According to the Polish version of a legend, the name comes from gniazdo, a nest: the hunter Lech, one of three brothers, settled where he found a white eagle guarding its nest.

Around 940 Gniezno, an important pagan cult centre, became one of the main fortresses of the early Piast rulers. After Mieszko I of Poland adopted Christianity, his son Bolesław I the Brave deposited the remains of Saint Adalbert in a church newly built on the hill, to underline the city's importance as the religious centre and capital of his realm. At the Congress of Gniezno in the year 1000 Bolesław received the Holy Roman Emperor Otto III, and they marked the founding of the Polish ecclesiastical province with an archbishopric at Gniezno. New bishoprics were set up at Kołobrzeg, Wrocław and Kraków beside the older one at Poznań.

The cathedral saw the coronations of Bolesław I in 1024 and of his son Mieszko II Lambert in 1025. In 1038 the Bohemian duke Bretislav I captured and destroyed Gniezno and Poznań, which led later Polish rulers to move the capital to Kraków. Bolesław II the Generous was crowned in the rebuilt cathedral in 1076, and Gniezno was again the coronation site in 1295 and 1300. The Teutonic Knights destroyed the city in 1331, and in 1419 its status as the capital of Christianity in Poland was confirmed when the archbishops received the title of Primate of Poland.

Prussia annexed Gniezno in the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 and renamed it Gnesen. After the Greater Poland Uprising of 1918–1919 and the Treaty of Versailles it became part of the Second Polish Republic. In the Second World War German troops took it on 11 September 1939 and annexed it to Germany.

Gniezno is the seat of Gniezno County in the Greater Poland Voivodeship and of the oldest archdiocese in Poland, whose archbishop is the Primate of Poland. Gniezno Cathedral is a designated Historic Monument of Poland. It holds the Romanesque Gniezno Doors and the coffin of Saint Adalbert.
goa: Goa lies on the southwestern coast of India, in the Konkan region, separated from the Deccan highlands by the Western Ghats. It covers 3,702 square kilometres, and its highest point, Sonsogor, rises to 1,167 metres. The climate is tropical monsoon, with over 90 per cent of the rain falling from June to September. Rock engravings at Usgalimal and Kajur are among the earliest known traces of human life in India.

In the 3rd century BCE Goa belonged to the Maurya Empire under Ashoka. Between the 2nd century BCE and the 6th century CE it was ruled by the Bhojas of Goa, then by the Chalukyas of Badami from 578 to 753 and the Rashtrakutas from 753 to 963. The Kadambas, who followed as feudatories of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, patronised Jainism.

In 1510 the Portuguese defeated the Bijapur sultan Yusuf Adil Shah with the help of a local ally, Thimmayya or Timoji, and set up a permanent settlement at Old Goa. Under Afonso de Albuquerque the city became capital of the Estado da Índia. The Goa Inquisition was established in 1560 and abolished in 1812, and the first printing press in India produced its first books in 1556. Old Goa was abandoned in the 19th century after outbreaks of disease. On 19 December 1961 the Indian Army invaded in Operation Vijay and annexed Goa, and on 30 May 1987 it became India's twenty-fifth state.

Goa is a state of India with Panaji as its capital and Vasco da Gama as its largest city. Konkani is its sole official language, with Marathi also permitted for official purposes. The census of 2011 counted 1,458,545 people, 66.1 per cent of them Hindu and 25.1 per cent Christian. The Bom Jesus Basilica and the churches and convents of Old Goa form its World Heritage Site; the basilica holds the remains of Saint Francis Xavier. Goan cooking, based on rice, fish and coconut, is heavily influenced by Portuguese cuisine.
gobi-desert: The Gobi is a large, cold desert and grassland region in southern Mongolia and North China. It measures about 1,600 km from southwest to northeast and 800 km from north to south, and covers approximately 1,295,000 square kilometres. The name comes from the Mongolian word Gov', meaning dryland, used for all waterless regions of the Mongolian Plateau; the Chinese term gēbì refers to rocky semi-deserts rather than sandy ones, and much of the Gobi is bare rock rather than sand.

It lies on a plateau roughly 910 to 1,520 m above sea level, with frost and occasional snow on its dunes, and an average of about 194 mm of rain a year. Its climate is one of great extremes, with changes of as much as 35 °C in 24 hours. Geographers divide it into five dry ecoregions, among them the Eastern Gobi desert steppe, the Alashan Plateau semi-desert and the Dzungarian Basin semi-desert; some regard the Tarim basin in the west as a separate Taklamakan Desert.

Little is known about early habitation. Lisa Janz has proposed three phases: Oasis I, the Mesolithic from 13500 to 8000 calibrated years before the present, when people began to use oases and made microblades, small milling stones and plain, low-fired pottery; Oasis II, the Neolithic from 8000 to 5000, when oases were used extensively; and Oasis III, the Bronze Age from 5000 to 3000.

A warm wet phase began around 8000 years ago, and lakes in the western Gobi peaked by 7500. Bronze Age herder burials, Karasuk bronze knives and Mongolian deer stones have been found. A period of desertification followed between 5000 and 4500 years ago, and increasing aridity between 3500 and 3000 led to a decline in habitation. The region was later inhabited mostly by nomadic Mongols, Uyghurs and Kazakhs.

The Gobi is a source of important fossil finds. The first dinosaur eggs, twenty-six averaging 23 cm in length, were uncovered there in 1923, and the Nemegt Basin in Mongolia is noted for early mammals, dinosaur eggs and stone implements some 100,000 years old. It supports black-tailed gazelles, wild Bactrian camels and the Mongolian wild ass, and large reserves include Gobi Gurvansaikhan National Park. The desert is expanding, mostly on its southern edge into China, which loses about 3,600 km2 of grassland a year, and China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program, begun in 1978, is meant to run through 2050 to slow it.
god-defend-new-zealand: The competition of 1876 was won by John Joseph Woods of Lawrence, Otago, who was Vandemonian-born and composed the melody in a single sitting on the evening after he learned of it. The song was first performed at the Queen's Theatre in Princes Street, Dunedin, on Christmas Day 1876, and sheet music was published in February 1878. In 1878 Thomas Henry Smith of Auckland, a judge in the Native Land Court, made a Māori version at the request of Premier George Edward Grey. The anthem has five verses in each language, and the Māori is not a direct translation of the English. Its structure is a prayer to God, with the refrain God defend New Zealand.

In 1897 Premier Richard Seddon presented a copy of the words and music to Queen Victoria. In 1940 the government bought the copyright and made the song the national hymn in time for the centennial celebrations. It was used at the British Empire Games from 1950, and at the Olympics in 1952, when it and God Save the King were played after Yvette Williams won the long jump. A campaign for its adoption as the anthem began after the 1972 Munich Games. With the consent of Queen Elizabeth II, the government of Robert Muldoon gazetted it as a second national anthem on 21 November 1977, on equal standing with the royal anthem.

Until the 1990s only the first English verse was commonly sung. After Hinewehi Mohi sang only the first Māori verse at a 1999 Rugby World Cup match between the All Blacks and England, it became usual to sing the first verse in Māori and then in English.

Some of the words, such as thy, thee, ramparts and assail, have been criticised as antiquated or obscure, and the melody as hard to sing at its original pitch, but no widely acceptable replacement has been found. The phrase Pacific's triple star has no official explanation; unofficial readings include New Zealand's three main islands and the three stars on the flag of Te Kooti, a 19th-century Māori leader. In 2013 the original score and lyrics were added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Aotearoa New Zealand register; the documents are kept at the Auckland Central City Library.
god-save-the-king: The author of the song is unknown, and it may originate as a plainchant, although an attribution to the composer John Bull has sometimes been made. In The Oxford Companion to Music, Percy Scholes notes similarities to an early plainsong melody, though the rhythm is distinctly that of a galliard. He quotes a keyboard piece by John Bull dated 1619 with some similarities to the modern tune, and a piece by Henry Purcell that sets the words God Save the King to its opening notes. Nineteenth-century writers mention a widespread belief that an old Scots carol, Remember O Thou Man, was its source.

The phrase itself is much older than the song. A text based on 1 Kings 1:38–40 has been sung and proclaimed at every coronation since that of King Edgar in 973, and by 1545 it was a watchword of the Royal Navy.

In the United Kingdom the song derives its official status from custom and use, not from a royal proclamation or act of Parliament. Beyond its consistent first verse it has many versions, and usually only one verse is sung. King George V considered himself an expert on how it should be played, and in 1933 an Army Order laid down its tempo and orchestration.

It spread with the British Empire, serving as the national anthem of each country, and declined in use in most states that became independent. In New Zealand it was the sole national anthem until 1977, when God Defend New Zealand was introduced as a second. In South Africa it was a co-national anthem from 1938 until 1957. In Australia it was declared the royal anthem on 19 April 1984.

The melody has served elsewhere with new words. It was the anthem of Prussia, Heil dir im Siegerkranz, from 1795 until 1918, the imperial anthem of Russia from 1816 to 1833, and the anthem of Switzerland from the 1840s until 1961. It remains the national anthem of Liechtenstein and the royal anthem of Norway, and it is the basis of the American song My Country, 'Tis of Thee. About 140 composers have used the tune, among them Beethoven, who wrote seven piano variations on it in 1802–1803.

In 1796 the philosopher Jeremy Bentham praised the melody for its beauty and simplicity. In 1951 the song became the first music played on a computer, programmed by Christopher Strachey at Manchester.
god-save-the-tsar: The anthem was chosen in a competition held in 1833 and first performed on 18 December 1833. The music was written by the violinist Alexei Lvov and the words by the court poet Vasily Zhukovsky. It served as the national anthem of the Russian Empire until the February Revolution of 1917. The Worker's Marseillaise was then adopted as the new anthem, and remained so until the Bolsheviks overthrew the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution of the same year.

The tune was also used as the royal anthem of the Principality of Bulgaria, where it had been imposed by the temporary Russian government and the Russian army commanders. Bulgaria gave up its use after the declaration of independence in 1908.

Many composers used the theme. Tchaikovsky quoted it in the 1812 Overture, the Marche Slave, his overture on the Danish national anthem and the Festival Coronation March. In the Soviet era the authorities altered such works, replacing the theme with other patriotic melodies, such as the Glory chorus from Mikhail Glinka's opera A Life for the Tsar. Charles Gounod used it in his Fantaisie sur l'Hymne National Russe, and later film scores, among them William Walton's for Three Sisters in 1970 and Maurice Jarre's for Doctor Zhivago in 1965, are built on it.

In 1842 the English author Henry Chorley wrote the words God, the Omnipotent! for Lvov's tune, and as the Russian Hymn it appeared in 19th- and 20th-century hymnals and still appears in several others. The melody also carries the words of many college and school songs. The Royal Scots Dragoon Guards still play the anthem at formal events as a tribute to Nicholas II, former colonel-in-chief of their predecessor regiment, the Scots Greys. In 1998 the rock artist Alexander Gradsky proposed reviving the theme as the Russian national anthem, with substantially different lyrics.
godfrey-of-bouillon: Godfrey was the second son of Eustace II, Count of Boulogne. His uncle, Godfrey the Hunchback, was murdered on 22 February 1076 without issue, having designated him as heir, and Godfrey became Lord of Bouillon through an inheritance from his mother's family. His claim was challenged by several rivals, among them his aunt Matilda of Tuscany, Albert III of Namur and Count Theoderic of Veluwe. Emperor Henry IV first gave the duchy of Lower Lorraine to his own infant son Conrad. Godfrey supported Henry during the Investiture Controversy and gained Lower Lorraine in 1087.

In 1096 Godfrey joined the First Crusade with his brothers Eustace and Baldwin of Boulogne. He either sold or mortgaged most of his estates to the bishops of Liège and Verdun to raise an army, reportedly 40,000 strong, which set out in August 1096. He reached Constantinople in November and, like most of the crusaders, agreed to a modified oath to Emperor Alexios I Komnenos promising to restore some lands. He took part at Nicaea, Dorylaeum and the Siege of Antioch.

The crusaders reached Jerusalem in June 1099, and the major attack took place on 14 and 15 July. Godfrey and some of his knights were among the first to take the walls. On 22 July a council met in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and after Raymond IV of Toulouse refused the crown, Godfrey agreed to rule, preferring the title Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre to that of king. Its meaning is disputed, since early chroniclers used the term princeps or his old rank of duke, while later ones wrote rex.

Godfrey defeated the Fatimids at the Battle of Ascalon in August 1099 and in 1100 made Acre, Ascalon, Arsuf, Jaffa and Caesarea tributaries. Godfrey died on 18 July 1100. The Arab chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi reports that an arrow killed him at Acre, but Christian chroniclers say he fell ill at Caesarea, and a disease like typhoid is thought more likely than poison. His supporters seized Jerusalem and his brother Baldwin succeeded him; Dagobert crowned Baldwin as first Latin king on 25 December 1100.

Later accounts idealized him as the crusade's military leader and as a legislator of the assizes of Jerusalem, and in the early 14th century he was chosen as one of the Nine Worthies. In reality he was one of several leaders, and the assizes developed gradually. He was the hero of Torquato Tasso's epic Jerusalem Delivered.
goiania: Goiania lies in the cerrado, a landscape of savanna crossed by gallery forests and stream valleys, on mostly flat land along the Meia Ponte River. It covers about 739 square kilometres and lies about 200 kilometres from Brasilia. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with a wet season from October to April and a dry one from May to September, and annual rainfall of around 1,300 millimetres.

The first state capital, Vila Boa, today the City of Goias, was chosen when the economy rested on gold. When cattle-raising and agriculture came to dominate, it was considered remote. Plans to move the capital were put forward in 1753 by Marcos de Noronha, who favoured Pirenopolis, and in 1863 by Jose Vieira Couto de Magalhaes, who proposed the Araguaia river. In 1891 the constitutional delegates included a transfer in the constitution, which was ratified in 1898 and again in 1918.

The idea became reality under Pedro Ludovico, appointed governor after the military revolt of 1930. A commission created in 1932 chose the municipality of Campinas, whose mayor Andrelino Rodrigues de Moraes donated about 242 acres of land. The city was founded on 24 October 1933 and planned for 50,000 people, with streets radiating like spokes from the Praca Civica, where the state and municipal governments were to sit. A local newspaper held a contest for the name in 1933, and Ludovico first used Goiania in 1935 in the decree creating the municipality. A decree of 1937 transferred the capital from the City of Goias, and the official inauguration took place in 1942 with the president of the republic present.

The first buildings, designed by Attilio Correia Lima, were inspired by art deco, and 22 of them are listed as National Heritage. On 13 September 1987 a radiotherapy source containing caesium-137 was stolen from an abandoned hospital. People attracted by its bluish glow took grains of the salt home, and four people died, with many more suffering radiation poisoning. Several city blocks had to be demolished.

Goiania is the capital and largest city of Goias, with 1,536,097 inhabitants and a metropolitan area of 2,890,418. It is the second most populous city of the Central-West Region after Brasilia. Its economy grew from agriculture in and around the city, and it is also a regional centre of industry and medicine. It has many parks, among them the Bosque dos Buritis and the Vaca Brava Park,. Goias is regarded as the cradle of sertanejo, a country music genre.
gojong-of-korea: Gojong was born into a distant branch of the royal House of Yi, a descendant of Grand Prince Inpyeong, the third son of King Injo. When King Cheoljong died without a son, the influential Andong Kim clan nominated him as the next king, and he was crowned on 13 December 1863. Queen Sinjeong acted as regent, assisted by his father, Heungseon Daewongun, who remained the dominant figure at court. The Daewongun was the chief proponent of isolationism and persecuted native and foreign Catholics, a policy that led to French and United States expeditions to Korea in 1866 and 1871. Gojong announced his direct rule in 1873, and after the Daewongun's retirement in November 1874 Queen Min and the Yeoheung Min clan controlled the court.

The Treaty of Ganghwa of 1876 was the first unequal treaty Korea signed with a foreign country. It gave Japanese citizens extraterritorial rights and opened the ports of Busan, Chemulpo (Incheon) and Wonsan to trade. In the Imo Incident of 1882, soldiers of the old army, unpaid for 13 months, rioted, and Queen Min asked the Qing Empire for help; about 3,000 Qing soldiers came to Seoul. The Kapsin Coup of December 1884 failed after three days. In 1895 Japanese agents, in a plot organised by the Japanese minister Miura Gorō, killed Queen Min in Gyeongbokgung. In February 1896 Gojong fled to the Russian legation in Seoul and governed from there for about a year.

On 13 October 1897 he proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Korean Empire at the altar of Hwangudan, with the era name Gwangmu, a gesture marking the end of Qing suzerainty. The constitution of 17 August 1899 granted him absolute power. His reforms improved the military, industry and education to some degree, and in 1898 he abolished the Independence Club. After Japan's victory in the Russo-Japanese War, Korea lost its diplomatic sovereignty in the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905. Gojong refused to sign it and appealed to other powers, including a letter to President Theodore Roosevelt, but without result.

Gojong was forced to abdicate on 20 July 1907, and his son Sunjong replaced him. He was confined to Deoksugung and made several attempts to escape, in 1910, 1915 and 1918, all unsuccessful. Korea was formally annexed by Japan on 22 August 1910, and Gojong received the title King Emeritus Yi of Deoksu. He died suddenly at Deoksugung on 21 January 1919, aged 66. The official cause was a cerebral haemorrhage, but suspicion that Japan had poisoned him arose around the time of his death and persists. His death and funeral were a catalyst for the March First Movement. He is buried with his wife at Hongneung in Namyangju, part of the Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
golan-heights: The Golan is a basaltic plateau at the south-western corner of Syria, generally bounded by the Jordan Valley on the west, the Yarmouk River on the south and the Sa'ar stream on the north, with its eastern limit at the Ruqqad or the Allan river. It is about 65 km long and 12 to 25 km wide and overlooks the Jordan Rift Valley and the Sea of Galilee. Volcanic eruptions that began about 4 million years ago formed it, and dormant volcanoes and cinder cones are scattered across it. The snow of Mount Hermon, 2,814 m high, feeds springs and rivers in the Jordan watershed.

The earliest evidence of habitation dates to the Upper Paleolithic, and settlement grew from the 2nd millennium BCE. After the Late Bronze Age collapse the kingdom of Geshur emerged; the Hebrew Bible describes David's marriage to Maacha, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, as a dynastic alliance. By the mid-9th century BCE Aram-Damascus had absorbed Geshur, and the Assyrians conquered the region in the 8th century BCE. Gaulanitis, the Greek name for the region, appears after Alexander the Great's conquest, under Ptolemaic and then Seleucid rule. In the middle of the 2nd century BCE the Itureans moved in, and the Roman and Byzantine periods left Diocletianic boundary stones and 25 ancient synagogues.

After the Battle of Yarmouk the Golan came under Muawiyah I, the future first Umayyad caliph, and then passed from the Abbasids to the Fatimids and the Seljuk Turks. Crusader forces held Banias in 1128–32 and 1140–64, and the Ayyubids under Saladin later ruled the area. The Mongols swept through in 1259 and were driven off by Qutuz at Ain Jalut in 1260. In the 1560s the Ottoman official Mustafa Lala Pasha made al-Qunaytira a regional centre.

When the French mandate ended in 1946 the Golan became part of the independent Syrian Arab Republic. Israeli forces captured the plateau on 9–10 June 1967 in the Six-Day War, and an estimated 80,000 to 130,000 people fled or were driven out. After the 1973 war a third of the plateau returned to Syrian administration. In 1981 the Knesset passed the Golan Heights Law applying Israeli law there, which the UN Security Council condemned in Resolution 497.
golconda-fort: Golconda, also called Muhammadnagar, is a fortified citadel and ruined city on the western outskirts of Hyderabad in Telangana. The name is thought to come from the Telugu Gollakonda, meaning Shepherd's hill. Its fortifications include four distinct forts within an outer wall with 87 semicircular bastions, eight gateways and four drawbridges, with royal apartments, halls, temples, mosques, magazines and stables inside. The outermost enclosure is entered by the Fateh Darwaza, the Victory gate, so called because Aurangzeb's army marched in through it. A hand clap beneath the dome there can be heard at the Bala Hisar pavilion, the highest point, almost a kilometre away.

The fort began as a small mud fort that tradition ascribes to the Kakatiya ruler Pratāparudra, and it is also thought that the Kakatiya ruler Ganapati built a stone hilltop outpost there to defend the western region. It was made over to the Bahmani Kingdom by sanad from the Rajah of Warangal, and under the Bahmani Kingdom it slowly rose to prominence. Quli Qutb Shah, sent by the Bahmanids as governor, made the city his seat around 1501 and formally became independent in 1518, founding the Sultanate of Golconda. Over 62 years the first three Qutb Shahi sultans turned the mud fort into a massive granite fortification. It remained the dynasty's capital until 1590, when the capital moved to Hyderabad.

Golconda flourished as a trade centre of large diamonds from the nearby mines, especially the Kollur Mine, and the diamonds believed to have come from its mines include the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond. In the early seventeenth century it also had a strong cotton-weaving industry, exporting muslin and calico to Persia and Europe and printed cloth to Java and Sumatra. In January 1687 Aurangzeb besieged the fort. After eight months it fell, the Qutb Shahi reign ended and the last king, Abul Hasan Qutb Shah, was taken captive.

The fort is listed by the Archaeological Survey of India. Inside stand the Jagdamba temple, visited by many Hindu devotees during the Bonalu festival, and the Taramati mosque. About a kilometre north of the outer wall are the Qutb Shahi tombs, in Indo-Islamic style within gardens. The fort, the Charminar and the tombs were submitted to UNESCO in 2010 and are on India's tentative list. The Golconda Artillery Centre of the Indian Army, raised in 1962, lies in and around the fort. In the Renaissance and early modern periods the name Golconda became a byword for vast wealth.
golden-bull-of-1356: The Golden Bull was a decree of the Imperial Diet at Nuremberg and Metz, headed by Emperor Charles IV, which fixed important parts of the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire for more than four hundred years. It was named for the golden seal it carried. The election of the King of the Romans by the chief ecclesiastical and secular princes was already established, but disputes over the process and papal involvement had caused controversy, most recently in 1314, when Louis of Bavaria and Frederick of Austria were elected by opposing sets of electors. Louis had tried to clarify matters in the Declaration of Rhense of 1338, which renounced papal involvement and limited the choice of a king to the prince-electors.

The Bull named the seven prince-electors and set out their largely ceremonial court offices. For the first time in the Empire it stated the principle of majority voting: four of seven votes sufficed to elect a king. The electoral principalities were declared indivisible and their succession regulated, and the electors received a number of privileges. The Bull also regulated the election in detail. It was to be held in Frankfurt, the coronation in Aachen and the first diet of a reign in Nuremberg, and electors who had not agreed within thirty days of taking their oath were to live on bread and water. Chapter 15 outlawed conspiracies and confederations, which meant the city leagues, and most of them were dissolved.

The Bull fixed the electoral vote on the Palatinate branch of the Wittelsbachs rather than on Bavaria, partly because Louis IV was of that branch, and Louis's sons protested. The Habsburgs, rivals of the House of Luxembourg, were left out altogether, and Duke Rudolf IV of Austria had the Privilegium Maius forged in retaliation. The Habsburgs held no electoral vote until they gained Bohemia in 1526. The Bull made no mention of papal confirmation of an election, and Pope Innocent VI did not protest because he needed Charles's support against the Visconti. It also helped the growth of largely independent states in the Empire, a process completed only centuries later. The Golden Bull was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in June 2013.
golden-gate-kyiv: The Golden Gate was the main gate in the 11th-century fortifications of Kyiv, the capital of the Kievan Rus', and one of three built by Yaroslav the Wise, at about the time of the Saint Sophia Cathedral. It was first called the Southern Gate, one of three main entrances to the walled city beside the Ladski and Zhydivski gates, which have not survived. The stone fortifications ran for only 3.5 kilometres. The name was probably given in imitation of the Golden Gate of Constantinople.

Once the Church of the Annunciation, or Blahovist Church, was built beside it, its golden domes were a landmark seen from outside the city, and the gate took the name Golden. Its passage was about 12 metres high and 6 metres wide.

For almost five hundred years the gate served as Kyiv's triumphal arch and a symbol of the city. A church over the passage, mentioned in the chronicle and in Metropolitan Ilarion's Word of Law and Grace, was meant to give the city heavenly protection and was also a place of worship. In 1240 Batu Khan's Golden Horde partly destroyed the gate, which remained in use for ceremonies into the 18th century while gradually falling into ruin. A gate in Vladimir, where Andrei I Bogolyubsky founded his own state, was later given a similar name. In 1832 Metropolitan Eugenius had the ruins excavated and surveyed, and works in the 1970s added a pavilion housing a museum.

Only two wall segments of the original, 24 and 13 metres long, of Roman brick and stone, survive. No images of the original gate survive either. The Soviet authorities rebuilt it completely in 1982, for the 1500th anniversary of Kyiv, a decision that has been intensely controversial because many competing reconstructions had been proposed.

Some art historians called for the reconstruction to be demolished so that the ruins could be seen. The medieval sections are protected as a monument of national significance, while the reconstructed outer parts are not listed. Inside is a branch of the museum Sophia of Kyiv, and a monument to Yaroslav the Wise stands beside it since 1997.
golden-horn: The Golden Horn, Altın Boynuz or Haliç in Turkish, is the estuary of the Alibey and Kağıthane Creeks. It is 7.5 kilometres long and 750 metres across at its widest, and about 35 metres deep where it flows into the Bosphorus. Its waters mark the northern boundary of the peninsula of old Istanbul, the ancient Byzantium and Constantinople, and separate the historic centre from the rest of the city. Its name is understood to refer to its horn-shaped outline. Historians think that the word golden refers either to the riches brought in through its harbour or to the yellow light on the water at sunset. The Turkish name means estuary and derives from the Arabic khaleej, a gulf.

Archaeological finds show a significant urban presence around the Golden Horn from at least the 7th century BCE, with smaller settlements back to 6700 BCE, from ancient ports and ships found during construction of the Yenikapı subway station and the Marmaray tunnel. The deep harbour was an economic and military asset, and Constantine I founded Nova Roma, later Constantinople, on the existing city of Byzantium for the same reason. The Eastern Roman Empire kept its naval headquarters there, and walls were built along the shore against attack from the sea.

A large chain was drawn across the entrance from Constantinople to the old tower of Galata, called the Megàlos Pyrgos by the Byzantines. It was broken or circumvented three times. In the 10th century the Kievan Rus' dragged their longships around Galata and relaunched them in the Horn, and the Byzantines defeated them with Greek fire. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, Venetian ships broke the chain with a ram, and the Latin Crusaders largely destroyed the tower. In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II, having failed to break the chain by force, towed his ships over greased logs past Galata into the estuary. The Genoese built a new tower in 1348, now the Galata Tower.

After the conquest of 1453 Mehmed II resettled Greeks in the Phanar, today's Fener. Balat had been inhabited by Jews in the Byzantine age, and Bayezid II invited the Jews expelled from Spain to settle there. In 1502 Leonardo da Vinci drew a single-span bridge of 240 metres over the Horn for Bayezid II, which was never built. Mehmed II founded the Haliç Shipyard in 1455, which worked into the 1960s.

Both shores of the Golden Horn are now settled, with parks, museums, university campuses, naval facilities and Muslim, Jewish and Christian cemeteries. The inlet is crossed by bridges including the Galata Bridge and the Atatürk Bridge, and ferries link its suburbs. Industrial waste polluted it until the 1980s, and it was later cleaned in two phases.
golden-temple: The Golden Temple, or Harmandir Sahib, stands in Amritsar and is the pre-eminent spiritual site of Sikhism. Guru Ram Das acquired the land for the site, by one account buying it from the village of Tung, by another receiving it as a gift from Emperor Akbar. The pool on the site was completed by Ram Das in 1577, and Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, finished the construction. In 1604 Arjan placed a copy of the Adi Granth in the temple.

The early history is hard to reconstruct for lack of records. The few Persian sources are biased, and the Sikh sources are reverential. Guru Arjan was arrested on the orders of the Mughal emperor Jahangir and executed in 1606. The shrine was repeatedly destroyed by Mughal and Afghan armies and rebuilt by the Sikhs.

The complex centres on the sanctum and the Amrit Sarovar, the pool of nectar, which is about 150 metres square, with the shrine in its middle reached by a causeway. The plan is square with four entrances, which Sikhs take to symbolise the welcome of people of all castes and ethnicities. It is entered by descending rather than ascending. Its architecture shows both Hindu and Islamic influences.

Ranjit Singh took Amritsar in 1802 and announced that he would rebuild the temple in marble and gold; he added marble flooring and the gilding. This is the origin of the name Golden Temple. In front of the sanctum stands the Akal Takht, founded by Guru Hargobind after his father's death, the chief of the five Sikh seats of authority. A langar, a free kitchen, serves vegetarian meals to visitors of every faith.

The complex is understood as the principal shrine and headquarters of Sikhism, and an exception is made to Sikhism's disapproval of pilgrimage because hymns are sung there constantly. Reformers of the Singh Sabha movement removed idols and images from the temple in 1905. After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919, the British transferred management to the elected Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. The Punjabi Suba movement, which led to the state borders of 1966, centred on the complex.

From 1 to 8 June 1984 the Indian Army carried out Operation Blue Star to remove Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and his followers, who had taken refuge in the buildings. Thousands of soldiers, militants and civilians died, and the Akal Takht was destroyed. The complex was rebuilt afterwards.
golestan-palace: The royal citadel of Tehran was built in the reign of Tahmasp I (r. 1524–1576) of the Safavid dynasty. Abbas the Great laid out a large garden in the northern part of its enclosure, later surrounded by a high wall, with a royal residence inside. The palace was later renovated by Karim Khan of the Zand dynasty (r. 1750–1779). Agha Mohammad Khan, founder of the Qajar dynasty, chose Tehran as his capital, and the citadel became the seat of the Qajars (1794–1925), with the palace of Golestan as their official residence. It was rebuilt to its present form in 1865 by Haji Ab ol Hasan Mimar Navai.

The complex is a group of royal buildings within a wall, most of them dating from the 19th century, and it holds Iranian and European crafts and gifts from the 18th to the 20th century. Its halls include the Marble Throne terrace, built in 1747–1751, the Mirror Hall, the Salam Hall and the Ivory Hall, a dining room decorated with gifts to Naser ed-Din Shah from European monarchs. The Edifice of the Sun, begun in 1865, carries a clock given by Queen Victoria. The Abyaz Palace, completed in 1883 to show Ottoman gifts, is neo-baroque and was designed by the shah himself. A photographic archive was created on the shah's order.

In the Pahlavi era (1925–1979) the palace was used for formal receptions. The coronation of Reza Shah in 1926 and that of Mohammad Reza Shah and Shahbanu Farah in 1967 took place in the Salam Hall. Between 1925 and 1945 a large part of the complex was destroyed on Reza Shah's order, because he believed historic Qajar palaces should not hinder the growth of a modern city, and commercial buildings were put up in their place. UNESCO proclaimed the palace a World Heritage Site on 23 June 2013 at a meeting in Phnom Penh.
goliath: Goliath is attested in the Biblical narratives of 1 and 2 Samuel. The Dead Sea Scrolls text of Samuel, Josephus and the Septuagint give his height as four cubits and a span, about 2.06 metres, while the Masoretic Text has six cubits and a span, about 2.97 metres. Many scholars think the smaller number grew in transmission. The name Goliath is not Semitic and has been linked with that of the Lydian king Alyattes. Tell es-Safi, the biblical Gath, was one of the largest Philistine cities until its destruction in the 9th century BCE. A potsherd found there, dated between the 10th and mid-9th centuries BCE, bears the names ʾLWT and WLT, which are etymologically related to Goliath.

In 1 Samuel 17 Saul and the Israelites face the Philistines in the Valley of Elah. For forty days Goliath comes out between the lines each morning and evening and challenges the Israelites to send a champion to decide the matter in single combat. Saul is afraid. David, a young shepherd, accepts, declines Saul's armour and takes his staff, sling and five stones from a brook.

Goliath curses him by his gods, and David answers that the battle is the Lord's. David's stone strikes Goliath in the forehead and David cuts off his head with Goliath's own sword. The Philistines flee, pursued as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron. Many scholars see the purpose of the story as showing that Saul, a head taller than anyone in Israel yet unwilling to take the challenge, was unfit to be king.

Another verse, 2 Samuel 21:19, says that Elhanan, son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, killed Goliath the Gittite. Most scholars regard this as the older account, which the authors of the Deuteronomistic history reworked to credit David.

The armour described in 1 Samuel 17 resembles Greek armour of the 6th century BCE, and a similar story appears in the Iliad, where Nestor recalls conquering the giant Ereuthalion. Other scholars hold that the description fits a Philistine warrior of the 10th century BCE. The Babylonian Talmud makes Goliath a son of Orpah, the sister-in-law of Ruth. The phrase David and Goliath has come to describe a smaller, weaker opponent facing a much stronger one.
gonaives: Gonaïves lies on a flood plain, below mountains that are largely unforested. Even among Haiti's port cities it has long been vulnerable to hurricanes for this reason. The Gulf of Gonâve takes its name from the town, which is also called Les Gonaïves, and in Haitian Creole Gonayiv.

The city was founded around 1422 by a group of Taíno, who named it Gonaibo, a locality of the cacicat of the Jaragua. In 1802 the Battle of Ravine-à-Couleuvres, an important engagement of the Haitian Revolution, was fought near it.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent from France on 1 January 1804 by reading the Act of Independence, drafted by Boisrond Tonnerre, on the Place d'Armes of the town. His wife, Marie-Claire Heureuse Félicité, died in Gonaïves in August 1858.

In the early 2000s the city saw substantial rioting and violence, motivated mainly by opposition to President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. On 5 February 2004 a group calling itself the Revolutionary Artibonite Resistance Front seized control of the city, which began the 2004 Haitian rebellion.

Storms struck the city twice in four years. In September 2004 Hurricane Jeanne caused major flooding and mudslides. Four years later Hurricane Hanna devastated it again and killed 529 people, mostly in the flooded parts of Gonaïves, where the destruction was described as catastrophic. At least 48,000 people from the Gonaïves area were forced into shelters, according to the mayor, Stephen Moise.

Gonaïves is a commune of Haiti and the capital of the Artibonite department. Its population was 356,324 at the 2015 census. The city has a public university, the Université Publique de l'Artibonite aux Gonaïves, as well as a law and economics school and La Providence Hospital. Its association football clubs include Eclair AC and Racing FC.
gondar: Gondar lies in the North Gondar Zone of the Amhara Region, north of Lake Tana on the Lesser Angereb River and south-west of the Simien Mountains. The name is first recorded under Amda Seyon I as that of a regiment stationed, probably in Wegera, to guard trade routes and control a restive population. In 1636 Emperor Fasilides chose the place as his katama, or royal camp, in the midst of Kémant country. It stood where caravans from Sudan and the Red Sea converged, which brought trading benefits to the court.

Fasilides ordered the building of Fasil Ghebbi, or Fasilides Castle, and founded five other churches. In 1648 a Yemeni ambassador, Hassan ibn Ahmad al-Haymi, described the palace as a great house of stone and lime. By Fasilides' death in 1667 the city was so well established that his successor Yohannes I did not seek a new capital. In 1669-1670 Yohannes ordered Muslims and Jews to live apart from Christians in quarters of their own. Iyasu I (1682-1706) added a castle and several churches, and under him the population was estimated to exceed 60,000. The French physician Charles Poncet was the first European observer to describe the city.

After the death of Iyasu I in 1706 the city declined. Oromo influence grew, and the warlord Ras Mikael Sehul became master of Gondar, killing Emperor Iyoas I in May 1767. The empire then entered the period of weak central rule known as the Zemene Mesafint. Early in the 19th century soldiers plundered the city repeatedly, and in 1864 Emperor Tewodros II ordered it violently sacked, calling it a town of priests who did not love him. Mahdist forces from Sudan burned its churches in January 1888 and attacked again the following June. The population, over 60,000 in the 18th century, was said to have shrunk to 8,000 in the 1870s.

Italian forces occupied Gondar without a fight on 1 April 1936, during the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. They laid out a piazza, new roads and buildings in the modernist style of the 1930s, and about 2,000 Europeans settled there within two years. British and Italian forces fought in the city from 13 to 17 November 1941.

Gondar has about 44 churches, more than any other Ethiopian settlement for many years, and is a centre of learning of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Its region is the homeland of most Ethiopian Jews. Fasil Ghebbi holds Fasilides' castle, Iyasu's palace, Dawit's Hall, Empress Mentewab's castle and three churches. Nearby are Fasilides' Bath, blessed each year in a ceremony, and the Debre Berhan Selassie Church. The University of Gondar includes Ethiopia's main faculty of medicine.
good-friday-agreement: When the Irish Free State was established in 1922, six northern counties of the island remained in the United Kingdom. In the decades that followed there were tensions, sometimes violent, between unionists who wished to remain with Britain and nationalists who wanted unification with the Free State, later the Republic of Ireland. From the late 1960s the conflict, known as the Troubles, became more intense, and over 3,500 deaths were attributed to it in more than thirty years.

Serious political efforts to end it began in the late 1980s, and ceasefires were declared and later broken. The talks that produced the Agreement were chaired by the United States special envoy George J. Mitchell, with Tony Blair and Bertie Ahern as the British and Irish leaders and Mo Mowlam as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland.

The Agreement consists of two documents agreed in Belfast on 10 April 1998: the Multi-Party Agreement between most Northern Ireland parties and the two governments, and the British–Irish Agreement between the governments. Among the eight parties were the Ulster Unionist Party, the Social Democratic and Labour Party, Sinn Féin and the Alliance Party. The Democratic Unionist Party was the only major group to oppose it.

It acknowledged as legitimate both the wish of a majority in Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom and the wish of many to see a united Ireland. Northern Ireland would stay in the United Kingdom until majorities in both Northern Ireland and the Republic wished otherwise. Strand 1 set up an Assembly and a power-sharing Executive, Strand 2 the North/South Ministerial Council, and Strand 3 the British–Irish Council. Participants committed to decommissioning of paramilitary arms, police reform and the early release of prisoners from groups keeping a ceasefire. A total of 428 were released by 28 July 2000.

Both parts of Ireland voted on 22 May 1998. In Northern Ireland turnout was 81% and 71% of votes were in favour, and in the Republic 56% voted and 94% supported the constitutional amendment, which removed the territorial claim in Articles 2 and 3. The British–Irish Agreement came into force on 2 December 1999, when power was devolved to the Assembly and direct rule from Westminster ended.

The Assembly has been suspended several times, sometimes for years, and parts of the rights provisions, such as a Bill of Rights for Northern Ireland, have not been fully implemented. Because it binds the British government on points of law, the Agreement has become part of the constitution of the United Kingdom.
gopal-krishna-gokhale: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was born on 9 May 1866 in Kotluk village in Ratnagiri district, then part of the Bombay Presidency. His family was relatively poor, but it made sure he received an English education, and he belonged to one of the first generations of Indians to attend a university. He studied at Rajaram College in Kolhapur and graduated from Elphinstone College in 1884. He became an admirer of Western political thinkers such as John Stuart Mill and Edmund Burke, and was deeply influenced by the social work of Justice Mahadev Govind Ranade.

Gokhale joined the Indian National Congress in 1889. He was a moderate who sought to petition the British authorities and win greater respect for Indian rights through dialogue. He later became joint secretary of Congress with Bal Gangadhar Tilak, whose early career had run parallel to his own, though they differed over methods: Tilak favoured protest, boycott and agitation. Their disagreement over the Age of Consent Bill of 1891–92, which Gokhale supported, and over control of the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha led Gokhale to found the Deccan Sabha in 1896.

He sat on the Bombay Legislative Council from 1899 and on the Imperial Council of the Governor-General from 1901. His statements before the Welby Commission and his budget speeches, rich in statistics, won praise, and he played a leading part in the Morley-Minto Reforms. At the Surat session of 1907, when rival camps backed different presidential candidates, the Congress split amid scuffles; Gokhale stood beside Tilak to protect him.

In 1905, as Congress president, he founded the Servants of India Society to promote Indian education. He also campaigned against indentured labour, and in 1910 his resolution in the Imperial Legislative Council helped end indentured migration to Natal.

Gokhale visited South Africa in 1912 at Mahatma Gandhi's invitation, and Gandhi's autobiography calls him his mentor and guide. Gandhi nonetheless rejected his faith in Western institutions and did not join the Servants of India Society. Gokhale, deeply concerned about the split of the Congress, hoped to see it reunited. He died on 19 February 1915, and Tilak paid tribute to him in an editorial in Kesari.
goppingen: Göppingen is part of the Stuttgart Region of Baden-Württemberg and the capital of the district of Göppingen. It lies at the foot of the Hohenstaufen mountain, in the valley of the river Fils. Its districts are Bartenbach, Bezgenriet, Faurndau, Hohenstaufen, Holzheim, Jebenhausen and Maitis, besides Göppingen itself.

Tradition holds that the town was founded by an Alemannic leader called Geppo in the 3rd or 4th century. A fire on 25 August 1782 destroyed most of it, and it was rebuilt at once. Industrialisation in the 19th century made the area a centre of industry, and companies such as Märklin and Schuler show its importance still.

Göppingen and the nearby village of Jebenhausen had a Jewish community from 1777 until the Holocaust. In that year the Baron von Liebenstein issued a letter of protection allowing Elias Gutmann and other Jews to settle in Jebenhausen. The community peaked in the middle of the 19th century, when its centre shifted from Jebenhausen to Göppingen, and many families emigrated to America by the late 19th century. The synagogue built in 1881 was destroyed in the Kristallnacht of 9 and 10 November 1938. Rabbi Aron Tänzer, who served the community from 1907 to 1937, collected detailed records and published a history of the Jews of Jebenhausen and Göppingen in 1927. The Jewish Museum in Jebenhausen opened in 1992.

A civilian airfield built north of the town in 1930 was taken over by the Luftwaffe in 1935 and expanded into a barracks. From 1945 to 1949 it housed displaced persons and refugees. It was renamed Cooke Barracks in 1949, and from late 1950 United States Army units were stationed there, among them divisions that used it as headquarters. The barracks were returned to the German government in 1992 and later returned to civilian use.

Göppingen is the home of the toy company Märklin and the headquarters of TeamViewer. The local handball club Frisch Auf Göppingen plays in the men's top division of the Handball-Bundesliga. The town has its own daily newspaper, the Neue Württembergische Zeitung, and its twin towns are Foggia in Italy, Klosterneuburg in Austria, Pessac in France and Sonneberg in Germany. Among its natives are the mathematician and astronomer Michael Maestlin, the mentor of Johannes Kepler, and the pietist theologian Friedrich Christoph Oetinger.
gordian-i: Gordian I's cognomen suggests that his family came from Anatolia, more specifically Galatia or Cappadocia, and his name Marcus Antonius suggests ancestors who received Roman citizenship under Mark Antony. The Historia Augusta, an unreliable source, names his mother as Ulpia Gordiana and his father as the senator Maecius Marullus; many modern historians dismiss the father's name as false. His career began relatively late in life. He commanded the Legio IV Scythica when it was stationed in Syria, governed Roman Britain in 216 and was a suffect consul during the reign of Elagabalus. Inscriptions in Britain bearing his name were partly erased, which may show imperial displeasure.

He gained great popularity through the games and shows he produced as aedile, and his retired life did not arouse the suspicion of Caracalla, in whose honour he wrote a long epic poem, the Antoninias. He kept his wealth and political influence through the chaotic years of the Severan dynasty, which suggests a dislike of intrigue. Philostratus dedicated his Lives of the Sophists to either him or his son. Under Alexander Severus he drew lots for the proconsular governorship of Africa Proconsularis and took it up in 237, by which time he was in his late sixties.

Maximinus Thrax had killed Alexander Severus at Mogontiacum and become emperor, and his oppressive rule bred discontent. In 238 a revolt broke out in Africa after Maximinus' fiscal curator was murdered in a riot. The people demanded that Gordian accept the throne, and he yielded to the clamour and took the cognomen Africanus; Herodian puts his age at about eighty. Because of his age he insisted that his son be associated with him. He entered Carthage with the support of the population and local leaders, and an embassy under Publius Licinius Valerianus won the Senate's confirmation, and many provinces sided with him.

Opposition came from Numidia, where the governor Capelianus, a loyal supporter of Maximinus, invaded the African province with the Legio III Augusta and veteran units. Gordian II, leading an untrained militia, lost the Battle of Carthage and was killed. Gordian I hanged himself with his belt. The two had reigned only 22 days, the shortest reign of any Roman emperor, and Gordian I was the first emperor to commit suicide since Otho in 69.

His reputation rests on his reportedly amiable character and his fondness for literature, though neither he nor his son had the skills or resources of capable rulers. The Senate, having embraced his cause, had to continue the revolt and appointed Pupienus and Balbinus as joint emperors, and by the end of 238 the recognised emperor was Gordian III, his grandson.
gordian-ii: Gordian II, in Latin Marcus Antonius Gordianus Sempronianus Romanus, was the only known son of Gordian I, who was said to be related to prominent senators. His first two names suggest that his paternal ancestors received Roman citizenship under Mark Antony or one of his daughters, and his cognomen Gordianus suggests family origins in Anatolia, especially Galatia and Cappadocia. His younger sister Maecia Faustina was the mother of the later emperor Gordian III.

The only surviving account of his early career is the Historia Augusta, a source that cannot be taken as reliable. It has him serve as quaestor under Elagabalus and as praetor and consul suffect under Severus Alexander, and it names his mother as Fabia Orestilla, a descendant of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, a claim modern historians dismiss. Some evidence suggests that his mother may instead have been a granddaughter of the Greek sophist Herodes Atticus. In 237 or 238 he went to the province of Africa Proconsularis as legate under his father, the proconsular governor.

Early in 235 mutinous troops at Moguntiacum, now Mainz, killed Emperor Severus Alexander and his mother Julia Avita Mamaea, and their leader Maximinus Thrax became emperor despite the disapproval of the Senate. In 238, probably at the end of March, a local elite that had just killed Maximinus's procurator forced Gordian I into a full-scale revolt. Because of his father's age, the younger Gordian, said to be 46, was joined to the throne and acclaimed augustus, and like his father received the cognomen Africanus. Because Maximinus was unpopular, the Senate and most of the other provinces ratified their claim.

Opposition came from the neighbouring province of Numidia. Its governor Capelianus, a loyal supporter of Maximinus who held a grudge against Gordian, invaded Africa with the legion III Augusta, the only legion stationed in the region, and other veteran units. Gordian II led a militia of untrained soldiers, lost the Battle of Carthage and was killed. According to the Historia Augusta his body was never recovered. On hearing the news his father killed himself.

Gordian II died in April 238, and because he died before his father his reign of about 22 days is the shortest recorded of any Roman emperor. The rebellion failed, but by the end of 238 his nephew Gordian III was recognised as emperor by the whole Roman world. Edward Gibbon, in The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, wrote that twenty-two acknowledged concubines and a library of sixty-two thousand volumes attested to the variety of his inclinations.
gordian-iii: Gordian III was born on 20 January 225, the son of Maecia Faustina, daughter of Emperor Gordian I and sister of Emperor Gordian II, and her husband Junius Balbus, who died before 238. Their names come from the unreliable Historia Augusta, and very little is known of his early life before his acclamation. In 238 a rebellion in the province of Africa proclaimed his grandfather and uncle joint emperors against Maximinus Thrax, but it was suppressed within a month by Cappellianus, the governor of Numidia and a loyal supporter of Maximinus.

The Senate, hostile to Maximinus, elected Pupienus and Balbinus as joint emperors. As these senators were not popular, it raised Gordian to the rank of Caesar. Maximinus' march met difficulties in an Alpine winter, and at Aquileia, short of supplies, he besieged the city; after four weeks his demoralized army mutinied and the Legio II Parthica murdered him. Pupienus and Balbinus then faced popular riots, military discontent and an enormous fire in Rome, and the Praetorian Guard killed them. Gordian was proclaimed sole emperor, probably around August, at the age of 13. Because of his youth, the imperial government passed to the aristocratic families who controlled Rome through the Senate.

In 240 Sabinianus revolted in Africa but was quickly defeated. In 241 Gordian married Furia Sabinia Tranquillina, daughter of the newly appointed praetorian prefect Timesitheus, who as father-in-law and chief of the Guard became the de facto ruler of the empire. Severe earthquakes in his reign led him to consult the Sibylline Books.

When the Sasanians under Shapur I invaded Mesopotamia, Gordian opened the doors of the Temple of Janus for the last time in Roman history and sent a large army east. The Sasanians were driven back over the Euphrates and defeated at the Battle of Resaena in 243. Timesitheus then died in unclear circumstances, and Gaius Julius Priscus and later his brother Marcus Julius Philippus, Philip the Arab, became the Praetorian Prefects. Around February 244 the Sasanians fought hard to halt the Roman advance to Ctesiphon.

The accounts of Gordian's fate differ. An inscription of Shapur I claims a major Sasanian victory near modern Fallujah and Gordian's death. Roman sources say the soldiers proclaimed Philip emperor, that he made a shameful peace, and that Gordian died as the army left; Zonaras says he fell from his horse in battle. One view holds that he was murdered by his frustrated army at Zaitha, and scholars regard the Sasanian version as better than the Roman one. Accounts of his burial also differ: David S. Potter says Philip brought the body to Rome and arranged his deification, while Edwell, Dodgeon and Lieu say it was buried at Zaitha.
gordion: Gordion lies at the site of modern Yassıhüyük, 70 to 80 kilometres south-west of Ankara, where the Sakarya and Porsuk rivers meet. The ancient road between Lydia and Assyria and Babylonia crossed the Sangarius river here. People lived on the site from the Early Bronze Age, about 2300 BCE, until the 4th century CE, and again in the 13th and 14th centuries. The Citadel Mound covers about 13.5 hectares, and at its largest the settlement spread over about 100 hectares.

In the Late Bronze Age Gordion belonged to the Hittite Empire, at the western edge of its heartland. A circuit wall and the East Citadel Gate were built in the Early Phrygian period of the 10th and 9th centuries BCE, and the gate still stands ten metres high, the best preserved in Anatolia. Tumulus W, about 850 BCE, is the first known tumulus burial in Anatolia. The megaron halls on the citadel include some of the earliest known pebble-mosaic floors. A fire about 800 BCE sealed this level. It was once blamed on a Cimmerian attack around 700 BCE, but radiocarbon dating and tree-ring analysis show it was about a century earlier and probably accidental.

After the fire the citadel was rebuilt on a similar plan, and the city grew into the capital of a kingdom controlling much of Asia Minor west of the Halys. Midas was probably on the throne by about 740 BCE, and Assyrian sources of about 718 to 709 BCE call him Mit-ta-a. Tumulus MM, over fifty metres high and about three hundred metres across, was built about 740 BCE. Excavated in 1957, it held a royal burial on purple and golden textiles in a log coffin, with bronze vessels and well-preserved carved wooden furniture. It is generally assumed to be the tomb of Midas' father Gordias.

Cyrus the Great's forces besieged Gordion in 546 BCE, and it passed to the Achaemenid Empire. Alexander the Great came in 333 BCE, and by tradition cut the Gordian Knot, which tied the yoke to the pole of a wagon on the acropolis; a prophecy said that whoever loosened it would rule Asia. Galatians settled there from the mid-3rd century BCE. The site was abandoned in the 1st century BCE and refounded under Rome.

Gustav and Alfred Körte excavated the site in 1900, and the University of Pennsylvania Museum worked there from 1950 under Rodney S. Young. Finds are displayed in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations in Ankara, the Istanbul Archaeological Museums and the Gordion Museum in Yassıhöyük. Gordion was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
gorgan: The present city of Gorgan is the capital of Golestan province and lies about 400 km north-east of Tehran and some 30 km from the Caspian Sea. North of it stretches the wide Dasht-e Gorgan, the Plain of Gorgan. The city has hot, humid summers and cool, wet winters, with about 584 millimetres of rain a year, while the Gorgan valley has a semi-arid climate. Some 150 km to the east is the Golestan National Park.

More than 50 archaeological sites lie on the Gorgan Plain, among them Tureng Tepe and Shah Tepe, with remains from the Neolithic and Chalcolithic periods. According to the Greek historian Arrian, Zadracarta was the largest city of Hyrcania and the site of its royal palace. Hyrcania became part of the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great or his successor Cambyses. The Great Wall of Gorgan was built in the Parthian and Sasanian periods, and under the Sasanians the name Gurgan was used for a city, a provincial capital and a province.

The region kept its independence as a Zoroastrian state even after the Arab conquest of Persia in the 7th century. In 1210 the city was invaded and sacked by the army of the Kingdom of Georgia under the Mkhargrdzeli brothers. Old Gorgan was destroyed during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century, and the centre of the region moved to Astarabad, which is the city now called Gorgan. Astarabad was an important political and religious city in the Qajar era.

The census of 2016 counted 350,676 people in the city, against 269,226 in 2006. It has several universities, among them Golestan University and Gorgan University. Among the people the city counts as its own are the 11th-century poet Fakhroddin Asaad Gorgani, composer of Vis and Ramin, the 11th-century grammarian Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani, and Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, Shah of Iran from 1789 to 1797.
gorgias: Gorgias was born about 483 BCE in Leontinoi, a Chalcidian colony in eastern Sicily allied with Athens. His brother Herodicus was a physician who sometimes travelled with him. Several ancient writers report that he studied under the philosopher Empedocles of Acragas, though it is not known when or for how long. In 427 BCE, when he was about sixty, his fellow citizens sent him to Athens as head of an embassy to ask for protection against Syracusan aggression.

After 427 BCE he seems to have settled in mainland Greece, living in several cities including Athens and Larisa. He was an itinerant teacher who gave public displays at Olympia and Delphi and charged fees. According to Aristotle his pupils included Isocrates, and he is thought to have influenced Thucydides and the tragic poet Agathon.

Gorgias is credited with bringing rhetoric from Sicily to Attica and with spreading the Attic dialect as the language of literary prose. He is held to be the first orator known to develop and teach a distinctive style, and he introduced paradoxical expression, called paradoxologia. His surviving rhetorical works are the Encomium of Helen, the Defense of Palamedes, On Non-Existence and the Epitaphios, which come to us through a rhetorical manual called the Technai; only the first two are believed to survive complete.

In the Encomium he argues that Helen should not be blamed for going to Troy, whether the gods, force, love or speech led her, and he compares the effect of speech on the soul to that of drugs on the body. The lost On Non-Existence is known only from paraphrases by Sextus Empiricus and the author of On Melissus, Xenophanes, and Gorgias. It argued that nothing exists, that if it did it could not be known, and that if known it could not be communicated. Because of it he has been called a nihilist, a label that most recent scholars reject.

Gorgias is reputed to have lived past a hundred. A gold statue of him was set up in the temple of Apollo at Delphi after his Pythian Oration. He died at Larisa in Thessaly. In antiquity Plato named a dialogue after him and portrayed him as a shallow orator, and Aristotle called him a sophist who aimed at profit. For most of western history he was a marginal figure, until writers in the nineteenth century, among them Hegel and George Grote, began to rehabilitate the sophists.
gorgon: According to Hesiod and Apollodorus, the Gorgons were daughters of the sea-god Phorcys and the sea-monster Ceto, and sisters of the Graeae. Hyginus makes them daughters of a single Gorgon, offspring of Typhon and Echidna. In Euripides' Ion the Gorgon is a child of Gaia, born to help the Giants against the Olympian gods. The name is associated with the Greek adjective gorgós, meaning grim, fierce or awesome when said of an eye or look. Where the Gorgons lived varies in the sources: Hesiod puts them far to the west beyond Oceanus, and Aeschylus in the far east on the plains of Cisthene.

Stheno and Euryale were immortal, but Medusa was mortal. In Apollodorus' version Polydectes ordered Perseus to bring back Medusa's head. Guided by Hermes and Athena, Perseus took the one eye and one tooth the Graeae shared and so learned the way to the nymphs, who gave him winged sandals and the cap of Hades. Hermes gave him an adamantine sickle. Perseus found the Gorgons asleep and beheaded Medusa while looking at her reflection in his bronze shield. Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from her neck. He gave the head to Athena, who set it on her aegis.

Homer and Hesiod, around 700 to 650 BCE, give the earliest literary accounts. In the Iliad the Gorgon is a dread monster whose head on the aegis is grim and glaring. Apollodorus describes Gorgons with dragon scales, tusks like a swine's, brazen hands and golden wings. By the 5th century BCE Pindar could call Medusa beautiful, and Ovid says she was once a beautiful maiden whom Minerva punished by turning her hair into snakes.

Gorgons were a popular subject in Greek, Etruscan and Roman art, with over six hundred representations catalogued. The earliest, of the mid-7th century BCE, are a Boeotian relief pithos and the Eleusis Amphora. Archaic Gorgons have snaky hair, menacing eyes, wide mouths with lolling tongues and tusks, and the head always faces the viewer.

The gorgoneion, the face alone, is the most frequent of Greek demon images. It is thought to have protected the object that bore it, and it appears on temple pediments, antefixes, shields, coins and the bases of cups. From the 5th century BCE Gorgons were increasingly shown as beautiful young women, and after the 4th century BCE full-bodied Gorgons were no longer made.
goris: Goris lies in the valley of the Goris, or Vararak, River, surrounded by the Zangezur Mountains, at an average elevation of 1,385 metres. It is 254 kilometres from Yerevan and 67 kilometres from Kapan, the provincial capital. The mountains to the south and east are known for medieval cave dwellings carved from the soft rock. The place has been called Kores and Gorayk, and one explanation derives the name from Indo-European prelanguage words for rock and to be, meaning a rocky place.

The area has been settled since the Stone Age. A cuneiform inscription of King Rusa I of Urartu, who reigned from 735 to 713 BCE, names Guria or Goriaya among 23 countries he conquered, and some scholars connect it with Goris. In the Middle Ages the settlement, called Kores, stood on the left bank of the river and appears in Stepanos Orbelian's 13th-century History of the Province of Syunik. In the early 16th century the region became part of Safavid Persia, and in 1813 the Treaty of Gulistan gave it to the Russian Empire.

The Russians founded the town in 1870 as the centre of the Zangezur uezd, and the new town was completed in 1876 near old Kores to a plan by a German architect. After the fall of the First Republic of Armenia in 1920, a congress at Tatev declared the Republic of Mountainous Armenia on 26 April 1921, with Goris as its de facto capital and Garegin Nzhdeh as leader. It capitulated on 13 July 1921 after Red Army operations, on Soviet promises to keep Zangezur in Soviet Armenia. Under Soviet rule the town was a regional centre, and its economy grew with hydroelectric plants and new industry.

Goris is a town in Syunik Province and the seat of the Diocese of Syunik of the Armenian Apostolic Church. The Cathedral of Saint Gregory the Illuminator was built between 1897 and 1904, and in February 1921 Nzhdeh was announced there as commander of the forces of the coming republic. The stone pyramids of Old Kores and the 4th-century basilica of Saint Hripsime stand in the old town. The archaeological museum opened in 1948, and a house museum of the writer Axel Bakunts has operated since 1970.
gorizia: Gorizia stands at the foot of the Julian Alps and the confluence of the Isonzo and Vipava valleys, on the border with Slovenia. Its name comes from the Slovene word gorica, little mountain. The place began as a watchtower or castle controlling the fords of the Isonzo. Sheltered from the cold bora wind, the town has a mild climate, and in the 19th century it was a summer resort of the Austrian nobility.

The name Goriza was first recorded on 28 April 1001, when Emperor Otto III gave the castle and village to the Patriarch of Aquileia and Count Verihen of Friuli. Count Meinhard is mentioned in 1107 and by 1127 styled himself Count of Gorizia. Between the 12th century and the early 16th, the town was the centre of the essentially independent County of Gorizia, whose lands at their height reached from Friuli and Istria to western Carinthia and East Tyrol.

The dynasty of the counts died out in 1500 and the county passed to Habsburg rule, after a short Venetian occupation in 1508 and 1509. Friulian, German and Slovene were all spoken in the town. The Archdiocese of Gorizia was established in 1751 after the suppression of the Patriarchate of Aquileia. Before the First World War the town had around 31,000 inhabitants, of whom about 48 percent spoke Italian or Friulian and 35 percent Slovene.

Italy entered the war in May 1915, and the hills west of the town became a scene of fierce battles on the Isonzo front. Italian forces took Gorizia in August 1916, and Austro-Hungarian forces regained it after Caporetto in 1917. It became part of Italy in 1920, and under the Fascist regime Slovene organisations were dissolved and the public use of Slovene was prohibited. After the Second World War the frontier of 1947 left Italy the old town and gave Yugoslavia about half the municipality's prewar area. Slovenia built Nova Gorica on its side from 1948.

Gorizia is a town of 33,620 people in the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Italy and Slovenia no longer control movement across their frontier since Slovenia joined the Schengen area on 21 December 2007, and Gorizia, Nova Gorica and Šempeter-Vrtojba form a cross-border metropolitan zone. Its sights include the medieval castle and Transalpina Square, divided by the border.
gorlitz: Görlitz lies on the Lusatian Neisse and is the largest town in Upper Lusatia and the easternmost town in Germany. Slavs settled the area in the Early Middle Ages and the Sorbs, a Slavic people, founded the town, as its name shows: it probably derives from a Slavic word for burned land, referring to a method of clearing land. Opposite stands the Polish town of Zgorzelec, which was the eastern part of Görlitz until 1945.

Görlitz, as Goreliz, was first mentioned in a document of Henry IV in 1071. It stood on the Via Regia, the old trade route linking western and eastern Europe, and the settlement gradually became a town in the 13th century. It passed between Bohemia and the Piast Duchy of Jawor before falling back to Bohemia in 1329. From 1346 it was a wealthy member of the Lusatian League with Bautzen, Kamenz, Lubań, Löbau and Zittau, and it was the capital of a duchy from 1377 to 1396.

The Reformation arrived in the early 1520s and the town became almost wholly Lutheran. In 1547 Ferdinand I, as King of Bohemia, punished it for disobedience in the Schmalkaldic War, taking away customs and toll rights. In 1635, in the Thirty Years' War, Upper Lusatia was ceded to the Electorate of Saxony. After the Napoleonic Wars the Congress of Vienna gave the town to Prussia in 1815, and it was administered within Silesia until 1945.

In March 1933 the SA set up the Leschwitz concentration camp in the town, dissolved that August. During the Kristallnacht of November 1938 the synagogue was set on fire but survived, because firefighters ignored the order not to put out the blaze, and it is the only synagogue in present-day Saxony to have outlasted Nazi rule. The number of Jews fell from 567 in 1925 to 134 in 1939. The town was spared major destruction in the war, but the Oder–Neisse line of 1945 divided it, and the eastern bank became Zgorzelec in Poland.

Görlitz has about 56,000 inhabitants and, with Zgorzelec, forms the Euro City of Görlitz/Zgorzelec. The border was open to visa-free travel from 1972 until East Germany closed it in 1980, and movement became unrestricted again when Poland joined the Schengen area on 20 December 2007. The old town has Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Neoclassical and Art Nouveau buildings, among them the Schönhof, one of the oldest civic Renaissance buildings in Germany, and the Silesian Museum.
gorm-the-old: Gorm was born before 900. He is reported to have been the son of the Danish king Harthacnut, who according to the chronicler Adam of Bremen came from Northmannia to Denmark in the early 10th century and deposed the young king Sigtrygg Gnupasson. Heimskringla has Gorm taking at least part of the kingdom from Gnupa by force, and Adam suggests the kingdom had been divided before his time. His name is a contraction of a traditional Germanic compound name, and suggested origins include Old Norse words for god and snake. He is also called Gorm the Languid.

Gorm is first mentioned in 936 as host of Archbishop Unni of Hamburg and Bremen. Because the Jelling Stones say that his son Harald Bluetooth won all of Denmark, it has been suggested that Gorm ruled only Jutland from his seat at Jelling. He married Thyra, whose parentage is given inconsistently by late sources.
