For her he raised one of the great burial mounds at Jelling and the oldest of the Jelling Stones, calling her tanmarkar but, Denmark's salvation or adornment. They had three sons, Toke, Knut and Harald. Saxo Grammaticus credits Thyra with building the Dannevirke, but excavations since 2010 show that its oldest phase dates from about 500 CE or earlier.

One theory puts his death in the winter of 958-959, since tree-ring dating shows the burial chamber in the northern mound at Jelling was made from wood felled in 958. A tradition tells that he died of grief the day after learning of the death of his son Knut. Some scholars think he was first buried in Thyra's mound and later moved by Harald into the first wooden church at Jelling, though this is much debated. In Gorm's time most Danes still worshipped the Norse gods, and under Harald Denmark officially became Christian. Gorm was called old because he was regarded as the ancestral head of the Danish monarchy.
gorno-badakhshan-autonomous-region: The official English name of the region is the Badakhshan Mountainous Autonomous Region. Gorno-Badakhshan is the Russian form and means mountainous Badakhshan, while Badakhshan itself derives from the Sasanian title bēdaxš or badaxš. The region makes up nearly forty-five percent of Tajikistan's land but only two percent of its population. It borders China's Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region to the east, Afghanistan's Badakhshan Province to the south and Kyrgyzstan's Osh Region to the north.

Its highest ground lies in the Pamir Mountains, which local people call the roof of the world. Three of the five peaks over 7,000 metres in Central Asia stand here, among them Ismoil Somoni Peak (7,495 metres), formerly Communism Peak and before that Stalin Peak. Its districts correspond to river valleys, while Murghob District, in the eastern two-thirds, is a desolate plateau.

Borders and authority in the Western Pamir were long contested by imperial powers. Between the 17th and 19th centuries several semi-self-governing statelets, including Darwaz, Shughnun-Rushan and Wakhan, ruled the lands that now lie partly in Tajikistan and partly in Afghanistan. In the late 19th century the emirates of Kokand and then Bukhara held authority until Russia completed its colonisation of the Western Pamir in 1896. In that year Russia and the British Empire fixed their shared border through the Pamir, which produced the Wakhan Corridor.

The region took its present western borders in 1925, within the Tajik Soviet Socialist Republic. Soviet ethnographers fixed the category of Pamiris, or Mountain Tajiks, and the region received resources as a borderland, including the Pamir Highway in 1935, and its people had easier access to higher education and office. When the Tajik civil war broke out in 1992 the local government declared independence, though it later withdrew the claim. The movement La'al-e Badakhshan, which demanded autonomy and democratic rule, joined the United Tajik Opposition in 1997. During the war the Ismaili development organization AKDN brought in supplies from Kyrgyzstan, which prevented starvation. In 2011 Tajikistan ratified a 1999 treaty ceding 1,000 square kilometres in the Pamirs to China.

About 226,900 people live in the region, most of whom identify as Pamiris, with a Kyrgyz minority in Murghob District. Khorog, with about 30,300 inhabitants, is the largest city. Tajik is the state language and Russian the language between peoples, but residents also speak Pamir languages including Shughni, Rushani, Wakhi, Ishkashimi and Sarikoli, several of them on UNESCO's endangered list. Most Pamiris are Ismaili Shia Muslims who follow the Aga Khan, and there are also Sunni Muslims.
gortyn-code: The code, also called the Great Code, is known only from the inscription itself, cut on the circular wall of what may have been a bouleuterion or other public building in the agora of Gortyn. The building was 30 m in diameter; the twelve surviving columns of text are 10 m long and 1.5 m high and hold some 600 lines. It has been dated to the first half of the 5th century BCE.

It belongs to a tradition of Cretan law, the only substantial body of Greek law from antiquity found outside Athens. Earlier laws, of about 600 to 525 BCE, were inscribed on the steps and walls of the temple of Apollo Pythios, and the Great Code is one of a series written on walls in or near the agora between about 525 and 400 BCE.

The code distinguishes the free, the serf, the slave and the foreigner. Anyone bringing a suit is forbidden to seize the accused before trial, on pain of a fine that varies with the status of the person detained. Rape is punished by fines set largely by the difference in status between victim and accused. Adultery is treated similarly, with higher fines when it took place in the house of the woman's father, husband or brother; the fine falls on the man, and the code provides no punishment for the woman.

A divorced woman keeps the property she brought to the marriage and half of the income derived from it. A child conceived before a divorce and born after it belongs to the father and, if he does not accept it, to the mother. A widower holds his wife's property in trust and may not act on it without her children's consent; when a father dies, the land goes to the sons, and a childless widow is compelled to remarry. Adopted children inherit as natural children do, but women may not adopt.

The first fragment was discovered in 1857 by Georges Perrot and Louis Thenon. In 1884 the Italian archaeologist Federico Halbherr found four more columns while excavating near a local mill, and with Ernst Fabricius he uncovered eight further columns whose stones had been reused in the foundations of a Roman odeion of the 1st century BCE. The wall has since been partly reconstructed. All the Cretan legal texts are fragmentary and show continuous amendment, and from them scholars have traced the development of the law, notably the diminishing rights of women and the increasing rights of slaves.
gospel-of-john: The gospel is internally anonymous. It identifies an unnamed 'disciple whom Jesus loved' as its source and, perhaps, its author, a figure who appears at key episodes such as the Last Supper and the Empty Tomb. The traditional attribution to John the Apostle is first found in Irenaeus. Many modern scholars still affirm it, but most prefer alternatives such as John the Elder or Lazarus, while holding that the beloved disciple is the source of much of the content. Most critical commentaries consider that it was probably composed at Ephesus.

The gospel is usually divided into a prologue (1:1 to 1:18), an account of the ministry often called the Book of Signs (1:19 to 12:50), the final night, passion and resurrection (13:1 to 20:31) and an epilogue in chapter 21. The first part presents seven signs that culminate in the raising of Lazarus, and the second the Farewell Discourse and the passion and resurrection. The prologue identifies Jesus as the Logos, the Word, and calls the Word God; it contains some of the clearest identifications of Jesus with God in the New Testament.

It differs from the Synoptic Gospels. The ministry lasts three years, marked by three Passovers, and the cleansing of the Temple comes at its start. The death of Jesus is presented as his glorification and return to the Father, and he speaks of being lifted up. In place of the institution of the Eucharist, Jesus washes his disciples' feet. About 85 percent of its content is unique to it.

There is evidence that the gospel was circulating by the early second century: the First Epistle of John, which depends on it, was cited by Papias of Hierapolis. The attribution to John son of Zebedee was widespread by the mid-second century. Since the 19th century scholars have agreed that its long discourses are less likely to be historical than the Synoptic parables, though it is not without historical value, for example in its topographical references to Jerusalem and Judea. Early in the 20th century many scholars saw Gnostic elements in it, but most now consider the question closed. Augustine of Hippo and Thomas Aquinas wrote commentaries on it.
gospel-of-luke: Together with the Acts of the Apostles the Gospel of Luke forms a two-volume work called Luke–Acts, which makes up 27.5 per cent of the New Testament, the largest share by a single author. The text does not name its author. A church tradition first recorded by Irenaeus (c. 130 – c. 202 CE) identifies him as the Luke named as a companion of Paul in three of the Pauline letters. Most scholars hold that the author met Paul as a travelling companion, though some point to differences between Luke–Acts and the authentic letters of Paul.

Most scholars date the work to about 80–90 CE, since it knows the Gospel of Mark and the destruction of Jerusalem but not the Pauline letters. Mark supplied the narrative outline, and about 550 verses, nearly half the gospel, are found only in Luke. In his preface the author addresses Theophilus, whom most interpreters take to be a Christian convert and literary patron.

After the preface and the birth narratives of John the Baptist and of Jesus, the gospel opens in Galilee, where Jesus preaches the kingdom of God. It then moves to the journey to Jerusalem, its central section, and to the confrontation with the leaders of the Temple, the last supper, the arrest and crucifixion. It ends with the events from the first Easter to the Ascension, which anticipate Acts.

The gospel sets out a salvation history in three stages: the Law and the prophets, the time of Jesus, and the period of the church. The Holy Spirit has a greater part in it than in the other gospels and is the basis of the Christian community. Luke also holds that Christians are no threat to the Roman order.

No original copy of Luke survives. Early manuscripts fall into two families, the Alexandrian and the Western, and the dominant view is that the Western text results from a deliberate revision in the second century. The fragment 𝔓4 is often cited as the oldest, dated to the late second century, although the dating is disputed. Papyrus 75 includes an attribution of the gospel to Luke. The oldest complete texts are the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae gives Luke in Greek and Latin on facing pages.
gotha: Gotha lies in a flat, fertile part of the southern Thuringian Basin, about 20 kilometres west of Erfurt and 25 kilometres east of Eisenach. It is one of the few ancient cities in Germany that does not stand on a river, so water supply was a problem in the Middle Ages. For that reason the Leinakanal, more than 25 kilometres long, was built in the 14th century to bring water from the Hörsel and Apfelstädt rivers.

A document signed by Charlemagne in 775 mentions the place as Villa Gotaha, from Old High German gotaha, meaning good waters. The Ludowingians received the village in the 11th century and founded the city in the late 12th century, making it their second most important city after Eisenach. It lay at the junction of the Via Regia and a north-south route from Mühlhausen to Franconia.

A cache of nearly 800 bracteates buried in 1185 is among the oldest evidence of its trade, and in 1180 it was first mentioned as a city. The Reformation came in 1524. Gotha declined after the Schmalkaldic War of 1547, and in 1572 imperial troops razed its castle, Grimmenstein.

The turn came in 1640, when Ernest the Pious founded the duchy of Saxe-Gotha and made Gotha his residence. In 1642 he introduced compulsory schooling up to the age of 12, which was the origin of the city's liberal education. Friedenstein Castle was built between 1643 and 1654. From 1826 to 1918 Gotha and Coburg were the two capitals of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. After the revolution of 1848 the Gothaer Nachparlament met in the city. In 1875 the SPD was founded there by merging the Social Democratic Workers' Party and the General German Workers' Association. The compromise, the Gotha Program, drew a critique from Karl Marx.

Gotha is the fifth-largest city in Thuringia, with a population of about 46,000, and the capital of the district of Gotha. Friedenstein Castle, one of the largest late Renaissance and early Baroque castles in Germany, holds several museums, including the Ekhof Theatre, a Baroque court theatre with its original stage machinery still working. The city has a museum of the insurance business, which has been important there since 1820, and the Ernestine Gymnasium, the oldest Gymnasium in Thuringia. Vehicle construction remains the leading industry.
gothenburg: Gothenburg lies on the west coast of southwestern Sweden, about halfway between Copenhagen and Oslo, at the mouth of the Göta älv, which feeds into the Kattegat, an arm of the North Sea. Scandinavia's largest drainage basin enters the sea there, and the position has helped the city grow as a trading centre. The archipelago off the city consists of rough, barren rocks and cliffs, typical of the coast of Bohuslän. Because of the Gulf Stream the climate is mild, and warmer than that of places at a similar latitude such as Stockholm.

In the early modern period the shape of Sweden's borders made Gothenburg strategically critical. It was the only Swedish gateway to the Skagerrak, the North Sea and the Atlantic, on a very narrow strip of Swedish territory between Danish Halland in the south and Norwegian Bohuslän in the north. After several failed attempts, King Gustavus Adolphus founded it by royal charter in 1621 as a heavily fortified, primarily Dutch, trading colony. An earlier city founded in 1604 had burned down in 1611.

During the Thirty Years' War he gave generous privileges, such as tax relaxation, to his Dutch allies, and he also attracted German and Scottish allies to populate his only town on the western coast. The city council of 1641 had four Swedish, three Dutch, three German and two Scottish members.

The charter of 1621 named the city Göteborg, after the Göta älv and other cities ending in -borg, and gave it at the same time the German and English name Gothenburg. Its trading status was furthered by the founding of the Swedish East India Company. In the eighteenth century the Company made Gothenburg an important trade city, and imposing stone houses in Neo-Classical style were erected around the canals. In the nineteenth century the wealthy bourgeoisie moved outside the city walls, while the working class lived in wooden houses in the overcrowded district of Haga. Gothenburg became a city municipality with an elected council when the first Swedish local government acts were implemented in 1863.

Gothenburg is the second-largest city in Sweden after Stockholm and the seat of Västra Götaland County. Its port is the largest in the Nordic countries, and trade, shipping and manufacturing have long been the pillars of its economy. Because all but the military and royal houses were built of wood, very few buildings survive from the seventeenth century; among them are Kronhuset, the Torstenson Palace and the fortresses Skansen Kronan and Skansen Lejonet. The East India House now holds the Göteborg City Museum, and the city is home to the University of Gothenburg and Chalmers University of Technology.
gothic-war-535-554: In 476 Odoacer deposed the western emperor Romulus Augustulus and made himself king. The eastern emperor Zeno sent the Ostrogoths of Theodoric the Great to Italy to remove him, and Theodoric ruled Italy as the empire's viceroy. The civil administration was staffed by Romans and the army was exclusively Gothic. The Italo-Romans were Chalcedonian Christians and the Goths Arian Christians, but the Goths practised considerable tolerance. The system worked under Theodoric and collapsed under his heirs.

In 533 Justinian I sent Belisarius to recover North Africa from the Vandals, and the swift victory encouraged him to try to recover the other lost western provinces. Amalasuntha, the Gothic regent, had let the Byzantine fleet use the harbours of Sicily. She was arrested by her cousin Theodahad and killed in early 535, and her death became a casus belli.

Belisarius, with only 7,500 men, landed in Sicily, which fell quickly. He crossed into Italy in 536 and took Naples in November, after about three weeks of siege, and his troops sacked it. The Goths, under their king Vitiges, were pushed back to Ravenna. In 538 Mediolanum, modern Milan, asked for help and was garrisoned, but 10,000 Burgundians sent by Vitiges, with Goths under Uraias, besieged and took it. In 539 a Frankish army of 100,000 crossed the Alps, defeated both Goths and Byzantines, and lost a third of its men to dysentery. Justinian offered a partition of Italy along the Po, which the Goths accepted but Belisarius refused to sign. Ravenna fell in 540.

The war then entered a second phase. Totila led a Gothic revival, helped by the plague that devastated the empire in 542, by war with Persia and by the disunity of the Byzantine generals. He defeated them at Faventia and Mucellium and took the south, and after he took Naples in 543 he treated its defenders and people humanely. By 550 the Goths controlled much of the peninsula. In 553 a Frankish army of about 75,000 invaded, and Narses all but annihilated it at the Volturnus.

In 554 Justinian issued a Pragmatic Sanction setting out Italy's new government, and Narses began a reconstruction. The last strongholds in the north, Verona and Brixia, held out until 562. Italy had been devastated and depopulated, and Rome and Milan became shadows of their former selves. The war is often regarded as a Pyrrhic victory, because it used up resources needed against threats in western Asia and the Balkans, and the Lombards invaded in 568. Some historians note that southern Italy, especially Sicily, recovered considerably and proved profitable to the empire.
goths: The Goths were a Germanic people, belonging with the Burgundians and Vandals to the East Germanic group. A crucial source is the Getica of the 6th-century historian Jordanes. Many scholars accept its claim that the Goths originated in Scandinavia and moved to Poland before settling north of the Black Sea, though how far it reflects Gothic tradition is debated. From the middle of the 2nd century the Wielbark culture shifted south-east towards the Black Sea, and by 200 CE Goths were probably being recruited into the Roman army. Their raids into the empire began with the sack of Histria in 238.

In 332 Constantine helped the Sarmatians settle on the north bank of the Danube against Gothic attacks. Around 375 the Huns overran the Alans and invaded the Gothic lands. Gothic refugees seeking shelter in the Roman Empire were mistreated by corrupt local officials and suffered famine, and Fritigern led a rebellion in Thrace. The Gothic War of 376–382 culminated in the Battle of Adrianople in 378, in which the Romans were badly defeated and Valens was killed.

Two groups then emerged: the Visigoths, led by the Balti dynasty, who lived inside Roman territory, and the Ostrogoths, led by the Amali, who were subjects of the Huns. A group under Alaric I sacked Rome in 410, and the successors of the Visigoths founded a kingdom in Spain at Toledo. Under Theodoric the Great the Ostrogoths established a kingdom in Italy at Ravenna. Byzantium destroyed it in the 6th century, and the Umayyad Caliphate largely conquered the Visigothic kingdom in the early 8th, leaving a remnant in Asturias. The Crimean Goths kept their identity into the 18th century.

Gothic is the Germanic language with the earliest written attestation, from the 4th century, known chiefly from the Codex Argenteus, a partial Bible translation credited to Ulfilas. The Goths were at first pagan and were gradually converted to Arianism in the 4th century through the missionary work of the bishop Ulfilas, who devised a Gothic alphabet. In the 370s the pagan king Athanaric persecuted Goths who converted. Archaeology shows the Visigoths were predominantly farmers growing wheat, barley, rye and flax.
gottfried-keller: Gottfried Keller was born on 19 July 1819. His father Rudolf Keller, a lathe-worker from Glattfelden, died of tuberculosis in 1824, and the family lived in constant poverty. Four of the couple's six children died, so that Keller was left with his sister Regula. His difficulties with his teachers kept him in continual disagreement with the school authorities, and a political mix-up got him expelled from the Industrieschule in Zürich. His first true passion was painting. He was apprenticed in 1834 to the landscape painter Steiger and in 1837 to the watercolourist Rudolf Meyer, and in 1840 he went to Munich to study at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts.

Keller returned to Zürich in 1842 and took up writing, publishing his first poems, Gedichte, in 1846. From 1848 to 1850 he studied at the University of Heidelberg, where the philosopher Feuerbach influenced him. He worked in Berlin from 1850 to 1856 and there chose literature as a career. He published the semi-autobiographical novel Der grüne Heinrich, Green Henry, which draws on his youth and his career as a painter up to 1842. The literary world received it coolly, but the second version of 1879 is a rounded artistic work. He also published his first collection of stories, Die Leute von Seldwyla, Seldwyla Folks, which includes Romeo und Julia auf dem Dorfe, set in a Swiss village.

In 1861 Keller became First Official Secretary of the Canton of Zürich. He published Seven Legends in 1872, the second volume of Seldwyla Folks in 1874 and the Züricher Novellen in 1878. After 15 years in office he retired in 1876 and wrote until his death. Collected Poetry appeared in 1883 and the novel Martin Salander in 1886.

Keller died on 15 July 1890. In his last years he lived as a bachelor with his sister Regula as housekeeper, and despite his reserve he had won the affection of his townspeople. His stories are set in an orderly bourgeois world and tell of the development of character under the relatively free conditions of Switzerland, an ideal that endeared them to German readers. In 1890 Lydia Escher invested the Escher fortune in a foundation named after him, the Gottfried Keller Foundation, which became an important collecting institution for art.
gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz: Gottfried Leibniz was born on 1 July 1646 in Leipzig, in the Electorate of Saxony, to Friedrich Leibniz and Catharina Schmuck. His father, a professor of moral philosophy at the University of Leipzig, died when he was six, and he inherited his father's library, to which he had free access from the age of seven. It let him read advanced philosophical and theological works he would not otherwise have met until college, and it led to his proficiency in Latin by the age of 12. At 13 he composed 300 hexameters of Latin verse in a single morning for a special event at school.

In mathematics Leibniz developed differential and integral calculus independently of Newton. Newton had developed his theory earlier, in 1666, but Leibniz's notation has been favoured as the conventional and more exact expression of calculus. He was the first to use the notion of a function explicitly, in 1692 and 1694, and he is credited with devising the modern binary number system, though the English astronomer Thomas Harriot had devised the same system decades before. In 1685 he was the first to describe a pinwheel calculator.

As a philosopher he dated his beginning to the Discourse on Metaphysics of 1686, and he published only two philosophical books in his lifetime, De Arte Combinatoria and the Théodicée of 1710. His optimism held that our world is, in a qualified sense, the best possible world that God could have created. Against Newton he argued that space, time and motion are relative, not absolute. In 1677 he called for a European confederation governed by a senate, and he noted that the hexagrams of the I Ching correspond to binary numbers.

Leibniz died on 14 November 1716, when his reputation was in decline. He was remembered for only one book, the Théodicée, whose argument Voltaire lampooned in Candide so influentially that many took the satire for an accurate description. His disciple Christian Wolff did him harm, and philosophical fashion was moving away from the rationalism of the 17th century. His reputation began to recover with the publication of his New Essays on Human Understanding in 1765. Only in 1895, when Bodemann completed a catalogue of his manuscripts, did the extent of his literary estate become clear: about 15,000 letters to more than 1,000 recipients and more than 40,000 other items.
gotthard-pass: The pass lies on the main watershed of the Gotthard massif, at the lowest point between the summits of Pizzo Lucendro to the west and Pizzo Centrale to the east. Its summit, at 2,106 metres, is in the canton of Ticino, about 2 kilometres south of the border with Uri. It joins the valley of the Reuss, called the Urseren, to the valley of the Ticino, called the Valle Leventina, with the towns of Andermatt and Airolo on either side. The saddle is a continental divide between the Rhine, which flows to the North Sea, and the Ticino, which reaches the Po and the Adriatic. The pass was formerly known as Monte Tremolo, and its southern slope is still called Val Tremola.

The pass was known locally in antiquity but was not generally used until the early 13th century, because travellers had to ford the turbulent Reuss in the narrow Schöllenen Gorge below Andermatt. Once a wooden bridge crossed the gorge, the pass quickly gained in importance. A chapel dedicated to Saint Gotthard of Hildesheim, patron saint of mountain passes, was built on the southern slope and consecrated by the archbishop of Milan in 1230, and the pass was known by his name by 1236.

The opening of the gorge was an important factor in the early Swiss Confederacy. The regions of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden gained imperial immediacy under the Hohenstaufen emperors, and the Pfaffenbrief of 1370 guaranteed peace along the road from Zürich to the pass. From 1331 the Swiss extended their influence south of the Alps through trade agreements to secure the route to Milan. In 1403 the upper Leventina became a protectorate of Uri, and a struggle with the Duchy of Milan in the 15th century ended in the Swiss conquest of Ticino.

A new road with the 60-metre Urnerloch tunnel, the first road tunnel in the Alps, was built in 1707/8. Only foot traffic and pack animals crossed until 1775, when the first carriage made the journey, and the Battle of Gotthard Pass took place on 24 September 1799.

A road wide enough for single-lane motorised traffic was built in 1830, and the first car is said to have crossed the pass in 1895. Three tunnels now carry most of the traffic beneath the massif, each the world's longest of its kind when built: the 15-kilometre Gotthard Rail Tunnel of 1882, which cost about 200 workers' lives, the 17-kilometre Gotthard Road Tunnel of 1980, and the 57-kilometre Gotthard Base Tunnel of 2016, which gives a nearly level railway route from Erstfeld to Bodio. With the Lötschberg it is one of the two main north-south routes through the Swiss Alps. Near the summit are several lakes, a hospice and a museum.
gotthold-ephraim-lessing: Lessing was born on 22 January 1729 in Kamenz, a small town in Saxony, the son of the Lutheran pastor and theologian Johann Gottfried Lessing. He studied at the Latin School in Kamenz and then at the Fürstenschule St. Afra in Meissen, and in 1746 enrolled at Leipzig University, where he pursued theology, medicine, philosophy and philology. There he met the actress Karoline Neuber, for whom he translated French plays. His first play, The Young Scholar, was produced by her in 1748.

From 1748 to 1760 Lessing lived in Leipzig and Berlin, working as a reviewer and editor for the Vossische Zeitung and other periodicals. In 1750 he and his cousin Christlob Mylius began a theatre journal that ran only four issues but marked him as a serious critic. He took his master's degree at Wittenberg in 1752, and from 1760 to 1765 served as secretary to General Tauentzien in Breslau, where he wrote Laocoön. He then worked at the Hamburg National Theatre as critic of plays and acting, which makes him the first dramaturg; the work formed the basis of the Hamburg Dramaturgy. Financial losses from pirated editions contributed to the theatre's closure.

In 1770 he became librarian at the ducal library in Wolfenbüttel. In 1773 he found Archimedes' cattle problem in a Greek manuscript there; it remained unsolved until 1880. He was initiated into Freemasonry in Hamburg in 1771 and married the widow Eva König in 1776. She died in 1778 after giving birth to a short-lived son. Lessing died on 15 February 1781, aged 52, during a visit to Brunswick.

In his critical writing Lessing turned against the theory of Gottsched and the neoclassical rules of the French Academy, advocated the outline of drama in Aristotle's Poetics and supported serious reception of Shakespeare; his views influenced the Sturm und Drang. Scholars see Miss Sara Sampson and Emilia Galotti as among the first bourgeois tragedies and Minna von Barnhelm as the model for many classic German comedies. In Laocoön he argued that painting is extended in space and poetry in time, so that each has its own character.

Lessing's friendship with Moses Mendelssohn sparked his interest in religious debates. He published fragments of an unpublished manuscript by Hermann Samuel Reimarus attacking the historicity of Christian revelation, which led to a dispute with the pastor Johann Melchior Goeze. Lessing was then silenced by a law ending his freedom from censorship, and in response wrote Nathan the Wise (1779). Its parable of the three rings implies that no single religion is the correct one. In The Education of the Human Race he set out his trust that human reason would develop even without divine revelation.
gottingen: Göttingen began as a village called Gutingi, whose name probably derives from a small stream, the Gote, that once flowed through it. Archaeology points to a settlement as early as the 7th century, with extensive commercial relations and developed craftsmanship. The Holy Roman Emperor Otto I mentioned it in a document of 953. At first it was overshadowed by the fortress of Grona, documented from 915 and used as an Ottonian imperial palace, which had 18 recorded visits by kings and emperors between 941 and 1025. The last emperor to use it, Heinrich II, had a church dedicated to Saint Alban built in Gutingi.

A trading settlement formed at the Leine river crossing to the west of the village, and the city was founded between 1150 and 1200 and took its name from it. The village remained distinct until about 1360, when it was incorporated within the town's fortification. In the Middle Ages Göttingen was a member of the Hanseatic League and a wealthy town. Between 1323 and 1329 its citizens, with their dukes, destroyed the fortress of Grone in battles against aristocratic knights. Under Ernest I the Principality of Göttingen, the poorest of the Welf principalities, remained separate from Brunswick for a long time.

A town council of 24 councillors dates from the 12th century, and in 1319 it took control of the new city district in front of the wall. From 1611 all citizens could elect the 24 councillors, a right previously restricted by income and profession. Later Duke Eric I the Elder annexed the principality into the Principality of Calenberg. The town refused to pay homage to him in 1504, and he had Emperor Maximilian I declare it outlawed; the resulting tensions weakened it economically until it paid homage in 1512. Luther's teachings became popular from 1528, the first Protestant sermon was preached in 1529 in the Paulinerkirche, and for many centuries nearly all of the population were Lutherans. Catholic services resumed in 1746.

Göttingen is a university city in Lower Saxony, the capital of its district, with the river Leine running through it. Its population was 124,548 in the 2022 census, of whom around 24,000 were students in 2004. Between 1772 and 1776 a group of poets who studied at the university formed the Göttinger Hainbund, disciples of Klopstock who revived the folksong and wrote Sturm und Drang lyric poetry, with an impact on German romanticism. Since the 1920s the town has been associated with the revival of interest in Handel's music through the Göttingen International Handel Festival, held each summer. Its coat of arms, first documented in 1278, shows three towers over the lion of the Welf dynasty, which ruled the area for 850 years.
gottlieb-daimler: Gottlieb Daimler was born on 17 March 1834 in Schorndorf, near Stuttgart, the son of a baker. He trained as a gunsmith under Hermann Raithel and passed his trade examination in 1852 with a pair of engraved pistols. The same year he turned to mechanical engineering and enrolled at Stuttgart's School for Advanced Training in the Industrial Arts.

In 1853 he found work at Rollé und Schwilque in Grafenstaden, where he was made foreman in 1856. He then spent two years at the Stuttgart Polytechnic Institute and became convinced that steam would be superseded. From the autumn of 1861 to the summer of 1863 he worked in England, including at Beyer, Peacock and Company in Manchester.

In 1863 Daimler joined the Bruderhaus Reutlingen, where he met the 15-year-old orphan Wilhelm Maybach. In 1872 he became factory manager at Nicolaus Otto's Gasmotoren-Fabrik Deutz and brought Maybach in as chief designer. The two men disagreed over small engines for transport, which Otto did not want, and Daimler was dismissed in 1880 with Deutz shares worth 112,000 gold marks as compensation. In summer 1882 he moved to Cannstatt, where he and Maybach worked in a summer house in the garden. Neighbours reported them to the police as suspected counterfeiters, but the police found only engines.

On 16 December 1883 they patented an engine fuelled by ligroin that ran at 750 rpm. In November 1885 a smaller version fitted to a wooden two-wheeler became the first internal combustion motorcycle, the Reitwagen. On 8 March 1886 they installed an engine in a coach, which became the first four-wheeled vehicle to reach 16 kilometres per hour. Karl Benz had meanwhile built his own automobile, and the two men never met during the period of invention.

Daimler wanted small, fast engines that could serve any form of transport, and he later summed up their uses on land, water and air in a sketch that became the basis of the three-pointed star. In 1886 the engine was used in a boat on the Neckar, the first motorboat, and boat engines became his main product for several years. In 1888 it drove a balloon over the Seelberg. Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft was founded on 28 November 1890.

He resigned in 1893 after disputes with the other directors, and a condition set by Frederick Simms over the British licences brought him back later in the 1890s. Licences went to Panhard et Levassor and Peugeot in France and to a company in the United States. In 1896 Daimler won a patent suit against Benz and Cie over hot tube ignition. He died in 1900. Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft and Benz and Cie merged on 28 June 1926.
gough-whitlam: Edward Gough Whitlam was born on 11 July 1916 in Kew, a suburb of Melbourne, the elder of two children. His father, Fred Whitlam, was a federal public servant who later became Commonwealth Crown Solicitor, and his interest in human rights was a strong influence on his son. The family moved to Sydney in 1918. Soon after the outbreak of war in 1939 Whitlam joined the Sydney University Regiment, and he entered the Royal Australian Air Force on 20 June 1942. That year he married Margaret Dovey.

After the war he practised as a barrister and tried to build a place in the Labor Party at Cronulla, where local supporters doubted him because of his privileged background. He was elected to the House of Representatives for Werriwa at a by-election on 29 November 1952. He became deputy leader in 1960 and leader in 1967, and he sought to widen Labor's appeal from its working-class base to the suburban middle class and to shift control of the party from union officials to the parliamentary party.

Labor won the election of December 1972 after 23 years of Coalition government. Without waiting for the full results, Whitlam had himself and his deputy Lance Barnard sworn in on 5 December as a two-man government, which held 27 portfolios for two weeks. Opposition in the Senate led him to call a double dissolution election in May 1974, followed by the only joint sitting of both houses under section 57 of the constitution. His second term was dominated by the 1973 oil crisis and a recession, and by the Loans affair, which cost two ministers their posts.

In October 1975 the Opposition under Malcolm Fraser deferred the appropriation bills in the Senate, where the Coalition had an effective majority of 30 to 29, and supply was due to run out on 30 November. Whitlam argued that a government with a clear majority in the House of Representatives was being held to ransom. The governor-general, Sir John Kerr, dismissed him in mid-November and commissioned Fraser as caretaker prime minister. Labor lost the election that followed by a landslide.

Whitlam stepped down as leader after losing again in 1977 and resigned from Parliament on 31 July 1978. He served as ambassador to UNESCO in Paris after 1983 and chaired the National Gallery of Australia from 1987. He died on 21 October 2014, and a state memorial service was held at the Sydney Town Hall on 5 November. The circumstances of his dismissal are still debated. Journalist Paul Kelly wrote that Whitlam achieved a paradoxical triumph: the shadow of the dismissal has obscured the sins of his government.
government-of-india: Elected representative government in India began under British rule. Before the Indian Councils Act 1909, known as the Morley-Minto reforms, governance rested with an all-European Legislative Council and the Viceroy's Executive Council, and no Indians sat at high levels of government. The Government of India Act 1919 expanded the Imperial Legislative Council and introduced diarchy in the provinces, and the Government of India Act 1935 brought provincial autonomy and laid the foundation for a federal structure. It was unpopular among Indians because it did not grant full self-rule or dominion status.

Between midnight on 15 August 1947 and 26 January 1950, India was an independent, self-governing dominion of the Commonwealth of Nations. It was a constitutional monarchy with a prime minister and a governor-general representing the head of state, George VI. Its unicameral legislature, the Constituent Assembly, was charged with drafting the constitution. The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950, making India a republic with a president as head of state. It was based on the Government of India Act 1935 and drew on the constitutions of the United Kingdom, the United States, Ireland, Canada and France.

The constitution calls the country a Union of States, and the union government is also called the central government. Both India and Bharat are official names for the Republic of India. The system is quasi-federal: states govern themselves under their own governments, while union territories are administered directly by the union government under a lieutenant governor or administrator.

The government is modelled on the Westminster system, with legislative power vested in a bicameral Parliament, executive power in the Union Council of Ministers and judicial power in the Supreme Court. Parliament consists of the Lok Sabha, the lower house, and the Rajya Sabha, the upper house. The president is head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and acts on the advice of the prime minister, who leads the Council of Ministers.

The council is responsible to the Lok Sabha. The permanent civil services carry out executive decisions, and the cabinet secretary is the senior-most civil servant. The judiciary consists of the Supreme Court, High Courts at state level and district courts, and its concepts and procedures resemble those of Anglo-Saxon countries. The government's formal seat is Parliament House in New Delhi.
gozo: Gozo, in Maltese Għawdex, was known in antiquity as Gaulos and later as Gaudos, from which the Arabic name derives. It is the second-largest island of the Maltese archipelago and is rural in character, less developed than the island of Malta.

Gozo has been inhabited since 5000 BCE, when farmers from nearby Sicily crossed the sea. Similar pottery of the Għar Dalam phase has led to the suggestion that the first colonists came from the area of Agrigento, but where in Sicily they came from is not known. During the Neolithic period the Ġgantija temples were built, which are among the oldest free-standing structures and the oldest religious structures in the world. The name means belonging to the giants, because Maltese and Gozitan folklore says that giants built them. Native tradition and some ancient Greek writers, notably Euhemerus and Callimachus, hold that Gozo is the island Homer described as Ogygia, home of the nymph Calypso.

The Carthaginians occupied Gozo and built a temple to Astarte. Local coins with a Greek inscription suggest that it fell to the Greeks at some time, and it was probably annexed by Rome about 218 BCE. In the 1st century BCE it minted its own bronze coins bearing the head of Astarte and the legend Gaulitōn.

In 1530 the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V gave Gozo, with Malta, to the Knights Hospitalier. In July 1551 an Ottoman force under Sinan Pasha and Dragut invaded and ravaged the island, enslaving most of its 5,000 inhabitants and taking them to Libya. Mainland Maltese repopulated the island between 1565 and 1580 under the Knights. Gozo has generally been governed with Malta. The exception came after the French garrison surrendered to the British under Captain Alexander Ball on 28 October 1798, when Gozo was briefly independent until the French garrison in Valletta surrendered on 4 September 1800. Malta and Gozo then became a British protectorate and in 1813 a Crown colony.

Gozo is part of the Republic of Malta and had about 39,287 inhabitants in 2021, called Gozitans. It has its own Roman Catholic bishopric, the only suffragan of the Archbishop of Malta. The main town is Victoria, and ferries link the port of Mġarr to Ċirkewwa on Malta.
gracanica-monastery: Gračanica was built to replace an older cathedral of the Holy Virgin of the 13th century, which stood on the same spot in the centre of the Eparchy of Lipljan. A founder's inscription on the southern wall, in the words of King Stefan Milutin, says that he saw the ruins of the temple and built it from the ground. After the Serbian Archbishopric became a Patriarchate in 1346, the bishops of Lipljan were called metropolitans of Lipljan or Gračanica.

The narthex and tower were added a few decades later to protect the frescoes of the west facade. The Ottomans damaged the narthex several times between 1379 and 1383, when the tower was burned and a fire destroyed a rich collection of manuscripts; it was rebuilt in 1383. Under Ottoman rule the monastery kept some of its lands. Metropolitan Nikanor, in office from 1528 to 1555, had icons painted for the altarpiece and in 1538-1539 set up a Cyrillic printing press, which published the Gračanica Octoechos. Patriarch Makarije Sokolović had new frescoes completed in 1570. Of the former compound only the church survives, and nuns renewed it as a convent after the Second World War.

The church has the form of a double inscribed cross, one inside the other, which lifts the central dome on a graded arrangement of masses. The dome rests on four free-standing pillars, with four smaller domes above the spaces between the arms of the cross. The walls are built in alternate courses of brick and stone. It is regarded as the culmination of medieval Serbian building in the Serbo-Byzantine tradition.

The frescoes of the nave were painted in 1321-1322 and show the earthly life of Jesus and the church calendar. In the narthex are portraits of the founders, King Milutin and Queen Simonida, with Queen Helen, the king's mother, as a nun, and Milutin as a monk. It also holds the earliest painted genealogy of the Nemanjić dynasty, from Stefan Nemanja to Milutin, and a large Last Judgment.

The paintings rank highest among the achievements of Milutin's period and show the influence of the Byzantine style known as the Paleologan Renaissance. The Church of Saint Sava in Belgrade takes Gračanica and Hagia Sophia as models, and a detailed replica, the New Gračanica church in Chicago, was consecrated in 1984. In 2006 the monastery was placed on UNESCO's World Heritage List, as an extension of the Visoki Dečani site, under the name Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.
grameen-bank: Muhammad Yunus, a professor at the University of Chittagong, was inspired by the Bangladesh famine of 1974 to lend a total of 27 US dollars to 42 people, mostly makers of bamboo stools, as start-up money free of predatory interest. He began a research project with the university and Janata Bank to test a way of giving credit to the rural poor, and in 1976 the village of Jobra became the first to be served. The project reached the Tangail District in 1979 and then more districts.

An ordinance dated 2 October 1983 turned it into the Grameen Bank, whose name means village bank in Bengali. The bankers Ron Grzywinski and Mary Houghton of ShoreBank, a community development bank in Chicago, helped Yunus incorporate it under a grant from the Ford Foundation.

The bank rests on the principle that loans are better than charity for reducing hardship. It lends to groups usually without access to formal finance, such as the poor, women and the illiterate, on terms of group lending and weekly instalments. No written contract is made with borrowers, and the system works on trust. Repayment rests on the individual, and no formal joint liability exists, though members often cover a defaulter's debt, since the bank gives no further credit to a group in which a member defaults. About 97 per cent of its members are women.

Borrowers recite the Sixteen Decisions, which encourage habits such as sending children to school. Funding came at first from donor agencies, from the mid-1990s chiefly from the central bank of Bangladesh, and since 1995, 90 per cent of its loans have been financed by interest income and customer deposits. The bank also runs a Village Phone programme for women entrepreneurs in rural areas.

The bank's Low-cost Housing Program won a World Habitat Award in 1998, and the bank and Yunus were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006. Its success has inspired similar projects in more than 64 countries, including a World Bank initiative to finance Grameen-type lending systems. In 2013 the Bangladesh parliament passed the Grameen Bank Act, replacing the ordinance of 1983.
gran-chaco: The Gran Chaco, also called the Chaco or Chaco Plain, covers about one million square kilometres across eastern Bolivia, western Paraguay, northern Argentina and parts of Brazil, and forms part of the Río de la Plata basin. It lies west of the Paraguay River and east of the Andes and is mostly an alluvial plain. The name comes from the Quechua word chaqu, meaning hunting land.

The region has historically been divided into three parts: the Chaco Austral south of the Bermejo River, the Chaco Central between the Bermejo and the Pilcomayo, both now in Argentina, and the Chaco Boreal north of the Pilcomayo as far as the Brazilian Pantanal, in Paraguay and partly Bolivia. The west is dry and sparsely vegetated, while the east has a seasonally flooded plain with palm savanna and quebracho trees, the source of timber and tannin. Jaguars, peccaries, armadillos and tapirs live there; the Chacoan peccary was thought extinct until 1975.

Nomadic peoples, notably the Guaycuru groups, occupied the Chaco and resisted Spanish control, often successfully, from the 16th until the early 20th century. Other peoples of the region include the Wichí, Qom, Pilagá, Guaraní and Ayoreo. The Spaniards treated the whole area as a colonial region called Chiquitos before independence.

The Chaco was disputed territory from 1810. Argentina claimed land north of the Bermejo River until Paraguay's defeat in the War of the Triple Alliance fixed its present border with Argentina. Over the following decades Bolivia pushed the indigenous peoples out and settled in the Chaco, while Paraguay paid little attention. After losing its Pacific coast in the War of the Pacific, Bolivia sought the Paraguay River as an outlet, and the conflict over the Chaco Boreal, and supposed oil there, led to the Chaco War of 1932–1935 between Paraguay and Bolivia.

The Argentine foreign minister Carlos Saavedra Lamas mediated a ceasefire and a treaty signed in 1938, which gave Paraguay three quarters of the Chaco Boreal and gave Bolivia a corridor to the Paraguay River with use of Puerto Casado.

Mennonites came to the Paraguayan Chaco from Canada in the 1920s, and more arrived from the the USSR in the 1930s and after the Second World War; they founded some of the region's largest and most prosperous municipalities. In the 1960s Paraguay built the Trans-Chaco Highway, and Argentina built National Routes 16 and 81, each running about 700 km from east to west. Kaa-Iya del Gran Chaco National Park in Bolivia was established in September 1995 and is administered by indigenous peoples, among them the Izoceño Guaraní, the Ayoreode and the Chiquitano.
gran-sasso: Gran Sasso d'Italia, meaning the Great Rock of Italy, is a massif of the Apennine Mountains. Its highest summit, Corno Grande, at 2,912 metres, is the highest in the Apennines and the second highest in Italy outside the Alps. The other main summits are Corno Piccolo and Pizzo d'Intermesoli, which a deep valley, Val Maone, separates from the other two. The ash colour of Corno Grande and Corno Piccolo comes from their limestone and dolomite, and their rough vertical walls attract rock climbers. Corno Piccolo is known as the Sleeping Giant for its profile of a reclined face.

The mid and lower slopes are grazed in spring, summer and autumn by sheep, cattle and semi-wild horses. The park is home to the Apennine wolf, the Marsican bear, the European wildcat and the Abruzzo chamois, as well as golden eagles and peregrine falcons. East of Corno Grande and Corno Piccolo lies Campo Imperatore, a high plain 27 kilometres long and 8 wide at about 2,000 metres.

The Hotel Campo Imperatore was Benito Mussolini's prison until September 1943, when Nazi commandos freed him in the Gran Sasso raid. On the southern edge of the plain lie three medieval hill towns once ruled by the Medici: Calascio, below the ruined fortress of Rocca di Calascio, Santo Stefano di Sessanio and Castel del Monte. Pope John Paul II visited the Gran Sasso several times, and in 2005 a peak of 2,424 metres once called the Gendarme was renamed John Paul II Peak.

A ten-kilometre motorway tunnel for the A24 was bored through the massif in 1984, with a second tunnel completed in 1995. Its construction included the Gran Sasso National Laboratory at Assergi, an underground physics laboratory beneath 1,400 metres of rock whose first large experiments began in 1989. Opposition to the tunnel and laboratory from Italian and international environmental groups is credited by some with spurring the Italian environmental movement and the creation of the Gran Sasso and Monti della Laga National Park in 1991.

The massif lies within the Gran Sasso and Monti della Laga National Park. Its low background radiation makes the laboratory a site for work on neutrinos, cosmic rays, dark matter and nuclear decay. Campo Imperatore has Italy's oldest continuously operating commercial ski area, reached by cable car from Fonte Cerreto, and a station of the Rome Observatory. The Alpine Botanical Garden of Campo Imperatore and Lake Pietranzoni are among its points of interest.
granada: Granada lies in Andalusia at the foot of the Sierra Nevada, at the confluence of four rivers, the Darro, the Genil, the Monachil and the Beiro. It sits on the Vega de Granada, at an average elevation of 738 m and about 50 km from the Mediterranean coast. The pomegranate, granada in Spanish, is its heraldic device. The meaning of its Arabic name, Ġarnāṭa, is uncertain and debated.

The area has been populated since at least 5500 BCE. The oldest ruins belong to an oppidum called Ilturir, founded by the Iberian Bastetani around 650 BCE, later known as Iliberri or Iliberis, which became a Roman colony in 44 BCE. After the Umayyad conquest from 711 CE, the main settlement in the area was Madīnat Ilbīra (Elvira), while a smaller fortified settlement, Ġarnāṭa, with a mainly Jewish population, stood on the Albaicín site. Granada became a major city of al-Andalus in the 11th century under the Zirid Taifa of Granada.

As Almohad rule collapsed after 1228, Castile took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248. Ibn al-Ahmar (Muhammad I) established the Nasrid dynasty, the last and longest reigning Muslim dynasty in the peninsula, ruling the Emirate of Granada. He became a vassal of Ferdinand III of Castile in 1246, and Granada thereafter was a tributary state of Castile, though wars often interrupted this. On 2 January 1492 Emir Muhammad XI, called Boabdil by the Spanish, surrendered the emirate to the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile. The city was progressively made a Christian city during the 16th century, and the University of Granada was founded in 1531 by Charles V.

Granada is the capital of the province of Granada, with a population of 233,532 in 2024. The Alhambra, a fortified palace complex on the Sabika hill and one of the best-preserved palaces of the historic Islamic world, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984. The Albaicín and other medieval monuments preserve Islamic-period influence, and the 16th century brought Mudéjar and Renaissance architecture. The Sacromonte, with cave houses dug into the hillside, has a reputation as a centre of flamenco.
grand-bassam: Grand-Bassam lies in south-eastern Ivory Coast, east of Abidjan, and is the seat of Grand-Bassam Department. The Ébrié Lagoon divides it in two. Ancien Bassam, the former French settlement, faces the Gulf of Guinea and holds the grander colonial buildings, some of them restored, as well as a cathedral and the Ivory Coast National Museum of Costume, housed in the former Governor's Palace. Nouveau Bassam lies across a bridge on the inland side of the lagoon; it grew from the African servants' quarters and is now the main commercial centre of the town. The name Bassam may come from an ancient African word for the mouth of the Comoé River.

The Nzema people have lived in the area since the 15th century, and the place grew into a fishing village and trading centre. In 1843, after signing a treaty with the African ruler of the region, the French built Fort Memours on the banks of the river. It became their main trading point in the region and, after the Berlin Conference of 1885, a base for the exploration of West Africa. Grand-Bassam was the capital of the French Colonie de Côte d'Ivoire from 1893. A devastating outbreak of yellow fever that decimated its population led the colonial administration to move to the nearby town of Bingerville.

The town remained a key seaport until Abidjan grew in the 1930s. At independence in 1960 the remaining administrative offices moved to Abidjan, and for many years the town was inhabited only by squatters. From the late 1970s it began to revive as a tourist destination and craft centre.

The historic centre of Grand-Bassam was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012 for its outstanding colonial architecture and town planning and for the juxtaposition of the colonial town with a traditional Nzema village. Large sections of the old town were abandoned for decades, which gave it the aura of a ghost town. It is the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, whose cathedral is the Cathédrale Sacré Cœur.
grand-duchy-of-lithuania: The name of Lithuania was first mentioned in 1009 in the Annals of Quedlinburg. Between 1180 and 1183 the Lithuanians began sustained military raids on Slavic provinces, including Polotsk and Pskov, which marked the consolidation of the Lithuanian lands in Aukštaitija. Mindaugas, duke of southern Lithuania, had by the mid-1230s acquired supreme power in the whole country. He was baptised in 1252 and crowned in 1253, and Lithuania was recognised as a Christian state until 1260, when he supported an uprising in Courland and, according to the German order, renounced Christianity. The pagan state was the target of crusades by the Teutonic Knights and the Livonian Order but survived.

Under Grand Duke Gediminas the state grew quickly. In 1320 most of the principalities of western Rus' were vassalised or annexed, and in 1321 he captured Kiev. He established the permanent capital at Vilnius, probably in 1323. His sons Algirdas and Kęstutis then ruled together, and the state continued to expand.

Algirdas's son Jogaila signed the Union of Krewo in 1386, which made a dynastic union between the grand duchy and the Kingdom of Poland and led to the conversion of Europe's last pagan state, which took place in 1387. The reign of Vytautas the Great, son of Kęstutis, brought the widest territorial expansion and the defeat of the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410. By 1440 the state was the largest in Europe, reaching from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. It was multi-ethnic and multiconfessional: Ruthenians, ancestors of modern Belarusians and Ukrainians, spoke Ruthenian, the language of most official documents.

Wars with the Teutonic Order and the loss of land to Moscow forced a closer alliance with Poland, and the Union of Lublin of 1569 created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. The grand duchy kept its own ministries, laws, army and treasury. The Constitution of 3 May 1791 was meant to unite the two states, but Russia invaded in 1792, and the partition of 1795, after the Kościuszko Uprising, divided the territory among Russia, Prussia and Austria.

Historians from Lithuania, Belarus and Ukraine still debate whether the state was essentially Lithuanian or Ruthenian-Lithuanian. The Lithuanian annexation of much of southern and western Ruthenia is held to have led to the lasting division between Ukrainians, Belarusians and Russians.
grand-duchy-of-moscow: Moscow is first mentioned in chronicles under the year 1147, as part of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal, and was made a fortified stronghold in the 1150s. It was sacked during the Mongol invasions of 1237 to 1238. It became a separate principality when Daniel, the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, received the city and its surroundings as an appanage, and his reign is dated 1263 to 1303.

By the end of the 13th century Moscow was one of the leading principalities within the Grand Principality of Vladimir, alongside Tver. Daniel's son Yury contested the title of grand prince with Mikhail of Tver, and the khan of the Golden Horde, who held suzerainty over the princes, made Yury grand prince in 1318.

Ivan I, who ruled from 1325 to 1340, regained the title and collected tribute for the khan from the other Russian princes, which increased Moscow's wealth. The seat of the Russian Orthodox Church moved from Vladimir to Moscow in his time. Dmitry, who ruled from 1359 to 1389, permanently united the thrones of Vladimir and Moscow and defeated the Tatars in 1380. Vasily I took advantage of the strife in the Golden Horde to expand the realm, but he had to resume paying tribute after Tatar raids, and in 1408 Edigu besieged Moscow. The city survived on payment of a large indemnity.

Vasily II, who ruled from 1425 to 1462, won a civil war against his uncle Yury of Galich, and the Russian Church declared autocephaly in 1448. Ivan III, who ruled from 1462 to 1505, absorbed nearly all of the Russian states. Novgorod surrendered in 1478, and Ivan abolished its system of government. His defeat of the Tatars in 1480 traditionally marks the end of Tatar suzerainty. Vasily III completed the annexation of the remaining appanages, including Pskov in 1510 and Ryazan in 1521, and captured Smolensk from Lithuania in 1514. Ivan IV was crowned as the first Russian tsar in 1547.

The unification gave the grand prince dominance, and he treated the country as his personal patrimony. The historian Sergey Platonov wrote that the prince was not only the ruler of the country but also its owner. The veche and other traditional institutions were abolished, and appanage princes became part of the boyar class. Ivan III and Vasily III created a small bureaucracy of state secretaries known as dyaki.

The great majority of the population were peasants, whose primary allegiance was to the commune, and its members were collectively responsible for paying taxes. Monasticism spread between the 14th and 16th centuries, and one estimate suggests about 250 cenobitic monasteries and convents were founded. Andrei Rublev led a distinct Moscow school of icon painting, and his Trinity dates from the early 15th century.
grand-duke-konstantin-pavlovich-of-russi: Konstantin was born at Tsarskoye Selo in 1779, the second son of Paul Petrovich and Maria Fyodorovna. His grandmother, Catherine the Great, named him after Constantine the Great, and a medal struck for his birth bore the inscription Back to Byzantium, alluding to her Greek Plan. She directed his upbringing, and Cesar La Harpe was his tutor-in-chief from 1783 to 1795. On 26 February 1796 he married Juliane of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, who left him in 1799 after his violent treatment of her. The marriage was annulled on 20 March 1820, and on 27 May he married the Polish Countess Joanna Grudzińska, who became Princess of Łowicz.

In the campaign led by Suvorov he lost the battle of Bassignana by his own fault but distinguished himself at Novi, and Paul gave him the title tsesarevich. In 1805 he commanded the Imperial Guards and shared responsibility for the defeat at Austerlitz, though he captured the first French Imperial Eagle of the coalition's wars. After the peace of Tilsit he admired Napoleon and in 1812 pressed for a quick peace. Barclay de Tolly twice sent him away from the army for disorderly conduct. At La Fère-Champenoise in March 1814 he was praised for his bravery.

Alexander I installed him in Congress Poland as de facto viceroy and commander-in-chief, adding in 1819 the command of the Lithuanian troops. After Alexander suspended the Sejm for five years and authorised him to keep order, Konstantin strengthened the secret police, replaced Poles with Russians in the administration and army, and often insulted and assaulted subordinates. Yet he supported Polish musicians such as Maria Agata Szymanowska and Frédéric Chopin.

When Alexander I died on 1 December 1825, Nicholas had Konstantin proclaimed emperor in Saint Petersburg; when the news reached Warsaw, Konstantin formally abdicated. The confusion over the succession gave the Decembrist conspirators their opening. After an assassination attempt in November 1830 and the outbreak of the November Uprising, he refused to use Russian troops, saying that the Poles had started the disturbance and Poles must stop it. On 3 December he withdrew towards Russia. He died of cholera at Vitebsk on 27 June 1831. Russians remembered his stands against the imperial family as brave, while in Poland he was viewed as a tyrant and appears in literature as a cruel despot.
grand-national-assembly-of-turkey: Turkey had parliamentary experience before 1920. The Ottoman First Constitutional Era lasted two years: the assembly was dissolved on 28 June 1877 after criticism of the Russo-Turkish War, and the second assembly was dissolved by Sultan Abdul Hamid II on 14 February 1878, which suspended the Ottoman constitution of 1876. The Second Constitutional Era began on 23 July 1908 with the Young Turk Revolution. In both eras the General Assembly of the Ottoman Empire was bicameral, with a Senate chosen by the sultan and an elected Chamber of Deputies.

After the First World War the Allied Powers planned to dismember the Ottoman Empire through the Treaty of Sèvres. In a speech of 19 March 1920 Mustafa Kemal announced that an assembly with extraordinary powers would gather in Ankara, and he said that members of the dispersed Ottoman Chamber of Deputies could also take part. Elections followed in the style of the earlier Chamber, and the new body held its first session on 23 April 1920. Until 1923 the provisional government was known as the Government of the Grand National Assembly.

Multi-party politics began unsteadily. The Progressive Republican Party, founded in 1924 at Mustafa Kemal's request, was closed after several months, and the Liberal Party of Ali Fethi Okyar, founded in 1930, was dissolved on 17 November 1930 after disorders. No further attempt was made until 1945. The Democrat Party, established the year after the National Development Party of 1945, won the general elections of 1950, and Celal Bayar became President and Adnan Menderes Prime Minister.

A military coup on 27 May 1960 arrested Menderes, Bayar, the ministers and the members of the Assembly and closed it. A Constituent Assembly drafted the 1961 Constitution, accepted in a referendum on 9 July 1961 by 61.17 percent of voters, which made parliament bicameral. After the coup of 12 September 1980 the 1982 Constitution, accepted by 91.37 percent on 7 November 1982, made it unicameral with 550 members and introduced a 10 percent electoral threshold. After the referendum of 2017 Turkey adopted a presidential system, and the number of deputies rose from 550 to 600.

The 600 deputies are elected for five years by the D'Hondt method of party-list proportional representation, from 87 electoral districts that represent the 81 provinces. Parties with at least 20 deputies may form a parliamentary group, and the work is divided among specialised committees. The Assembly has met in three buildings. The first was converted from the Ankara headquarters of the Committee of Union and Progress, designed by Hasip Bey, and is now the War of Independence Museum. The second, by Vedat Tek, served from 1924 to 1960 and is now the Republic Museum. The present building in the Bakanlıklar neighbourhood of Ankara was designed by Clemens Holzmeister.
grand-palace: Construction of the Grand Palace began on 6 May 1782 at the order of King Phutthayotfa Chulalok, Rama I, who had seized the crown from King Taksin of Thonburi and meant to build a capital for his new Chakri dynasty. He moved the seat of power from Thonburi, on the west side of the Chao Phraya River, to the east side at Bangkok, where canals dug along the east side made the new capital an artificial island, named Rattanakosin. The old royal palace at Thonburi was small and sandwiched between two temples, Wat Arun and Wat Tai Talat, which prevented its expansion.

The new palace was built on a rectangular plot on the western edge of the island, between Wat Pho to the south and Wat Mahathat to the north, with the river on the west. The land had been occupied by a Chinese community, which Rama I ordered to move to an area south of the city walls, now Bangkok's Chinatown. The castellated walls were built in 1782 and extended southwards under Rama II.

The palace is a rectangle of about 218,400 square metres, surrounded by four walls with twelve gates and seventeen small forts, on the banks of the river. It is not a single building but numerous halls and pavilions set round lawns, gardens and courtyards, and its asymmetry and mixed styles come from two centuries of additions and rebuilding by successive kings, especially Chulalongkorn, Rama V.

It is divided into the Temple of the Emerald Buddha, the Outer Court with public buildings, the Middle Court with the main throne halls, the Inner Court and the Siwalai Gardens. The Temple of the Emerald Buddha, Wat Phra Kaew, built in 1783, is a royal chapel rather than a temple, as it has no living quarters for monks, and follows the tradition of the royal chapels at Sukhothai and Ayutthaya. In the Phra Maha Prasat group Rama I built a copy of an Ayutthaya throne hall, where he held his full coronation; lightning burned it down in 1789.

The king, his court and his government were based in the palace until 1925. The Outer Court, historically called Fai Na, held ministerial offices, a theatre, elephant stables, barracks, the royal mint and an arsenal. The Inner Court, Fai Nai, was reserved for the king and his queens and consorts, their children and a multitude of ladies-in-waiting and servants, and was a town within itself with its own shops, government and schools. Royal polygamy ended in practice under Rama VI and was outlawed by Rama VII. After the abolition of absolute monarchy in 1932 all government agencies left the palace. It is now partly open as a museum, and royal ceremonies and state functions are still held within its walls.
grand-trunk-road: The road follows an ancient route called the Uttarapatha, the Northern Road, which Buddhist literature mentions before the Maurya Empire and which Pāṇini also names. Its precursor was built on the orders of the emperor Chandragupta Maurya and was inspired by the eastern stretch of the Persian Royal Road, the Great Khurasan Road. In Mauryan times overland trade between India, Western Asia and Bactria passed through the north-western cities of Takshashila and Purushapura. The Greek diplomat Megasthenes, who spent fifteen years at the Mauryan court, records that Chandragupta had a department of officials to maintain it.

The road is said to have been built in eight stages linking Purushapura, Takshashila, Hastinapura, Kanyakubja, Prayag, Patliputra and Tamralipta, a distance of around 2,600 kilometres. The emperor Ashoka recorded in an edict that he had trees planted, wells dug at every half kos and rest-houses built along the route.

In the 16th century Sher Shah Suri of the Sur Empire repaired the road, rerouted it at Sonargaon and Rohtas and widened it. He added caravanserais, kos minars and baolis, and gardens beside some sections. His son Islam Shah Suri built an additional sarai between each of his father's on the way to Bengal, and the Mughals built more. Jahangir decreed that all sarais be of burnt brick and stone, planted broad-leaved trees between Lahore and Agra and bridged the water on the route. Sher Shah's road was called Sadak-e-Azam, and the Mughals called it Badshahi Sadak. Over the centuries it served as a major trade route and carried both travellers and the post.

The Afghan end was rebuilt under Mahmud Shah Durrani. In the 1830s the East India Company began a programme of metalled roads for commerce and administration, and the road from Calcutta through Delhi to Kabul was rebuilt at a cost of £1,000 a mile; the rebuilding ran between 1833 and 1860. It appears in the writing of Rudyard Kipling, who in Kim described the Brahmins, bankers, tinkers and pilgrims, all the world going and coming, on a road bearing India's traffic like a river of life.

Today the Indian sections coincide with parts of the National Highways NH 19, NH 112 and NH 44, and in Pakistan the road coincides with the N-5. India submitted the historic sites along it to the tentative list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 2015.
grand-vizier: The title Grand Vizier, in Ottoman Turkish Vezir-i Azam or Sadrazam, comes from Classical Persian, while its components derive from Arabic. The word vizier comes from wazīr, from a root meaning to bear a burden, which reflects the official's role in carrying the burdens of the state for the sovereign. The rank was formally established as a state office in the Abbasid Caliphate, where the term was used in the 8th century. The Ottomans took the office from the Seljuks of Anatolia in the early 14th century, and in the first phase of the state vizier was the only title in use.

The first Ottoman vizier to be called Grand Vizier was Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Elder, in the reign of Murad I. The title distinguished the holder of the sultan's seal from other viziers. He was the first holder with a military background, and the first of a political family that rivalled the Ottoman dynasty itself. His grandson Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Younger opposed the siege of Constantinople and was executed two days after Mehmed II won it. After this the post went almost exclusively to men of the kul system and the devshirme, who were easier for the sultan to control.

Power was centralised in the office in the Köprülü era. Köprülü Mehmed Pasha, appointed in 1656 under Mehmed IV, sent the sultan away from the city on hunting trips, removed officers suspected of corruption and executed those who stayed. On his deathbed five years later he persuaded the sultan to appoint his son Köprülü Fazıl Ahmed Pasha. After the Tanzimat of the 19th century, Grand Viziers came to resemble the prime ministers of Western monarchies.

The Grand Vizier held the imperial seal and could convene all other viziers. In conference they were called the Kubbealtı viziers, after the Kubbealtı in Topkapı Palace, and the Grand Vizier's offices stood at the Sublime Porte. In Ottoman legal theory the sultan was supposed to conduct state affairs only through him, but the arrangement was often circumvented. As the Ottomanist Colin Imber writes, the sultan often had closer contact with the pages of the privy chamber and other courtiers than with the Grand Vizier.

Elsewhere the office had its own course. In the Mughal Empire holders included Bairam Khan, who led the forces of Akbar to victory at the Second Battle of Panipat. In Qajar Iran the chief minister was styled sadr-e aʿzam, a title adopted in the Ottoman manner.
grande-armee: The Grande Armée was formed in 1804 from the Armée des côtes de l'Océan, also called the Armée d'Angleterre, the field army of over 100,000 men that Napoleon had assembled at the port of Boulogne for a planned invasion of the United Kingdom. When the Third Coalition formed against France after his coronation as Emperor of the French, the army turned east in 1805. At its formation it consisted of six corps led by Napoleon's marshals and senior generals.

In 1805 rapid marches surrounded General Karl von Mack's Austrian army at Ulm, which yielded 60,000 prisoners for the loss of some 2,000 French soldiers. On 2 December 1805 the Grande Armée defeated a combined Russian and Austrian army at the Battle of Austerlitz, and the Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December. After the stalemate at Eylau, victory at the Battle of Friedland on 14 June 1807 brought the Treaties of Tilsit. The army was dissolved in October 1808 and its parts formed into the Army of Spain and the Army of the Rhine.

In 1812 Napoleon assembled the largest field army he had ever commanded to invade Russia. After the capture of Smolensk and the battle of Borodino, the French reached Moscow on 14 September 1812, but disease, desertion, exhaustion and long supply lines had already reduced the army. On the retreat, cold, starvation, disease and harassment by Cossacks and partisans destroyed it as a fighting force, though its pontoon builders saved it from complete annihilation at the Berezina River. Later armies fought on in 1813, notably at the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig, and the Hundred Days of 1815 ended its campaigns.

The army was divided into corps, usually five to seven, each of between 10,000 and 50,000 men, commonly 20,000 to 30,000. Each corps was a self-contained army of combined arms, commanded by a marshal or a general, and the corps marched on separate routes within a day's march of one another. They were small enough to live by foraging, so fewer supplies had to be carried. The Imperial Guard formed a single corps of its own and served as a reserve.

Soldiers could rise through the ranks regardless of class, wealth or national origin. More than one-third of the troops who marched into Russia were not French and came from 20 countries. Each soldier carried four days' provisions, and Napoleon encouraged his men to live off the land. Every regiment included women called cantinières, married to soldiers, who sold food and drink and fed the troops when other arrangements broke down.
graubunden: The canton lies in the Alps and, unlike any other Swiss canton, extends fully on both sides of the main Alpine barrier, from the northern plains at Maienfeld to the southern plains at Roveredo. Much of it belongs to neither side: the Engadin is a large inner Alpine valley that drains through the Inn to the Danube. Parts of the canton lie in four of the country's five drainage basins, drained by the Rhine, the Po, the Adige and the Inn. Its heraldic symbol is the Alpine ibex.

The deep valleys were first settled by the Raetians. Archaeological evidence of settlement at Chur goes back to the Pfyn culture, 3900 to 3500 BCE. Most of the land became part of the Roman province of Raetia, established in 15 BCE, with Chur as Curia, and later lay in the territory of the diocese of Chur.

In the late Middle Ages three leagues formed. The League of God's House was founded in 1367 to resist the rising power of the Bishop of Chur. The Grey League followed in 1395 in the Upper Rhine valley, named for the homespun grey clothes of its people, and that name was used exclusively after 16 March 1424. In 1436 the people of ten bailiwicks of the former Toggenburg countship, whose dynasty had died out, formed the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. An alliance of 1471 produced the Three Leagues, which before the end of the 15th century became an ally of the Old Swiss Confederacy. The Grey League's name gave the canton its German name, meaning the Grey Leagues.

Chur is the capital and the only sizable city; most people live in mountain valleys, and the canton has 200,096 inhabitants. Romansh has official status here and has been a national language of Switzerland since 1938; in 1996 it was declared an official language of the Confederation. It consists of five dialect groups, with a common written form, Rumantsch Grischun. Since the late Middle Ages it has lost more than half its original territory, which included Liechtenstein and parts of western Austria.

Three World Heritage Sites lie in the canton: the Benedictine Convent of Saint John, the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona and the Rhaetian Railway in the Albula and Bernina landscapes. The church of Zillis holds a Romanesque painted ceiling added about 1130, and the canton has many medieval castles, among them Tarasp in the Engadin.
graz: Graz lies on both sides of the river Mur in southeast Austria, about 150 kilometres southwest of Vienna and some 50 kilometres north of Maribor in Slovenia. It is in the Graz Basin on the eastern edge of the Alps, with the city centre at 353 metres, and the Schlossberg, or Castle Hill, 475 metres high, dominates the old town. Because the basin is open only to the south, the climate is warmer than expected at that latitude.

The oldest settlement on the site dates to the Copper Age, but there is no continuity of settlement before the Middle Ages. The name most likely derives from the Slavic gradec, small castle, though the city itself was founded by Bavarian settlers who arrived shortly after the Slavs and intermixed with them. They called it Bayrischgraz, Bavarian Graz, to distinguish it from the older Windischgraz, Slovenian Graz, which it soon eclipsed.
