Mendel died in Brno on 6 January 1884 of chronic nephritis, and Leoš Janáček played the organ at his funeral. His successor as abbot burned his papers to end the tax dispute. In 1900 Hugo de Vries and Carl Correns, working independently, repeated his experiments and found his writings, and both acknowledged his priority. In 1936 Ronald Fisher judged his data too close to expectation, but Daniel Hartl and Daniel Fairbanks later rejected the charge of falsification.
gregory-of-tours: Gregory was born Georgius Florentius at Clermont in the Auvergne, into the upper stratum of Gallo-Roman society. His father Florentius was a senator of Clermont, and relatives of his held the bishoprics of Tours, Lyon and Langres at the time of his birth. After his father's death he was raised by his uncle Gallus, bishop of Clermont, and by Gallus's successor Avitus, who ordained him deacon. A serious illness led him to visit the tomb of Saint Martin at Tours, and he recovered.

When the see of Tours fell vacant, the clergy and people chose Gregory as bishop. Deputies overtook him at the court of King Sigebert of Austrasia, and he was consecrated on 22 August 573, at the age of 34, though he accepted much against his will. He spent most of his career at Tours, on the Loire, where Frankish influence from the north met Gallo-Roman influence from the south. As the centre of the cult of Saint Martin it was a pilgrimage site and a political sanctuary. He dealt with four Frankish kings, Sigebert I, Chilperic I, Guntram and Childebert II. After rumours that he had slandered Chilperic's wife Fredegund, Chilperic had him arrested and tried for treason.

His main work, the Decem Libri Historiarum or Ten Books of Histories, known as the History of the Franks, begins with the Creation and moves quickly to the spread of Christianity into Gaul, the conversion of Clovis I and the history of the Frankish kings. Books V to X, covering the years from 575 to 591, rest largely on his own knowledge. He added an epilogue in 594. He wrote in Late Latin and apologised for his rough style. He opens with a statement of his Catholic orthodoxy against Arianism. Recent scholarship holds that his underlying purpose was to set the vanity of secular life against the miracles of the saints.

He also wrote the Life of the Fathers, twenty lives of holy men, and the Book of the Glories of the Martyrs, begun in 587, which tie saints and relics to local shrines in Gaul. Historians value the History of the Franks as the central source for the Franks' rise, and it is often compared with Herodotus.
gregory-the-illuminator: In the Armenian tradition the standard life of Gregory derives from a fifth-century hagiographic history attributed to Agathangelos. It makes him the son of the Parthian nobleman Anak, who at the urging of the Sasanian king Ardashir I assassinated the Arsacid king of Armenia, Khosrov. The Armenian nobles put Anak and his family to death, but Gregory escaped with the help of his nurse and was taken to Caesarea in Cappadocia, where he received a Christian upbringing. Some modern scholars distrust this account. Marie Louise Chaumont suggested he was probably a Greek from Cappadocia. According to Movses Khorenatsi, Gregory married Mariam and had two sons, Aristaces and Vrtanes.

Gregory entered the service of King Tiridates III, son of the murdered Khosrov. When he refused to sacrifice to the goddess Anahit, the king had him tortured, and on learning whose son he was, had him thrown into the deep pit of Khor Virap near Artaxata, where he stayed for thirteen or fifteen years. Agathangelos says he was brought out after the king's sister Khosrovidukht had a vision. He then healed the king, whom the history describes as driven into animal madness for his sins, and Tiridates and his court accepted Christianity.

Gregory raised shrines to the martyrs Gayane and Hripsime at Vagharshapat, later called Ejmiatsin, and destroyed pagan temples. He was consecrated bishop of Armenia at Caesarea by Leontius of Caesarea, and his successors went there to be confirmed until the death of Nerses I. He built churches in place of the temples, founded schools teaching in Greek and Syriac, and baptized the king, the army and the people in the Euphrates. The conversion is traditionally dated to 301, but modern scholarship considers a date near 314 more likely, and holds that the spread of Christianity was more gradual than Agathangelos depicts.

Gregory appointed his younger son Aristaces as his successor and lived as an ascetic in the cave of Manē in Upper Armenia. According to Khorenatsi he was last seen after Aristaces returned from the Council of Nicaea in 325, and he died in seclusion, buried by shepherds who did not know who he was. His descendants, the Gregorids, held the patriarchate of Armenia, with some interruptions, until the death of Patriarch Isaac in the fifth century. The Armenian Church is sometimes called lusavorchakan, "of the Illuminator", or Gregorian. The Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches commemorate him on 30 September.
greifswald: Greifswald lies on the River Ryck, near its mouth into the Danish Wiek, a sub-bay of the Bay of Greifswald on the Baltic coast. The city stands roughly midway between the two largest Pomeranian islands, Rügen and Usedom,. Its name derives from the dukes of Pomerania, the House of Griffin, and means Griffin's Forest.

In the Middle Ages the site was unsettled woodland on the border between the Danish Principality of Rügen and the Pomeranian County of Gützkow. In 1199 the Rugian Prince Jaromar I allowed Danish Cistercian monks to build Hilda Abbey, later Eldena Abbey, at the mouth of the Ryck. The lands granted to the monks included a natural salt pond beside an important trade route, and the town grew there. In 1241 Prince Wizlaw I and Duke Wartislaw III both granted market rights, and in 1250 Wartislaw gave a charter under Lübeck law.

Eldena Abbey and the main buildings of the town were raised in North German Brick Gothic. By the end of the 13th century Greifswald was one of the earliest members of the Hanseatic League. In 1456 the mayor Heinrich Rubenow laid the foundations of the university.

The Reformation ended Eldena's life as a monastery, and the friaries within the walls were secularised. During the Thirty Years' War Imperial forces held the town from 1627 to 1631. Swedish troops besieged it on 12 June 1631, and it surrendered four days later. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden came to supervise the siege and received the university's homage. After the war the town became part of Swedish Pomerania, which remained Swedish until 1815, when it passed to the Kingdom of Prussia. By 1630 the population had shrunk by two thirds.

The town expanded beyond its medieval walls for the first time about 1900. It survived the Second World War without much destruction: in April 1945 Colonel Rudolf Petershagen defied orders and surrendered it to the Red Army without a fight. From 1949 to 1990 it belonged to the German Democratic Republic, and its population peaked at about 68,000 in 1988.

Greifswald is the seat of the district of Western Pomerania-Greifswald in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The 2021 population was listed at 59,332, many of them students and staff of the University of Greifswald, which has about 12,000 students. The Pomeranian State Museum holds works by Caspar David Friedrich, who was born in the city and often painted the ruins of Eldena Abbey.
greiz: Greiz lies in eastern Thuringia, 100 kilometres east of the state capital Erfurt, on the White Elster river. It stands at the confluence of the White Elster and its tributary the Göltzsch, a position that helped the town grow fast. The place name, originally Grouts, is of Slavic origin and means gord, a fortified settlement.

The first documented mention of the settlement dates from 1209. From the 12th century it was governed by advocati, or Vögte, and in 1236 it came into the possession of Gera. It was recognised as a town in the 13th century. The House of Reuss, a ruling dynasty whose male members were all named Heinrich, later built two castles there, the Upper Castle and the Lower Castle, both by noted architects. Greiz became the capital of the Principality of Reuss-Greiz, which lasted until 1918. Fire destroyed the town entirely in 1494 and almost totally in 1802.

Between 1934 and 1943, 809 people were forcibly sterilised by the Nazis in the district hospital, and a local old people's home and care home sent 122 sick people to the Aktion T4 euthanasia programme. During World War II prisoners of war and people from occupied countries worked as forced labourers at Sorgwald and elsewhere, and at least 102 died; there is a memorial in the Old Cemetery. A monument honours the officer Kurt von Westernhagen, shot by the Gestapo in April 1945 for refusing to blow up the bridge and defend the town. Three of the five bridges were destroyed, but the town was not otherwise much damaged. Ulf Merbold, the first West German astronaut, was born there in 1941.

Greiz is the capital of the district of Greiz and has about 20,400 inhabitants. It has a large park, classified as an English garden, in its centre, the Fürstlich Greizer Park, and streets of Jugendstil houses. Its economy includes mechanical engineering, plastics, medical technology, printing and breweries. Like many towns in the former East Germany it has lost population.
grenadines: The Grenadines are a chain of small islands lying on a line between the larger islands of Saint Vincent and Grenada in the Lesser Antilles. Neither Saint Vincent nor Grenada counts as one of them. Nine are inhabited and open to the public: Bequia, Mustique, Canouan, Union Island, Petit St Vincent, Palm Island and Mayreau, all in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Petite Martinique and Carriacou in Grenada. Several privately owned islands, such as Calivigny, are also inhabited.

The chain is divided between two island nations at the Martinique Channel. The northern two-thirds, about 32 islands and cays, belong to Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and the southern third to Grenada. Carriacou is the largest and most populous of the Grenadines. Petit Nevis was formerly used by whalers.

The history of the Grenadines is not well studied, because of their relative lack of geopolitical importance and the scarcity of original documents. The Kalinago sparsely populated the islands, using them mainly for fishing and food gathering. When the French claimed Grenada in 1650 the Grenadines were included, while Saint Vincent to the north remained Kalinago country.

Their small size, dangerous reefs and lack of fresh water led the French to use them mainly for fishing, turtle catching and lime-making; smugglers and pirates also used them. Permanent settlement began about 1740. When the British took over in 1762 there were a fair number of French plantations on Bequia and Carriacou. In 1791 the islands were divided between Grenada and Saint Vincent.
grenoble: Grenoble lies where the river Drac flows into the Isère at the foot of the French Alps. It is surrounded by mountains, with the Chartreuse to the north, the Vercors to the south and west and the Belledonne range to the east, and it is regarded as the capital of the French Alps. The Bastille, a series of fortifications on the mountainside, overlooks the city from the north. It was begun in the Middle Ages and extended in later centuries, and it has been credited as the most extensive example of early 18th-century fortification in France, on what was then the Alpine frontier with the Kingdom of Sardinia.

The first references to the place date to 43 BCE, when Cularo was a village of the Allobroges, a Gallic tribe, near a bridge over the Isère. The Emperor Gratian visited it and made it a Roman city, and in 381 it was renamed Gratianopolis, the city of Gratian, which through regular sound shifts became Graignovol in the Middle Ages and then Grenoble.

After the fall of the Roman Empire the city became part of the first Burgundian kingdom in the 5th century and then of the Kingdom of Burgundy until 1032, when it was integrated into the Holy Roman Empire. Grenoble grew significantly in the 11th century, when the Counts of Albon chose it as the capital of their scattered territories, and when they took the title of Dauphins it became the capital of the State of Dauphiné. The Parlement of Dauphiné sat in a Renaissance palace built around 1500 until the French Revolution.

The revocation of the Edict of Nantes by Louis XIV caused 2,000 Protestants to leave Grenoble, which weakened the economy but also the glove industry of Grasse, and so left Grenoble's glove makers without competition. At the start of the 18th century 12 glovers made 180,000 gloves a year, and by 1787 there were 64 making 1,920,000.

Grenoble is the prefecture and largest city of the Isère department in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region. The commune had 156,140 inhabitants in 2023 and its metropolitan area 727,380, the largest in the Alps. It is a significant European scientific centre, and its post-war boom was symbolised by the Olympic Winter Games of 1968.
grigori-rasputin: Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin was born a peasant in the village of Pokrovskoye on the Tura River in the Tobolsk Governorate, on 21 January 1869 by official records. His father Yefim was a peasant farmer and church elder who also worked as a government courier. Like most Siberian peasants he was not formally educated and remained illiterate well into early adulthood. In 1897 he left on a pilgrimage, for reasons that are unclear: some sources say to escape punishment for horse theft, others that he had a vision. At the St Nicholas Monastery at Verkhoturye he was deeply humbled by an elder called Makary, and he returned a changed man, a vegetarian who abstained from alcohol. He then spent years as a strannik, a holy wanderer.

In 1904 or 1905 he gained a reputation in Kazan as a wise starets, and church leaders sent him to Saint Petersburg, where aristocrats curious about the occult welcomed him. He met Nicholas II and Empress Alexandra Feodorovna in November 1905. From late 1906 he acted as faith healer for their son Alexei, who had haemophilia. In 1912, when the boy lay close to death after a hemorrhage, Rasputin telegraphed that the Little One would not die, and the bleeding stopped within days. In 1907 clergy in Pokrovskoye denounced him as a heretic. His power was at its height in 1915, when Nicholas left Saint Petersburg to oversee the army.

A group of nobles led by Purishkevich, Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich and Prince Felix Yusupov decided that his influence over Alexandra threatened the empire. He was murdered early on 30 December 1916 at Yusupov's home, dying of three gunshot wounds, one at close range to the forehead. Little else is certain, and historian Douglas Smith writes that what really happened will never be known. Historians often suggest that his scandalous reputation helped discredit the tsarist government and precipitate the overthrow of the House of Romanov shortly after. Accounts of his life were often based on rumour.
grigory-potemkin: Grigory Potemkin was born on 11 October 1739 (30 September in the old style) in the village of Chizhovo near Smolensk, into a family of middle-income noble landowners. After his father's death in 1746 his mother, Daria Vasilievna Kondyreva, took charge of the family and moved to Moscow, where he studied at the gymnasium attached to the university. He enlisted in the army in 1750 at the age of eleven, as noble children customarily did, and won the university's gold medal in 1757. He later lost the sight of his left eye, under circumstances the sources tell differently.

Potemkin returned to court in January 1774, and by February had become Catherine's lover and favourite. The offices that followed included Governor-General of Novorossiya, General-in-Chief and Commander-in-Chief of the Cossacks. Their surviving letters show a relationship of laughter and mutual admiration. He pursued the Greek Project, which aimed at a new Byzantine Empire around Constantinople, and by July 1783 he had engineered the peaceful annexation of Crimea and Kuban. Catherine rewarded him with one hundred thousand roubles, which he used to build the Tauride Palace in Saint Petersburg.

He became a field marshal in 1784 and governed the southern provinces as Prince of Taurida. His firm dealing with the Cossacks, notably the breaking of the Zaporozhian host in 1775, defined his rule. He founded or developed cities: Kherson, begun in 1778 as a base for the Black Sea Fleet; Sevastopol; Simferopol; and Nikolayev, founded in 1789. His effort to build Yekaterinoslav, now Dnipro, was his biggest failure. When a second Russo-Turkish war began in August 1787 he was commander-in-chief, and his army besieged Ochakov.

Potemkin fell ill at Iași, where he oversaw peace talks, and died on 16 October 1791 (5 October in the old style) on the open steppe, 60 km from the town. Some historians have suggested poisoning, but Simon Sebag Montefiore proposes bronchial pneumonia. Catherine bought the Tauride Palace and his art collection and paid his debts. When Paul I succeeded in 1796 he tried to undo Potemkin's reforms. The Potemkin village, a ruse of painted façades to impress visiting officials, is associated with his rule but is probably mythical. The battleship Potemkin, named in his honour, took part in the Russian Revolution of 1905.
grodno: Grodno stands on the Neman River, about 300 km from Minsk, 15 km from the Polish border and 30 km from the Lithuanian. Its name is considered Slavic, derived from the Ruthenian horod, fortress, and the town grew from a small fortress and fortified trading outpost kept by Rurikid princes on the border with the lands of the Baltic Yotvingians. Before East Slavs arrived in the 10th and 11th centuries the area was inhabited by Yotvingians.

Grodno became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 13th century, and Lithuanians rebuilt the stronghold. In 1276 Duke Traidenis sheltered there Yotvingians fleeing a massacre by the Teutonic Knights, who attacked the town repeatedly between 1283 and 1377. The union of Lithuania with Poland in 1385 made it a town of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which gave it a charter in 1441 and used it as a royal residence. Stefan Batory made the Old Castle his principal residence and died there in December 1586.

Jews began to settle in the city in the 14th century, a privilege said to have been granted by Vytautas in 1389, though the YIVO Encyclopedia describes that document as a forgery of the early 16th century. They were expelled in 1495 and allowed back in 1503. Russia annexed the city in the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, and on 25 November that year Stanisław August Poniatowski, the last Polish king and Lithuanian grand duke, abdicated in the New Castle.

Germany occupied Grodno on 3 September 1915. In September 1939 the Soviet invasion brought heavy fighting in the Battle of Grodno, after which the Soviets massacred over 300 captured Polish defenders. Since 1945 the city has been part of Belarus, and most of its Polish inhabitants were expelled or fled to Poland in 1944–1946 and 1955–1959.
groningen: Groningen lies at the northernmost point of the Hondsrug area. The origin of its name is uncertain: a folk story tells of exiles from Troy led by a figure called Gruno, one modern theory takes it to mean among the people of Groni, from an old Frisian personal name, and another derives it from a word for green fields. The Dutch sometimes call it Martinistad, after the Martinitoren tower.

The oldest document referring to the city dates from 1040, though Saxons had occupied the area centuries earlier. It gained city rights de facto in 1245, but no written record of a formal grant survives. Isolated from the successive Dutch centres of power in Utrecht, The Hague and Brussels, it long relied on itself and nearby regions. As a Hanseatic city it belonged to the North German trade network and later became chiefly a regional market centre. In the 13th century its people built a city wall, and the Gronings dialect became common in the surrounding lands.

Its most influential period came at the end of the 15th century, when the province of Friesland was administered from Groningen and the Martinitoren was built. At the height of its power it could be considered an independent city-state. In 1536 it accepted Emperor Charles V as its ruler, which ended its autonomy. Dutch and English forces under Maurice of Nassau captured it in the Siege of Groningen of 1594, after which the city and the province joined the Dutch Republic. The University of Groningen was founded in 1614, and the city grew rapidly, with a new wall.

In the Siege of Groningen of 1672, during the Third Anglo-Dutch War, the bishop of Münster, Bernhard von Galen, failed to take the city, an event still marked on 28 August as Gronings Ontzet. In 1811 Napoleon I annexed it to the French Empire, until 1813. In April 1945, in the Battle of Groningen, the main square and the Grote Markt were largely destroyed, though the Martinitoren, the Goudkantoor and the city hall were undamaged.

Groningen is the capital of its province and the largest city of the northern Netherlands, with 244,807 inhabitants. The University of Groningen is the second oldest university in the country, and students make up about a quarter of the population.
gross-domestic-product: Sir William Petty devised a concept of gross domestic product to calculate the tax burden, and to argue that landlords were unfairly taxed during the warfare between the Dutch and the English between 1652 and 1674. Charles Davenant developed the method further in 1695. The economist Simon Kuznets, who developed the first comprehensive set of measures of national income, warned of the uses and abuses of such measurements in his second report to the United States Congress in 1937. The international standard for measuring GDP is the System of National Accounts, prepared by representatives of the International Monetary Fund, the European Union, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the United Nations and the World Bank.

Gross domestic product is the total market value of all final goods and services produced during a specific period, usually a year, by a country or countries. It can be determined in three ways that should in theory give the same result: the production approach, which sums the value added at each stage of production, the income approach, which adds the incomes paid to the factors of production, and the expenditure approach, which sums consumption, investment, government expenditure and net exports. Nominal GDP does not account for inflation, so comparisons over time use real values, and comparisons between countries are often adjusted for differences in the cost of living. GDP defines its scope by location, whereas gross national income defines it by ownership.

GDP is widely used as a broad measure of economic progress, but it has been criticised for leaving out externalities such as environmental harm, unpaid domestic work, non-market transactions and economies where little money is used. It also does not account for how income is distributed. In the 1980s Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum developed the capability approach, which looks at what people are able to achieve rather than at aggregate output. A commission including Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen and Jean-Paul Fitoussi proposed in 2009 a well-being framework to broaden the focus beyond GDP.
grosseto: Grosseto stands in the centre of the Maremma, on the alluvial plain called the Piana Grossetana, where the Ombrone valley meets the Tyrrhenian Sea. The Metalliferous Hills lie to the north, Mount Argentario and the Uccellina Mountains to the south and Mount Amiata to the east. In the past most of the plain was occupied by Lake Prile, which has almost disappeared after land reclamation completed between the 18th and 20th centuries. The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, as remains in the Fabbrica Cave and the Scoglietto Cave show.

In the Etruscan period the city did not exist; the area belonged to Rusellae, a few kilometres north, most splendid in the 6th century BCE. The Romans conquered it in 294 BCE, and under the empire it became a colonia with a forum, basilica, amphitheatre and baths. It became a Christian bishop's seat, first attested in 499. Rusellae declined from the 6th century, and a first nucleus of Grosseto formed in the early 7th century, after the Lombard conquest. It is first mentioned in 803 as a fief of the Aldobrandeschi counts.

Sienese rule ended in 1559, when Charles V handed the duchy to Cosimo I de Medici, first grand duke of Tuscany. In 1564-65 the Medicean walls were begun to the design of Baldassarre Lanci, as part of making Grosseto a stronghold on the southern border. Malaria spread in the swamps, and the population, estimated at 7 000 to 8 000 before the Black Death of 1348, fell to about 600 under Medici rule. Under the House of Lorraine the town flourished and became capital of the new Maremma province. At Italian unification it had about 4 700 inhabitants, and growth followed the land reclamation completed under the Fascist regime. The Allies heavily bombed it in 1943.

Grosseto is the capital of its province and the most populous city of the Maremma, with 82,284 inhabitants in its comune. Its economy rests on services, agriculture and seaside tourism. The Medicean walls are now a public park and walking area, and the Romanesque cathedral of St Lawrence, begun at the end of the 13th century by Sozzo Rustichini of Siena, is its main monument. Andrea da Grosseto, a 13th-century writer who translated Albertano of Brescia's moral treatises in 1268, was born in the city.
grover-cleveland: Stephen Grover Cleveland was born on 18 March 1837 in Caldwell, New Jersey, the son of Richard Falley Cleveland, a Congregational and Presbyterian minister, and Ann Neal. After his father died in 1853 he left school to help support his family, and in 1855 he decided to move west. He started his own law practice in 1862, and in January 1863 he became assistant district attorney of Erie County, New York. A Democrat from the start, he was elected mayor of Buffalo in 1881, on a ticket meant to attract voters tired of corrupt party machines, and governor of New York in 1882.

In 1884 reform-minded Republicans called Mugwumps denounced the Republican nominee, James G. Blaine, as corrupt and supported Cleveland, whose slogan was 'A public office is a public trust'. As president he said he would not dismiss Republicans who did their work well, and he vetoed hundreds of private pension bills for Civil War veterans, 414 vetoes in his first term, more than four times as many as any earlier president.

He signed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 and the Dawes Act, which led Native Americans to cede about 100 million acres between 1887 and 1934. On 2 June 1886 he married Frances Folsom in the White House, the only president to marry there. In 1888 he won the popular vote but lost the electoral college to Benjamin Harrison.

He defeated Harrison in 1892. The Panic of 1893 struck shortly before his second term, and he persuaded Congress to repeal the silver coinage provisions of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, which alienated the agrarian wing of his party. In 1894 the Pullman Strike put 125,000 railroad workers on strike; Cleveland obtained an injunction and sent federal troops into Chicago and 20 other rail centres, and the use of troops hardened organised labour against him. An anti-imperialist, he opposed the annexation of Hawaii and investigated the 1893 coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani. By the end of his second term he was highly unpopular, even among Democrats.

After leaving the White House, Cleveland served as a trustee of Princeton University. He joined the American Anti-Imperialist League in protest at the Spanish-American War of 1898, and he died on 24 June 1908. He was the first Democrat elected president after the Civil War and the first president to serve non-consecutive terms.
gruyeres: The medieval town stands at the top of an isolated hill 82 metres high, overlooking the Saane Valley and the Lake of Gruyère, at 810 metres above sea level and 4.5 kilometres south-south-east of the district capital Bulle. It lies in the foothills of Mount Moléson, where the Saane, called the Sarine in French, leaves the Fribourg Alps. Graves of the Hallstatt and La Tène eras and traces of the Bronze Age have been found at Épagny, together with the remains of a Roman villa of the 2nd or 3rd century CE.

The origins of the House of Gruyères remain mysterious. According to a legend, the founder Gruerius captured a crane, in French grue, and chose it as his heraldic animal, which gave the town its name. The town grew up beneath the counts' castle. By the end of the 12th century it was a market town with a central street and walls, and in 1397 Count Rudolph IV confirmed an older town charter modelled on that of Moudon. On 22 June 1476 Gruyères took part in the Battle of Morat against Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, and with the Old Swiss Confederacy routed the Burgundian army.

Nineteen counts are recorded between the 11th and 16th centuries. The last, Michel, was in financial trouble nearly all his life and went bankrupt in 1554. His creditors, the cantons of Fribourg and Bern, divided his county between them. From 1555 to 1798 the castle was the residence of the bailiffs and then of the prefects sent by Fribourg. It was sold in 1849 to the Bovy and Balland families, who restored it with the help of painter friends, and the canton of Fribourg bought it back in 1938 and made it a museum.

Gruyères has always been a rural town. Cheese and animals were traded there, and agriculture still specialises in milk and cattle, supplying the Gruyère cheese that carries the town's name. Most people speak French. The whole village is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and Gruyères Castle, Saint-Germain Castle and the town's fortifications are heritage sites of national significance. The castle holds a regional museum and an arts museum, and in 1998 the painter and sculptor H. R. Giger acquired Saint-Germain Castle, which now houses a museum of his work.
guadalajara-spain: Guadalajara lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula at about 685 metres above sea level, on the left bank of the Henares river, between the river and the moors of La Alcarria. The historic core stands on a small rise between two small watercourses, which gave an easily defended site. Control of the scarce water supply was fought over by the local nobility.

A Roman mansio called Arriaca is presumed to have stood in the region, though there is no archaeological proof. The town was founded in the Islamic period, in the 9th century, and was officially known as Madīnat al-Faraŷ, after a person named Faraŷ. It was later known as Wādī al-Ḥijāra, from which the present name comes. It belonged to the Middle March of Al-Andalus, governed by the Masmuda Berber clan of the Banū Sālim for the Umayyad rulers of Córdoba. A fortress, walls and the bridge over the Henares date from the Muslim period.

Alfonso VI of León and Castile annexed it in 1085 with the Taifa of Toledo, and the town surrendered without resistance, although tradition says a force led by Álvar Fáñez de Minaya seized it by night. Alfonso VII gave the first fuero in 1133. Henry IV granted city status in 1460. The Mendoza family, Dukes of El Infantado from 1475, dominated the city for generations and patronised the arts, so that it was called the Atenas alcarreña, Alcarria's Athens. A large Jewish community maintained four synagogues until the expulsion of 1492.

The 17th century was a time of crisis, made worse by the expulsion of the moriscos in 1610, which took 10 percent of the population, and the Mendozas left for good in 1657. In the War of the Spanish Succession the city was sacked and its population fell to about 2,200. The French took Guadalajara in 1808 during the Peninsular War, and it became a provincial capital in 1833.

Guadalajara is the capital of its province in Castilla–La Mancha, with 93,470 registered inhabitants, and has grown quickly since 1959, when it was included in plans to relieve the congestion of Madrid's industrial estates. The Palacio del Infantado, the bridge over the Henares, built on Roman foundations, and the Mudéjar co-cathedral of Saint Mary are among its monuments. In March 1937, in the Spanish Civil War, Republican forces defeated an Italian expeditionary force near the city.
guadalcanal-campaign: After the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, Japanese forces captured the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Burma, the Dutch East Indies, Wake Island, the Gilbert Islands, New Britain and Guam. In summer 1942 the Allies decided to mount offensives in New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, to defend the sea lines to Australia and eventually to attack the major Japanese base at Rabaul. The campaign followed the Allied defensive successes at the Battle of the Coral Sea and the Battle of Midway in May and June 1942.

Allied forces were under Robert L. Ghormley, reporting to Chester W. Nimitz, and Major General Alexander Vandegrift's 1st Marine Division moved from the United States to New Zealand. The Japanese defence rested on the Combined Fleet under Isoroku Yamamoto and the Seventeenth Army under Harukichi Hyakutake.

On 7 August 1942 mainly U.S. Marines landed on Guadalcanal, Tulagi and Florida Island, taking the Japanese defenders by surprise. Within days a Japanese force of seven cruisers and one destroyer under Vice Admiral Gunichi Mikawa defeated Allied screening ships at the Battle of Savo Island. The Marines formed a perimeter around Lunga Point and finished the airfield, named Henderson Field on 12 August. Japanese attempts to retake it came in mid-September and in late October.

The Japanese brought troops by fast destroyers at night, the runs the Allies called the Tokyo Express, while American aircraft at Henderson Field controlled the daytime. Naval battles followed, including the Eastern Solomons, Cape Esperance and the Santa Cruz Islands, and the Allies won the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal in mid-November. Japanese troops were short of supplies by late November. On 12 December the Japanese Navy proposed abandoning Guadalcanal, and imperial headquarters agreed on 26 December. In January 1943 the U.S. XIV Corps under Alexander Patch took over operations, and the last Japanese forces were evacuated by 9 February 1943.

Guadalcanal was the first major Allied land offensive against Japan. With the battles at Milne Bay and Buna–Gona on New Guinea, it marked the Allies' change from defence to offence and passed the strategic initiative to them. Failure to win air superiority forced Japan to rely on barges, destroyers and submarines for reinforcement, and the campaign strained the resources of both sides.

Afterwards Guadalcanal and Tulagi became major Allied bases, with extra fighter and bomber airfields and large port facilities for the advance up the Solomons. The campaign drew many war correspondents, among them Richard Tregaskis, whose Guadalcanal Diary was a bestseller in 1943.
guadalquivir: The Guadalquivir drains an area of about 58,000 km2 and rises at about 1,350 m above sea level, at a place known as Cañada de las Fuentes in the Sierra de Cazorla. Near the mouth the marshy lowlands called Las Marismas border the Doñana National Park. It is the only major navigable river in Spain. The modern name comes from the Arabic al-wādī l-kabīr, the great river.

During much of the Holocene the western valley was occupied by an inland sea, the Tartessian Gulf. The Phoenicians established the first anchorages and dealt in precious metals. The Romans, who called the river the Baetis, settled at Hispalis, now Seville, in the 2nd century BCE and made it an important river port. By the 1st century BCE it was a walled city with shipyards building boats to carry wheat,. In Roman times the river was navigable as far inland as Córdoba. Under Arab rule between 712 and 1248 the Moors built a stone dock and the Torre del Oro to reinforce the port's defences.

In the 13th century Ferdinand III expanded the shipyards, and grain, oil, wine, wool and many other goods were exported throughout Europe from Seville. After the discovery of the Americas the city became the economic centre of the Spanish Empire, because its port, under the Casa de Contratación, held the monopoly of trans-oceanic trade. Navigation was already becoming harder, and by 1500 much heavy cargo was handled downstream at Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Seville finally lost its monopoly to Cádiz. In the 16th century silting, and weirs built to power water mills, halted barge traffic between Seville and Córdoba, which had given Córdoba cheap transport to the sea. The Corta de Merlina, a canal built in 1794, began the modernisation of the port of Seville.

The Guadalquivir is 657 km long and is the fifth-longest river in the Iberian Peninsula. It flows through Córdoba and Seville and reaches the Gulf of Cádiz at Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Seville is its main port, and a lock protects the port entrance from tides.
guadalupe-victoria: Guadalupe Victoria was born on 29 September 1786 at Tamazula, in the province of Nueva Vizcaya in New Spain, now the state of Durango. His parents died early in his childhood and he lived with his uncle, the parish priest. In 1807 he went to Mexico City, entered the College of San Ildefonso and graduated as a Bachelor of Laws on 24 April 1811.

In 1812 he joined the insurgents and fought beside José María Morelos at the siege of Cuautla. For his part in the assault on Oaxaca on 25 November 1812 he was given command of the insurgent army in Veracruz, and he took the name Guadalupe, for the Virgin of Guadalupe, and Victoria, for the victory. Using guerrilla tactics, he held the Puente del Rey, the crossing between Xalapa and the port of Veracruz, and attacked royalist convoys until 1815, when he was defeated.

He then spent almost four years hiding in the jungle, while most insurgents accepted a viceregal pardon and only Vicente Guerrero kept fighting. He reappeared on 30 December 1820 and joined the Plan of Iguala in 1821. When Agustín de Iturbide became emperor, Victoria wanted a republic and was jailed in 1822, but escaped. He joined Antonio López de Santa Anna's revolt in December 1822, and the Plan of Casa Mata forced Iturbide to abdicate on 19 March 1823. On 31 March Congress made Victoria, Nicolás Bravo and Pedro Celestino Negrete the Supreme Executive Power.

Seventeen states voted for Victoria in the presidential election of 1824, and on 2 October 1824 he was declared the first president of the United Mexican States. His constitutional term began on 1 April 1825. He had to rebuild an economy devastated by the war and the Spanish embargo. Spending averaged about 18 million pesos a year against half that in revenue, and two British loans, each of over 3 million pounds, averted bankruptcy.

He won recognition from the United Kingdom, the United States, the Federal Republic of Central America and Gran Colombia, and ratified the border with the United States under the Adams-Onís Treaty. In 1829 he handed the presidency to Vicente Guerrero, and he was the only president to complete his term in more than 30 years of independent Mexico. He later served as senator, governor of Puebla and president of the Senate, and died on 21 March 1843 at the fortress of Perote, where he was being treated for epilepsy.
guadiana: The Guadiana defines a long stretch of the border between Portugal and Spain, separating Extremadura and Andalusia from Alentejo and the Algarve. Its basin reaches from La Mancha and the eastern part of Extremadura to the southern provinces of the Algarve, and about 82 per cent of the basin lies in Spain and about 17 per cent in Portugal. The river runs east to west across the southern Iberian plain until near Badajoz, where it turns south, and it enters the Gulf of Cádiz between Vila Real de Santo António in Portugal and Ayamonte in Spain.

Its exact source in Castilla-La Mancha is disputed, but it is generally believed to rise at the Ojos del Guadiana, in Villarrubia de los Ojos, about 608 metres above sea level. Pliny the Elder introduced a classic theory that the river rose from the Lagunas de Ruidera and ran underground for part of its course. The belief that it disappeared and reappeared persisted until the 19th century, although no such underground course exists. The Cigüela and Záncara rivers are now regarded as part of its headwaters.

Ptolemy's Geography recorded the Celtiberian name as Anas, meaning a marshy area. The Romans adapted it as Flūmen Anās and explained it as the River of Ducks. After the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula the name became Wādī Āna, which Portuguese and Spanish settlers passed on as Ouadiana and then Odiana. From the 16th century it slowly took the form Guadiana, like other Andalusi river names beginning with wadi, such as Guadalquivir, Guadalete and Guadarrama.

The river marks the border twice on its way to the sea, between the Caia and the Ribeira de Cuncos and again from the Chança to the mouth. Between the Olivença and Táliga ravines the border is a disputed section, claimed by both countries and administered in practice by Spain as part of Extremadura.

The Guadiana is navigable from the Atlantic as far as Mértola, 68 kilometres inland, and above Mértola lies Pulo do Lobo, the highest waterfall in southern Portugal. Its flow varies greatly from year to year, with large floods and severe droughts, in a semi-arid climate. The estuary is a saltmarsh with a maximum width of 550 metres, and two nature reserves protect parts of it, the Marismas de Isla Cristina in Spain and the Castro Marim and Vila Real de Santo António marsh in Portugal. More than 30 dams stand in the basin. The Alqueva Dam, near Moura, creates a reservoir of 250 square kilometres, the largest in Western Europe.
guadix: Guadix lies at an altitude of 913 metres in the centre of the Hoya of Guadix, a high plain at the northern foothills of the Sierra Nevada, in a landscape of gullies and badlands formed by erosion from small rivers. The sediments of the rivers Fardes and Guadix have made the area fertile, and its land is used for fruit trees, especially peaches, for poplar groves and for cereals, legumes and vegetables.

Evidence of settlement around Guadix goes back to at least the Bronze Age. Guadix el Viejo, 6 kilometres to the north-west, was the Roman Acci, mentioned by Pliny and by Ptolemy, who placed it among the Bastetani. Excavations have documented an oppidum with a well-defined urban plan from the 6th century BCE. Julius Caesar established the Roman colony of Julia Gemella, which minted coins and left a Roman theatre and a network of sewers. According to tradition it was the seat of the first bishopric in Hispania, in the 2nd century, and the city was among the first on the Iberian Peninsula to adopt Catholicism.

After 711 it became a Moorish fortress and trading station, renamed Wadi 'Ashi. After the decline of the Caliphate it lay on the border between the territories of the Zirids of Granada and the Banu Jayrán of Almería, and it later passed through the Almoravid and Almohad empires into the Emirate of Granada. The poet Ḥamda bint Ziyād lived there. In January 1362 a small Castilian army was routed there by the forces of Muhammed VI, Sultan of Granada. Civil wars in the kingdom of Granada made Guadix the capital of a short-lived kingdom under Muhammad XII, and in 1489 it surrendered without a siege to Ferdinand and Isabella.

The main sights are the cathedral, built from the 16th to the 18th century over a Moorish mosque with a Baroque façade, the Church of Santiago of 1540 with a Plateresque portal, the Moorish Alcazaba and the Barrio de Santiago, whose houses are cut into the tuff rock. The novelist Pedro Antonio de Alarcón was born there in 1833. By the end of the 19th century Guadix was known for its cutlery.
guan-yu: Guan Yu came from Xie County in Hedong Commandery, in present-day Yuncheng, Shanxi. His original courtesy name was Changsheng. He fled his hometown for unknown reasons and went to Zhuo Commandery. When the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out in the 180s, he and Zhang Fei joined a volunteer militia formed by Liu Bei and helped a colonel, Zou Jing, to suppress the revolt. The main historical source for his life is Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, annotated in the fifth century by Pei Songzhi.

After Liu Bei seized Xu Province, he left Guan Yu in charge of the provincial capital Xiapi. In 200 Guan Yu served briefly under Cao Cao. At the Battle of Boma in 200 he recognised the parasol of Yuan Shao's general Yan Liang, charged, killed him and returned with his head; Emperor Xian made him Marquis of Hanshou Village. He told Zhang Liao that he had sworn to follow Liu Bei until death, and he rejoined Liu Bei at about the time of the Battle of Guandu.

From 212 to 214, while Liu Bei campaigned in Yi Province, Guan Yu guarded Jing Province. In 219 Liu Bei made him General of the Vanguard, and he besieged Cao Ren at Fancheng. Autumn floods on the Han River destroyed Yu Jin's seven armies; Yu Jin surrendered and Pang De refused and was executed. Cao Cao allied with Sun Quan, and Xu Huang broke the siege. Lü Meng's troops, hidden in disguised vessels, disabled Guan Yu's river watchtowers and took Jiangling.

Most of Guan Yu's soldiers deserted to rejoin their families. He withdrew to Maicheng and was captured in an ambush with his son Guan Ping, and both were executed at Linju. Sun Quan sent Guan Yu's head to Cao Cao, who buried it with a noble's honours. Chen Shou judged that Guan Yu was unrelenting and conceited, and that this contributed to his downfall.

He was deified as early as the Sui dynasty. Taoist worship began in the Song dynasty, and Chinese Buddhists revere him as Sangharama Bodhisattva, a protector of monasteries. As Emperor Guan or Lord Guan he has temples across China and elsewhere. The 14th-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which he is one of the most altered and aggrandised characters, shaped his popular image as a model of loyalty and martial courage.
guanabara-bay: Guanabara Bay is an oceanic bay in south-eastern Brazil, in the state of Rio de Janeiro. Rio de Janeiro and Duque de Caxias lie on its western shore, and Niterói and São Gonçalo on its eastern shore. It is the second largest bay in Brazil by area, after All Saints' Bay, covering 384 square kilometres with a perimeter of 143 kilometres. It is 31 kilometres long and 28 kilometres wide at most. Its mouth, 1.5 kilometres wide, is flanked by the Pico do Papagaio on the eastern tip and the Pão de Açúcar, or Sugar Loaf, on the western tip.

The name comes from the Tupi language, goanã-pará, from gwa, bay, nã, similar to, and ba'ra, sea. Other suggested meanings include hidden water, lagoon of the sea and bosom of the sea. More than 130 islands dot the bay.

Tamoio and Tupiniquim people lived on the shores of the bay when the Portuguese explorers Gaspar de Lemos and Gonçalo Coelho first reached it on 1 January 1502, and they named it Rio de Janeiro. It is widely believed that they mistook the bay for a river mouth, but they probably knew it was a bay and called it a river because the term was then applied to other bodies of water, such as bays and rias.

No significant European settlement followed until 1555, when French colonists and soldiers under the Huguenot admiral Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon invaded to found France Antarctique. They stayed briefly on Lajes Island and then moved to Serigipe Island, near the shore, where they built Fort Coligny. After Portuguese military expeditions expelled them, the colonial government built fortifications at several points on the bay, among them the forts of Santa Cruz, São João, Lajes and Villegaignon, which formed a crossfire of heavy naval guns and made the bay almost impregnable to attack from the sea. Other islands were later fitted by the Navy for storehouses, hospitals, drydocks, oil reservoirs and the National Naval Academy.

The Rio-Niterói Bridge, 13.29 kilometres long, crosses the bay, and ferries and ships use it heavily. The Port of Rio de Janeiro and the city's two airports, Galeão on Governador Island and Santos Dumont on reclaimed land, stand on its shores, and the main campus of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro is on the artificial Fundão Island. The Guapimirim Environmental Protection Area protects part of it, chiefly in the municipality of Guapimirim.

Urbanisation, deforestation and pollution have damaged its mangroves, and an oil leak from a Petrobras pipeline in 2000 released 1,300,000 litres into the bay. It was once a whaling ground, and a population of botos, river dolphins, still lives there.
guangdong: Guangdong faces the South China Sea on the south and has 4,300 km of coastline. The Leizhou Peninsula lies at its south-western end. The Pearl River Delta, where the East River, North River and West River converge, is filled with hundreds of small islands. A few mountain ranges collectively called the Nan Mountains separate the province from the north, and its highest peak is Shikengkong, at about 1,900 metres. The name means east of Guang: the Chinese character guang, meaning wide, has been linked with the region since Guang Prefecture was created in 226, and under the Song the Two Guangs were separated into Guangnan East and Guangnan West circuits.

The Neolithic began in the Pearl River Delta about 7,000 years ago, and in the north of the province the Shixia culture dates from about 4600 to 4200 years ago. The region was originally inhabited by a mixture of tribal groups known to the Chinese as the Baiyue, the Hundred Yue. It first became part of China under the Qin dynasty, which after unifying China expanded southwards and set up Nanhai Commandery at Panyu, near present Guangzhou. Chinese administration and reliable historical records began with the Qin. An independent kingdom, Nanyue, then controlled the region between the fall of Qin and the reign of Emperor Wu of Han.

The Han administered Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam as Jiaozhi Province, and its southern part was a gateway for traders from the west, as far away as the Roman Empire. Under the Wu Kingdom of the Three Kingdoms period, Guangdong was made its own province, Guang Province, in 226. After the Qin unified Lingnan, immigrants from the Central Plains moved in and formed a local culture of its own, whose languages, music, cuisine and opera spread across China and Southeast Asia.

In the early 1920s Guangdong was the staging area where the Kuomintang prepared the Northern Expedition against the warlords, and the Whampoa Military Academy near Guangzhou trained its commanders. Sun Yat-sen, born in the province, declared a military government there. At the end of the Chinese Civil War Guangzhou was briefly the Kuomintang's provisional capital before the People's Liberation Army took the province.

Guangdong is the most populous province of China, with a population of 126,012,510 in the 2020 census, and Guangzhou is its capital. Shenzhen, the first special economic zone, lies in the Pearl River Delta, and Hong Kong borders the province to the south. The Cantonese, Hakka and Teochew make up much of the Han population, and Guangdong is the traditional heartland of Yue Chinese. It is the ancestral home of many overseas Chinese, including most of the 19th-century railroad labourers in Canada, the western United States and Panama.
guangxi: Guangxi is in the far south of China, bordering Vietnam and the Gulf of Tonkin, with Yunnan to the west, Guizhou to the north, Hunan to the northeast and Guangdong to the east. Its mountainous terrain placed it on the frontier of Chinese civilisation for much of history. Karst landforms, with steep mountains and large caverns, cover 37.8 per cent of the land. The name Guang means expanse and has been associated with the region since the creation of Guang Prefecture in 226; the abbreviation Gui comes from Guilin, the provincial capital under the Ming and Qing.

The region was originally inhabited by tribal groups the Chinese called the Baiyue and first became part of China under the Qin. In 214 BCE the general Zhao Tuo claimed most of southern China for Qin Shi Huang, and after the emperor's death he set up the separate kingdom of Nanyue, which collapsed in 111 BCE when the Han expanded south. The Southern Han gained minimal control and was annexed by the Song in 971. The name Guangxi comes from the Song circuit Guangnanxi. The Zhuang leader Nong Zhigao led a revolt in 1052, but his kingdom was short-lived.

The Yuan established Guangxi as a proper province. The Zhuang Cen clan ruled parts of it under the Ming and Qing as recognised local rulers, and the Qing imposed direct rule in 1726. The 19th century was one of constant unrest, including the Jintian Uprising, the beginning of the Taiping Rebellion, in January 1851. The Guangxi Army repulsed the French at the Battle of Zhennan Pass on 23 March 1885. After the Wuchang Uprising Guangxi seceded from the Qing on 6 November 1911. It joined the People's Republic in December 1949. The Guangxi Massacre of 1967 and 1968 during the Cultural Revolution killed 100,000 to 150,000 people.

Guangxi became an autonomous region in 1958, and its capital is Nanning. It has the largest ethnic minority population in China, and a 2021 report put the Zhuang at 31.36 per cent. Languages spoken include Zhuang, Pinghua, Kam, Cantonese, Hakka and Min alongside Mandarin. Major cities are Nanning, Liuzhou, Guilin and Beihai.
guangxu-emperor: The Guangxu Emperor, personal name Zaitian, was born on 14 August 1871, the second son of Yixuan, Prince Chun, and of Yehenara Wanzhen, a younger sister of Empress Dowager Cixi. When the Tongzhi Emperor died without a son on 12 January 1875, the dowager empresses Ci'an and Cixi chose Zaitian, breaking the convention that a new emperor must belong to a generation after his predecessor. The sons of Prince Gong were passed over because they were distrusted as a bad influence on Tongzhi, while Zaitian was younger, Cixi's nephew, and the son of a prince known as a scholar and a supporter of patriotic policies.

The Sino-French War broke out in 1884 over influence in Vietnam. By 1885 the French had destroyed the Chinese fleet at Fuzhou, occupied part of Taiwan and ended Vietnam's status as a tributary of China. Even after Guangxu began to rule in his own right, the court still depended on Cixi, who decided appointments to the Grand Council and the Six Ministries. In 1894 the First Sino-Japanese War began over influence in Korea. Guangxu was associated with the pro-war faction, in contrast to Cixi and the Viceroy Li Hongzhang, who wanted a peaceful settlement.

In early June 1898 the grand councillor Weng Tonghe introduced Guangxu to the reformer Kang Youwei, and the emperor began issuing reform decrees on 11 June. The first edict called on all subjects to strengthen China through Western learning while respecting traditional morals, and Cixi approved it. The programme proved too radical for the conservative elite and did not win the army's support. Cixi rallied its opponents in a coup in late 1898, and Guangxu was confined on Yingtai Island at Zhongnanhai, never ruling alone again.

Guangxu died without children on 14 November 1908, aged 37, a day before Cixi. Her choice of heir, his nephew Puyi, succeeded him. In 2008 forensic tests found that the arsenic in his remains was 2,000 times the level in ordinary people. Most historians have inclined to think that Cixi poisoned him, though another theory names Yuan Shikai, and there are no reliable sources to show who did it. Imperial power in the Qing dynasty reached its lowest point under Guangxu, and he was the only Qing emperor put under house arrest during his own reign.
guangzhou: Guangzhou lies on the Pearl River in south-central Guangdong, about 120 km northwest of Hong Kong and 145 km north of Macau. The old town stood near Baiyun Mountain on the east bank, about 130 km from the river's junction with the South China Sea, and commanded the alluvial plain of the Pearl River Delta, with its link to the sea guarded at the Humen Strait. The city name comes from the ancient Guang Prefecture, whose seat it became.

Before the Han conquest the area was inhabited by non-Chinese tribes known collectively as the Baiyue. A settlement now called Nanwucheng was present by 1100 BCE, and some traditional Chinese histories place its founding in the reign of King Nan of Zhou. Under the name Panyu the city was founded on the east bank of the Pearl River in 214 BCE. Incorporated into the Han dynasty, Panyu became a provincial capital, and in 226 CE it became the seat of Guang Prefecture, which gave it its modern name. The Old Book of Tang describes it as an important port.

Relations with foreign traders were sometimes violent. Arab and Persian pirates sacked the city on 30 October 758, during the An Lushan Rebellion. In 878 the rebel Huang Chao killed about 200,000 foreigners there, along with the city's Jews, Christians and Parsis, and the port was closed for fifty years. For a long time Guangzhou was the only Chinese port accessible to Europeans. It was captured by the British in the First Opium War and lost its monopoly, though it remained a major entrepôt. In the late Qing period it was the site of the revolutionary uprisings of 1895 and 1911.

Guangzhou, also called Canton, is the capital and largest city of Guangdong and a major port and transport hub. The 2020 census recorded a registered population of 18,676,605. Cantonese culture, including Cantonese cuisine and Cantonese opera, is its main cultural heritage. The Canton Fair, formally the China Import and Export Fair, was inaugurated in the spring of 1957 and is held each April and October. Its metro, the fourth underground railway in mainland China, opened in 1997.
guantanamo-bay-naval-base: The base occupies 45 square miles (117 km2) of land and water on the shore of Guantánamo Bay, at the south-eastern end of Cuba. It is the oldest overseas American naval base. The bay divides the station into sections: Leeward Point holds the airfield, while Windward Point holds most of the base's activities. The highest point is John Paul Jones Hill, at 495 feet (151 m), and many coves and peninsulas along the shore provide anchorage for ships.

The area was first inhabited by the Taíno people. Christopher Columbus arrived on 30 April 1494, on his second voyage, spent the night and named the bay Puerto Grande. During the War of Jenkins' Ear a British expeditionary force held the bay briefly and renamed it Cumberland Bay, but withdrew after an attempt to march to Santiago de Cuba was repulsed by Spanish troops. In 1898, during the Spanish–American War, the American fleet attacking Santiago secured the harbour for protection during the hurricane season, and marines landed with naval support.

The war ended with the Treaty of Paris of 1898. In 1901 the Platt Amendment provided that Cuba would sell or lease to the United States lands for coaling or naval stations. After initial resistance by the Cuban Constitutional Convention it was incorporated into the Cuban constitution, which took effect in 1902, and land at Guantánamo Bay was granted the following year. The lease of 1903 has no fixed expiration date. It left ultimate sovereignty with Cuba while giving the United States sole jurisdiction during its occupation, at a rent of $2,000 a year in gold coin.

Since the Cuban Revolution the Cuban government has protested against the American presence, arguing that the base was imposed by force and is illegal under international law; only one rent payment has been accepted since 1959. In 1961 both sides completed minefields around the perimeter, some 55,000 mines in all, and at least ten people died in explosions between 1961 and 1965. President Bill Clinton ordered the American field cleared in 1996. In 1964 Cuba stopped the flow of water to the base, and the commander had the pipelines cut. Water was first imported from Jamaica by barge, and a desalination plant was then moved from San Diego.
guarani-language: Guarani, called avañe'ẽ in the language itself, belongs to the Tupi-Guarani branch of the Tupian family. It was written down only after the arrival of Jesuit missionaries, so its earlier stages can be reconstructed only by comparison with related languages. Written records begin with the Jesuits Antonio Ruiz de Montoya and Alonso de Aragona. Montoya's Tesoro de la Lengua Guaraní, a dictionary of 1639, gave examples of how words were used, and his grammar, the Arte de la lengua Guaraní of 1640, is regarded as the starting point for all later grammatical work. Aragona's teaching grammar was finished in 1629 but not printed until 1979.

Guarani is one of the two official languages of Paraguay, with Spanish, and is spoken by the majority of the population; half of the rural population speak only Guarani. It is one of the most widely spoken Native American languages, with more than four million speakers. In South America it is the indigenous language most widely spoken among non-indigenous people, and unlike most American languages it has resisted a shift to the colonial language. Variants are spoken in north-eastern Argentina, south-eastern Bolivia and south-western Brazil, and it is one of the three official languages of Mercosur.

The language is highly agglutinative, often described as polysynthetic. Its syllables are open, consisting of a consonant and a vowel or a vowel alone, and it shows an unusual degree of nasal harmony. Everyday speech in Paraguay is Jopará, a mixture of Spanish and Guarani, spoken by an estimated 90 per cent of the population, with more Spanish used in official and business matters and more Guarani in art and daily life.

Modern scholarship shows that Guarani was always the main language of colonial Paraguay, inside and outside the Jesuit reductions. The Jesuits avoided direct loans from Spanish and built new terms from Guarani parts, rendering communion as Tupârahava, from Tupâ, God, while speakers outside the missions simply took in Spanish words, so that communion became komuño. After the Jesuits were expelled in the 18th century, the residents of the reductions moved gradually towards Asunción, and the regulated Jesuit variety gave way to the spoken form that became Jopará.

Since independence Paraguayan governments have repressed Guarani for most of the time, and it was forbidden in state schools for over 100 years, though populists used pride in the language to appeal to nationalist feeling. The constitution of 1992, with the arrival of democracy, made it equal to Spanish. It is also an official language of Bolivia.
guarani-people: The Guaraní are a group of culturally related Indigenous peoples, distinguished from the related Tupi by their use of the Guaraní language. Their traditional range lies in what is now Paraguay between the Paraná River and the lower Paraguay River, the Misiones Province of Argentina, southern Brazil and parts of Uruguay and Bolivia. Before they met Europeans they called themselves Abá, meaning men or people. When Europeans first met them they are estimated to have numbered about 400,000. They were sedentary farmers living on manioc, maize, game and honey, in communal houses that each held several families under a chief.

In 1537 Gonzalo de Mendoza met the Guaraní and founded Asunción. The first governor encouraged intermarriage between European men and Indigenous women, but modern historians describe the process as one of sexual and economic coercion: the Guaraní custom of giving women to newcomers to cement alliances gave way after 1541 to violent mass seizures, and women were sold and exported as slaves to Portuguese settlements on the coast.

In the early 17th century Jesuit missionaries, backed by the Spanish crown after protesting against the enslavement of Indigenous people, gathered Guaraní into mission towns. The first Guayrá mission, Loreto, was founded in 1610. Slave raiders from São Paulo attacked them, and within two years of 1629 about 60,000 converts had been carried off to be sold. In 1732 there were 30 missions with 141,252 Guaraní, defended by an army of 7,000. The Treaty of Madrid of 1750 transferred seven Uruguay missions to Portugal, and the Guaraní, who were absent from the negotiations, resisted in a war from 1754 to 1756. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767 the missions declined, and the census of 1801 counted fewer than 45,000 Guaraní.

The Guaraní number around 280,000 and live mainly in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay. Guaraní is one of the two official languages of Paraguay, with Spanish, and is learned there at school and in daily life. It is also an official language of Bolivia. In Paraguay Guaraní lineage predominates in the population, and in modern Spanish Guaraní can also mean any Paraguayan national. The Bolivian Guaraní, once called Chiriguanos, are represented by the Assembly of the Guarani People.
guarino-guarini: Camillo Guarino Guarini was born in Modena on 17 January 1624 into a deeply religious family; he and his four brothers all joined the Theatine Order. At fifteen he became a novice and was sent to the monastery of San Silvestro al Quirinale in Rome, where he stayed from 1639 to 1648 and studied the work of Francesco Borromini, Gian Lorenzo Bernini and Pietro da Cortona.

From Borromini he learned to use complex geometry as the basis of floor plans. He also trained in theology, philosophy and mathematics. Back in Modena as an ordained priest in 1648, he became a lecturer in philosophy at the Theatine College two years later, and in 1649 he began his career as an architect for the Order with the rebuilding of San Vincenzo.

In 1655 Guarini was elected provost of the Theatine house in Modena against the wishes of Alfonso IV d'Este, who banished him from the city. He reached Messina in 1660, where he built the façade of Santa Maria Annunziata, and in 1665 he published in Paris a large mathematical and philosophical treatise, the Placita Philosophica. When he arrived in Turin towards the end of 1666 he submitted a new design for San Lorenzo, and work on it began in 1668. The church has a centralized nave and a dome of criss-crossing hyperbolic ribs, with windows of different shapes breaking up the surfaces between them.

In 1679 Guarini was commissioned by Prince Emmanuel Philibert of Carignano to build the Palazzo Carignano outside the medieval walls of Turin. It was completed in 1683 as a three-winged building, not the four wings first planned. Its brick façade is formed of two S-curves around a tall oval pavilion, an innovation in Italian Baroque palace design. He also built the Chapel of the Holy Shroud (1668-94), the Castle of Racconigi and the Colegio dei Nobili. He wrote on mathematics, astronomy, fortification and architecture, roughly a book every other year.

Guarini died on 6 March 1683. In 1686 the Theatines published 33 engraved plates of his designs, and in the 1730s, with the help of the architect Bernardo Antonio Vittone, his treatise Architettura civile appeared in 1737. In it he wrote that vaults are the main thing in architecture and that architecture aims at the gratification of the senses.

His diaphanous domes found no imitators among his contemporaries in Italy outside Piedmont, and in the later 18th century Neoclassicism led to attacks such as Francesco Milizia's. His book was widely read in Austria and Germany and influenced Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach, Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt and Balthasar Neumann.
guatemala: Guatemala is mountainous. Two mountain chains enter it from west to east and divide it into three regions: the highlands, the Pacific coast to the south and the Petén region, a sparsely populated northern lowland. All major cities lie in the highlands and on the Pacific coast. The highlands lie along the Motagua Fault, which produced a 7.5 magnitude earthquake on 4 February 1976 that killed more than 25,000 people. Two of the three moves of the capital were caused by volcanic mudflows in 1541 and earthquakes in 1773.

The first evidence of human habitation dates to 12,000 BCE, and maize cultivation had been developed by 3500 BCE. Archaeologists divide the pre-Columbian past into the Preclassic period (2000 BCE to 250 CE), the Classic (250 to 900) and the Postclassic (900 to 1500). The Classic period matches the height of Maya civilisation, with the largest concentration of sites in Petén. That civilisation collapsed around 900 and many cities of the central lowlands were abandoned; the cause is debated, though the drought theory is gaining currency. In the Postclassic, regional kingdoms such as the Itza and Kowoj in Petén and the K'iche', Kaqchikel and Mam peoples in the highlands preserved many aspects of Maya culture.

Most of the territory was conquered by the Spanish in the 16th century and claimed as part of the viceroyalty of New Spain. Guatemala became independent from Spain and Mexico in 1821 and was part of the Federal Republic of Central America from 1823 to 1841. Jorge Ubico was overthrown in 1944, beginning a decade of reform that ended with a military coup in 1954. A civil war ran from 1960 to 1996 and included genocidal massacres of the Maya population by the military; 83 percent of the victims of the 626 massacres reported in the 1980s were Maya. A peace accord negotiated by the United Nations ended it.

Guatemala is a constitutional democratic republic with its capital and largest city at Guatemala City. The sole official language is Spanish, and twenty-one Mayan languages, Xinca and Garifuna are recognised as national languages. Indigenous Guatemalans, mostly Maya, are 43.6% of the population according to the 2018 census. The country is divided into 22 departments.
guatemala-city: Guatemala City lies in a mountain valley called the Valle de la Ermita, in the south-central part of Guatemala. Four stratovolcanoes are visible from the city, two of them active, and the nearest and most active, Pacaya, at times sends up a considerable amount of ash. The Guatemalan highlands lie on the Ring of Fire and are frequently shaken by earthquakes; the last large one to strike the region came in 1976, on the Motagua Fault.

Human settlement on the site began with the Maya, who built a large ceremonial centre at Kaminaljuyu. It was the biggest Maya settlement outside the lowlands of the Yucatán Peninsula and rose to prominence about 300 BCE through the mining and trade of obsidian, a volcanic glass valued across Mesoamerica. The centre is now a park within the city.

The old colonial capital, now Antigua Guatemala, was left in ruins by the earthquakes of 1773, the third to strike it after those of 1717 and 1751, and the Spanish decided to move to a safer place. In 1776 the capital was moved to the valley where Guatemala City stands. The Metropolitan Cathedral on the central plaza was built mostly between 1782 and 1815 and completed in 1871. The Act of Independence of Central America, declared in the city in September 1821, ended Spanish rule, and for several decades the city was the capital of the federation of the United Provinces of Central America. In August 1847 Guatemala declared itself an independent republic and Guatemala City became its national capital.

The earthquakes of 1917 and 1918 almost completely destroyed the city, and its reconstruction brought wider streets and grid layouts. Under President Jorge Ubico, who held power for 13 years, the National Palace was built between 1939 and 1943. He was overthrown in the Guatemalan Revolution of 1944.

Guatemala City is the national capital and largest city of Guatemala, and its metropolitan area is the largest in Central America. Its formal name is Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción, in honour of the Virgin of the Assumption, whose feast on 15 August is the city's feast day. The University of San Carlos of Guatemala, founded in 1676, is the oldest institution of higher education in Central America.
guayaquil: Guayaquil stands on the west bank of the Guayas River, about 60 km north of the Gulf of Guayaquil and near the Equator. The climate is tropical savanna: hot, humid and rainy from January to April, and dry from May to December because of the cooling Humboldt Current. The city lies on soft sediments and on the ring of fire, so it faces a serious earthquake threat.

After several failed attempts and fires, the Spanish settled the city as a port and shipyard. The name is older than the Spanish. A local tradition derives it from a leader called Guayas and his wife Quil, while historians point to a chief named Guayaquile, whose lands were held by the chonos of the Milagro-Quevedo culture. In colonial times it was the chief Spanish shipyard in the Pacific and a stopover for the Manila galleons. Most of the region's enslaved people lived there in the late eighteenth century, and María Chiquinquirá won her freedom in court in 1794. English and French pirates looted it on 20 April 1687, and Woodes Rogers and William Dampier did so in 1709.

On 9 October 1820 civilians and soldiers under the Peruvian Colonel Gregorio Escobedo arrested the Spanish authorities almost without bloodshed and declared the Free Province of Guayaquil, with José Joaquín de Olmedo as civil chief. Antonio José de Sucre sailed from the city to lead the army that won the Battle of Pichincha. On 26 July 1822 José de San Martín and Simón Bolívar met there. Peruvian troops occupied it for seven months in 1829. A fire destroyed large parts of it in 1896, and a three-day general strike in 1922 ended after at least 300 people were killed by the military and police.

Guayaquil is the capital of Guayas Province and the largest city of Ecuador, with more than 3,000,000 inhabitants. Its port handles most of the country's international trade. The oldest part of the city, with the cathedral, the Malecón along the river and the Las Peñas neighbourhood, draws visitors. The University of Guayaquil was founded in 1867.
guayas-province: Guayas lies on the Pacific coast of Ecuador, bordered by Manabí, Santa Elena and the Gulf of Guayaquil to the west, Los Ríos and Bolívar to the north, Chimborazo, Cañar and Azuay to the east, and El Oro to the south. Its capital, Guayaquil, is the largest city and main port of Ecuador. The province has no elevations except the Coastal Range, which runs from Guayaquil to Manabí. The land west of the range is desert, with an average temperature of 23 °C, while the land east of it belongs to the Guayas watershed and is humid and fertile.
The Daule River flows from the north to join the Babahoyo River and form the Guayas river. The province is part of the largest river basin in South America west of the Andes.

The native culture living in the province before the European arrival was the Huancavilca, and their descendants make up a large part of the population. Guayaquil was founded on 14 August 1534, although its foundation is marked on 25 July, and during the Spanish conquest it became one of the most important ports in South America. The city became free on 9 October 1820, and the Guayaquil Department, one of the original subdivisions of Ecuador, was founded soon afterwards. It consisted of Manabí Province and Guayaquil Province, which was later renamed Guayas.
The Guayaquil Province included the area of what is now Peruvian Tumbes and today's Los Ríos and El Oro. The provinces were separated from Guayas in 1860 and 1884, respectively.

Guayas is the most populous province in Ecuador, with a census population of 4,391,923 in 2022, and the seventh largest by area. It has grown rapidly, from 612,417 in 1950 to over 1.4 million by 1970, as people moved from rural areas to Guayaquil. The 2010 census recorded 67.5% of residents as mestizo, 11.3% as Montubio, 9.8% as white, 9.7% as Afro-Ecuadorian and 1.3% as indigenous, and there are also communities descended from Italians, Lebanese and German people. The province is divided into 25 cantons.
gubbio: Gubbio lies in an upland valley of the Apennines, on the lowest slope of Monte Ingino, in the north-east of Umbria. The area is a transitional one, close to Marche on the east and Tuscany on the west, and Gubbio has historically had strong political and cultural ties to both. The valley floor is a basin that was once a lake. The surrounding land is fertile and is especially productive for olives.

The oldest evidence of human habitation in the valley dates to the Middle Palaeolithic, and relatively permanent settlements appear in the Neolithic, between 6000 and 3000 BCE. By the Archaic period settlement had moved to the lower slopes of Monte Asciano, and Monte Ascoli served as a religious sanctuary, where dozens of bronze figurines dated between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE have been found.

Coins struck in the Umbrian period carry the forms Ikvvini and Ikvvins, which show that the Umbrian and Roman towns were the same community. Iguvium obtained Roman citizenship before the Social War, and its inhabitants were enrolled in the Clustumina tribe. Roman accounts say the Iguvini were entrusted with the custody of the captured King Gentius.

In the early Middle Ages the city came under the Heruli and then the Ostrogoths. A general of Totila captured and destroyed it, and it was rebuilt with help from Narses. In the 11th century it became a free municipality with civic institutions, though conflicts with feudal lords and bishops continued. In 1516 Pope Leo X appointed Lorenzo de' Medici as duke and forced Francesco Maria I into exile, but Francesco Maria recovered the duchy on Leo's death. Gubbio joined the Kingdom of Italy on 14 September 1860.

Gubbio is a municipality in the province of Perugia with a population of about 30,000. The Palazzo dei Consoli, built between 1332 and 1349 to a design by Angelo da Orvieto, and the Palazzo dei Priori stand opposite one another and show the medieval commune's civic life. The Roman theatre, completed around 20 BCE, held about 6,000 spectators. Every year on 15 May the Festa dei Ceri takes place on the eve of the feast of the patron, Saint Ubald, who died in 1160. Three wooden structures called Ceri are carried through the town to the Basilica of Sant'Ubaldo on Monte Ingino.
guben: Guben lies in the south-east of the state of Brandenburg, in the district of Spree-Neiße. The town sits on the banks of the Lusatian Neisse between two plateaus, a position that favoured its early economic development. The plateaus are ground moraines left by the Weichselian glaciation, and the surrounding land is covered with pine forests and lakes. Its coat of arms shows a red wall with three gates and three towers, with small shields for the Kings of Prussia, the Kings of Bohemia and the Electors of Saxony, its historic rulers.

A trade settlement existed here from the 11th century, and in the early 11th century it belonged to the early Polish state under Bolesław I the Brave before falling to the March of Lusatia. A document of Duke Henry the Bearded mentions it as Gubin in 1211. On 1 June 1235 Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, granted the settlement on the eastern bank Magdeburg rights and declared it a town, while a Benedictine nunnery developed on the western bank as a suburb. King John of Bohemia besieged the town unsuccessfully in 1319.
